The Festive Academy of „Gordonia“ in Będzin
[Będzin — youth movements; „Gordonia“.]
On Monday the great festive academy (commemorative assembly) of „Gordonia“ took place, in connection with the 10 years of existence of the „Gordonia“ movement and the 12th yahrzeit of A. D. Gordon.
In a packed hall of the „Nowości“ cinema Mr. Yehuda Anzlowicz[?] opens the academy by honouring, through rising, the deceased leader of the Eretz-Israel workers, Aharon David Gordon, and gives a survey of the development of the „Gordonia“ movement in the course of its 10 years of existence.
After that the floor is given to the „Gordonia“ member Yona Goldberg, who lectures on „10 years of existence of „Gordonia“.
Then Dr. Arie Tartakower delivers a successful lecture on the role of Gordon's work for the Jewish people and especially for the Jewish working class.
The second, artistic part made, with its rich content, a colossally good impression. Especially distinguished were the staging „Oygn[?] geyen heym avek“ [„Eyes(?) go off home“], performed by Riva Warszawska, the recitation „Di brik“ [„The Bridge“], performed by Blima Weisbart, and the choir conducted by Mordechai Krzesiwo. The stage sets were executed by Ch. Glecer and S. Klajman.

[Będzin area — accident.]
Yesterday morning in the village of Łagisza, near Będzin, a collision occurred between a lorry and a cart on which several Christians from Wojkowice were sitting.

[Taxes — new ordinance.]
In the „Dziennik Ustaw“ [Journal of Laws] no. 10 of 1[?] February an ordinance of the Ministry of Finance has been published, by which the ordinance of the year 1932 is amended — the one providing that from the time the taxpayer receives the „upomnienie“ [reminder] until the time of the „zajęcie“ [seizure] at least 14 days must pass; according to the present ordinance it will be possible to carry out a „zajęcie“ already 9 days after the taxpayer has received the demand to pay the tax.

The general strike in Paris passed off quietly; in the provinces, by contrast, the strike bore a stormy character.
—o—

—o—

—o—

A harsh decree for the small traders.
It is already quite some time since the municipality rebuilt the area at "Zavade" [probably Zawodzie] behind the town, in order to move the market traders from the New and the Old Market to that site, which is very inconvenient for the Jewish traders, because in the first place it is by no means a safe place and it is simply a danger to go there, and in particular trade will be greatly weakened.
Lately, however, the authorities have set about carrying out the plan, and the decree is to be implemented in the very near future.
In connection with this, meetings of the small traders have been taking place lately; they are seeking various means to soften this decree, which is catastrophic for the small-trading class, which consists exclusively of Jews.
Perhaps these interventions would have yielded some results, but the calamity is that Częstochowa has 2 small traders' unions. Taking advantage of the occasion that the handful of Jews are to be driven from the municipal markets, the two small traders' unions have set about fighting each other, in the form that each wants to outdo the other with positive deeds, and all this meanwhile goes on at the expense of the poor small traders...
—o—
Antisemitic attacks on Jews again.
About 2 weeks ago a member of the Endecja [National Democrats] was punished with a year and a half in prison for assaults and for wanting to kill a Jewish editor.
It appears that the Endek youth of Częstochowa were little frightened by the verdict and are renewing their antisemitic deeds.
Last week the pupils of the Christian artisans' evening courses spread out through the town and beat the Jewish passers-by. Larger groups formed along the avenues, smashing several shop windows of Jewish stores, and they went about their work undisturbed as far as the New Market, where they beat Mr. Yaakov Frein[?] murderously.
The kehilla has sent 2 memoranda, to the police inspector and to the town commissioner.

A victim of the strong wind.
The terrible gale did not spare Częstochowa either and caused considerable damage.
On the Lubliniec–Częstochowa highway the owner of the vinegar factory, Mr. Moshe Frankenberg, was travelling with his carter Kryszynski[?].
At a certain moment the flat wagon ["platforme"] overturned, crushing both passengers. The carter was killed on the spot, while the factory owner was noticed by peasants passing by, who took him in a gravely injured condition to the municipal hospital.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Changes in Katowice Kehilla Life

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, kehilla.] The rabbinate's income reduced. — For the first time a fee is fixed for the slaughter of poultry.
Under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Meyer [מייער], a meeting of the Katowice kehilla council took place, which dealt with the new kehilla budget.
After a lengthy discussion the budget was adopted according to the board's draft, but with the exception of several items, which were altered by the kehilla council.
The changes introduce new chapters into the life of the Katowice kehilla. As is known, the slaughter of poultry was free of charge for the Jewish population of Katowice. But because of the financial crisis, which also affects the income of the community (gmina), it was decided to take a fee for the slaughter of poultry.
The fee is: 50 groszy for a turkey, 30 groszy for a goose or a duck, 20 groszy for a hen and 10 groszy for a chicken (kurczak) or a pigeon.
The hitherto existing system of schooling has also been abolished. Tuition will be charged for every child who studies in the community schools. The scale of the fee is as follows: those who pay a kehilla tax („etat“) of 30 to 60 zł. will pay tuition of 2 zł. per child; from 60 to 150 — 3 zł.; from 150 to 250 — 4 zł.; from 250 to 500 — 6 zł. Whoever has 3 children in the school will pay for only 2.
The Orthodox faction put forward a proposal that with the income from the shechita and from the schools a town[?] building should be built, in which there would be a Talmud Torah, a mikveh and the like.
The proposal was rejected.
The kehilla council struck out the sum of 4 thousand zł. which the rabbinate received for teaching religion in the community schools, and also abolished the income which the rabbinate had from weddings and funerals.

In the night from Saturday to Sunday thieves got into the jeweller's shop of Mr. Garncarczyk [גארנטשארטשיק]. The latter heard it, went out into the street and called the police. Moshe Feinkind

[Literature — jubilee.] (On his 50-year literary jubilee.)
Quietly and modestly, without noise and tumult, the 50-year literary jubilee of the well-known writer and national communal worker, R. Moshe Feinkind, was celebrated last Sunday in Piotrków.
At the age of 17 Moshe Feinkind specialised in Jewish studies (Chochmat Yisrael) under Dr. Cassel, Lazarus, Dr. Hildesheimer and others, and translated into Hebrew poems by the German classics.
Moshe Feinkind begins his activity as a writer in the year 1884, in "HaNitzanim", in "HaTzefirah", and later, in the Jewish and Jewish-Polish press of Warsaw, Łódź and Lemberg, Moshe Feinkind occupies an honourable place and becomes popular through his dozens of publicistic and historical articles.
Among the readers of the Warsaw Jewish press in general, and of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" in particular, the esteemed jubilarian is likewise well liked for his frequent articles on historical dates, especially for his articles on the history of the Będzin kehilla.
At the age of 68 our esteemed contributor R. Moshe Feinkind celebrates his 50-year literary jubilee. He has honestly earned it; it is a jubilee of serious work, of tireless creation not only in the literary field — he also has great merits as an ardent, devoted national Jew, and we wish the old-young jubilarian long life, to go on freely spinning the thread of his literary activity.

The budget of the Będzin kehilla

And so we have had the opportunity to look on and observe how the Będzin Jewish kehilla administration adopted the budget for the current year, and we must admit that this kind of tactics. The whole proceeding is a riddle to us. We cannot understand how people can calmly sit down and make such budgets as our kehilla representatives have now made.
It seems that the institution is a completely dead one, backward[?] in every respect of any activity whatsoever, so that it occupies no place at all in public life — and yet its representatives have the nerve to make budgets that make one's eyes go dark. What do the public, the broad Jewish street, the institutions, the suffering population get from the Jewish kehilla as such? Nothing, it seems. Which philanthropic, cultural or educational establishments does it maintain? It seems that it has none such on its account, and yet it allows itself to hand out subsidies right and left. And the subsidies — woe and alas to them. They make a kind of "chaluka", handing out "Sabbath fruit" [shabes-oyps, i.e. little treats] of a couple of hundred zł. each. And with this they want to show that everywhere they lend a hand and everywhere they have a say. As soon as there is some little society that exists from today until tomorrow and is no more than a toy, they toss it at least a hundred-złoty note, just so that they can prove that subventions are being given for cultural and social welfare ["shuts"]. And this "welfare" amounts to no more and no less than 62 thousand zł. It goes without saying that we would not be against these subsidies if the town had the proper benefit from them. On the other hand, the tactic of handing out "Sabbath fruit" for the sake of demonstration, for the sake of amusement, must be rejected [the text says "ignored"]. And to distribute sixty-two thousand zł. just like that, for form's sake, is in today's critical time certainly a crime. Nor should one forget that the budget comes out raised by 50 per cent over last year's. And the question arises: has the Jewish situation improved in the course of the last year, so that the increase is justified? Has the kehilla administration already collected the whole etat [communal assessment] of the past year and distributed to the institutions their subsidies, so that it can go on and permit itself to raise the present budget? We, however, know the opposite: it has neither paid out the subsidies, nor is it able to collect the greater part of the etat. It is, after all, no secret to anyone that there is no money even to pay the office staff.
It goes without saying that we are certain the authorities will not approve the greater part of the subsidies; there are no two opinions about that. So the question arises: what is this needed for? Why should we have the slap in the face — for in the end it is vexing when the authorities meddle in our internal affairs and strike out what we find necessary, right and expedient.
But what kind of face do our representatives have in the eyes of the authorities when they see that, despite the fact that the financial state of the kehilla is so lamentable, no heed is nevertheless paid to all that, and one can even allow oneself to raise the budget considerably. They must then surely come to the conviction that Jews can give, only they do not want to — for the best proof is that their own representatives approve a raising of the budget.
We have already pointed out above that we could still have understood an increase if the population were to get something out of it, if the kehilla were to create something useful, urgently needed, something that would ease and beautify Jewish life. But what turns out? Of creating anything new there is no talk at all, and even what has been established since times of old is not looked after either, but on the contrary — neglected and held cheap.
What institutions and properties does this kehilla representation of ours have that are to be looked after and kept up as is proper? Yes, the only thing it had in its possession was the mikveh, which could not be managed by it and which it had to lease out, until it turned into a ruin, despite the fact that it has already cost the town no end of money.
True, we know that the presently existing representation is not to blame for all this — it could, with the best will, accomplish nothing; but precisely for that reason: when one takes over an abnormal economy, one must first of all bring it to some sort of order, everything must be put on a sound footing, and only then can one permit oneself to introduce improvements — which, by the way, they have so far not had in mind. On the other hand, one surely cannot make the economy healthy by raising the budget and earmarking the greater part of it for distributing subventions, which, by the way, will not be paid either, and even if they are, none of the recipients will be helped by them at all.
Yes, subsidies, donations can be handed out when one is rich, when one has the possibility of making it real; but one can never permit oneself luxuries when they cannot be realised.
We know from practice that if a firm has a deficit one year and the second year has not picked up either, it must reduce the budget of the current year, so that it should not begin to sink deeper and so that things should not be brought to a catastrophic state.
Our kehilla representatives apparently hold to the principle that "there is no such thing as a poor community", and they take no account of the situation prevailing in the kehilla. We had supposed that they would first of all pay off the debts, reduce the expenses, collect the etat tax more intensively wherever that is possible, and only then, once they had got onto the straight line, would the Jewish[?] situation be reckoned with and the budget be made with the greatest caution and calculation.
Meanwhile we see quite the reverse phenomenon: nothing is being improved, there is no new initiative, and instead they set about an enormous raising of the budget, into which subsidies are put to be handed out like "Sabbath fruit" — which must not be allowed to happen.
Surely no one will doubt that the authors of the budget would also know how to act that way if it were a matter of their private businesses. No one, after all, wants in his own affairs to crawl ever deeper into the mud, if only he has a way out. So why do our kehilla representatives do it?
By no manner of means may the budget be raised, and money must not be handed out like some kind of "chaluka". Above all when it serves no purpose. The town is being fleeced and the institution gets nothing out of the hundred-złoty note. It is unheard-of to act like this. In the present hard time one must not hold cheap Jewish money, which is as hard to earn as in the worst of times.
Is it really necessary to start agitating among our kehilla representatives that at the present moment it is a crime to take by compulsion monies that bring no great benefit? Do these representatives really not know how hard life is for the Jewish masses and how hard it is for them to pay a tax?! And since they know it, since they see it — what is the point of this light-mindedness, what is the point of sucking out of people monies that they cannot give and that, by the way, bring the community no great benefit.
We, on the other hand, understand things quite differently; we understand that the communal institutions ought to be supported — and not only supported but indeed wholly maintained — provided they bring one-hundred-per-cent benefit; if that is not so, it is a pity to support such ones.
The gmina [kehilla] does not support these institutions with such subsidies that they could maintain themselves, and it does not supervise them so as to know how far the institution is needed by the public and how far order reaches there; so what is the raising of the budget needed for? Perhaps only in order to make the Jewish situation, heavy enough as it is, still heavier?
The kehilla representatives want to have modernised budgets, enlarged as far as it will possibly go, whereas the institution itself they want to go on running in the old-fashioned way. Why do the representatives not enter into the situation of its members, who in fact get nothing from the kehilla, and as soon as a member needs something he has to pay separately for every trifle — so what are the enlarged budgets needed for? What benefit do they bring the community?
It is interesting and characteristic: this year the kehilla undertook to carry out the coal campaign; firstly, it has not yet finished it, and despite the fact that winter is already nearly over, it is only now getting ready to draw up a "black list" of those who will not bring their coal donations into the kehilla treasury; and secondly, it gives itself no account whatever that the citizens perhaps have more right to demand of the kehilla that it give coal to the needy out of its own treasury, into which the community's monies are paid — and not the other way round.
And one more thing: begging [shnorerai] has taken on unbearable forms among us; the citizens are fleeced and one is never done paying; at the same time all sorts of machinations and thefts occur, which lead to unheard-of deeds. Incidents often take place in open shops at which we turn red with shame when non-Jews look on at these unheard-of impudences.
We have dealt with the question more than once in the columns of our newspaper; we have thrown precise light on it and pointed to the unheard-of humiliations that this element causes us Jews, and we pointed out then that the only institution that ought to occupy itself with the matter is the Jewish kehilla representation. But with it, apparently, this has gone "into the left sidelock" [i.e. it could not care less]; that they have no time for it, that they have more fitting[?] business, that they must busy themselves with working out big budgets — that goes without saying.
It is, upon my life, high time to put an end to this spectacle, which merely looks like some toy with which one amuses oneself in a time of leisure, and afterwards it lies as a burden on the whole Jewish population.
R. Let.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (7)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; serial, instalment 7 (conclusion).] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
With a "bombshell" the gubernia [provincial government] was surprised at about ten o'clock in the morning, on the day of the elections, in the very heat of the election campaign.
"Chevre-layt" [the fellows of the gang] telegraphed to the governor that great falsifications were taking place at the elections on the part of Graubart's party, begging him for mercy's sake to invalidate the elections without even waiting for the result of the elections.
But the main attack was made only after the elections.
No fewer than two complaints against the elections were lodged, by two different kinds of groups, asking the governor to annul them because they had been conducted unlawfully, and so on [?].
In one complaint it is further mentioned that the deceased rabbi, although he was a great and capable man, nevertheless accomplished nothing for the good of the kehilla, because he was sickly, on account of which everything was neglected; and to introduce order there is only one single capable man, and that is Rabbi R' Dovid Bornstein [Bornsztajn].
Będzin, as a large town — it is underlined — must have an authority as its spiritual leader, and not an underage young man who can have no influence whatsoever among Jews...
Various abuses that occurred at the elections are also cited, namely: in the writing-out of the ballot slips for those who cannot write; that Rabbi Graubart promised the voters to pay the "etat" [community tax] for them and then to free them of it altogether, if they would vote for him; that in the polling office and in the taverns next to the polling office there was canvassing for Rabbi Graubart; that etat-payers were struck off the list; that the election committee consisted in its majority of members from Rabbi Graubart's side, and so on [?].
For all these facts the complainants invoked dozens of witnesses, who were supposed to confirm the gossip and the informing.
The gubernia sent the complaint on to the nachalnik [district chief] to conduct an investigation into all of this.
From the report which the nachalnik sent back to the governor in response it can be seen that all the accusations made against the elections by the opponents are unfounded; he defends the legality of the elections with great knowledge of the matter. He declares himself in favour of the candidacy that the Jewish intelligentsia wanted, and so on [?].
The Będzin burmistrz [mayor] Ris [?] too, who was the chairman of the election committee and was personally present at the elections, declares himself on the legality of the elections and in favour of the candidacy of Rabbi Graubart.
It must also be underlined here that even the opposing side did not find fault with the personality of Rabbi Graubart, but only maintained that he was too young to be a leader of the great kehilla of Będzin, which is a centre of trade and industry.
In the midst of this a third party also latched on, writing to the governor that, since Passover is approaching, they ask, for the sake of peace, that the governor put an end to the quarrels that are taking place in the town because of the rabbinate question, and that he immediately confirm one of the two candidates as rabbi in Będzin...
In the gubernia they were in no hurry at all with the Będzin rabbinate question.
It was found out that Rabbi Graubart had indeed been under age when he passed the examination as a rabbi in Płock, where the local rabbi, R' Yona Mordechai Zlotnik [Złotnik], had also issued him the "heter hora'ah" [rabbinical ordination]. An inquiry about this was made to the governor of Płock, and the latter answered that he had indeed made a mistake. On the grounds that Rabbi Graubart had been under age at the time of the examination, the governor of Piotrków, on 21 February 1914, annulled the elections on formal grounds, fixing new elections for 20 [?] June 1914;
meanwhile the rabbi of Modrzejów [printed „מאנדזשעוו״], R' Shaye Englard, bestirs himself and writes a petition all the way to the Emperor himself in Petersburg: whereas his little town of Modrzejów went up entirely in smoke five months ago and the Jews keep leaving the town, he has been left with nothing but a rabbinical seat, without Jews and without a livelihood; but in neighbouring Będzin there is a vacancy for a rabbi — so let the Emperor have mercy on him and install him in Będzin as rabbi...
This characteristic petition was sent by the proper authorities to Piotrków to be dealt with.
So Jaczewski [Yachevsky], „דער פיקוח״ [?; perhaps "the shrewd one"], had the poor rabbi of Modrzejów informed, through the Będzin nachalnik, that he may put forward his candidacy at the coming elections.
Rabbi Englard, poor man, was disappointed in his hope — having reckoned that if he wrote to the Russian Tsar, the latter would at once, by virtue of his patriotism, seat him upon the rabbinical chair of Będzin..
What happened further in Będzin the yellowed sheets of the Piotrków archive no longer tell.
(The End.)
On the "Hachshara" Question

[Zionism — the hachshara question; polemical article.] In the turmoil of the struggle which the spokesmen of the various Zionist ideologies have lately been waging among themselves, people have forgotten to give its due place to a question that today plays an enormous role in Zionist life, namely the hachshara question.
There is no doubt whatsoever that years ago, when the halutz (pioneer) movement began, halutzism had to be set up in such a way that every young Zionist who wanted to make aliyah to Eretz Yisrael had to go through a certain spiritual and physical preparation for the new life in Eretz Yisrael. This had to be so, in the first place, because years ago the youth did not go to Eretz Yisrael for material reasons, but chiefly driven by the Zionist ideal, in order to take part personally in the realisation of the idea of the Jewish renaissance. That youth was recruited years ago mostly from the Jewish middle-class (ba'al-habatish) circles, in which the children were not accustomed to physical labour and to the discomforts connected with it.
In order to avoid disappointments among the youth making aliyah to Eretz Yisrael, hachshara was introduced, that is, physical preparation, which was meant to protect the youth from disappointment and at the same time to guarantee the Zionist movement the selection of elements suited to Eretz Yisrael.
We are most deeply convinced that this very "hachshara" has in the course of time lost its right to exist, because there now stream to Eretz Yisrael not merely the children of middle-class parents, but children of all the strata and classes that are represented in the Jewish people.
Today there can be no talk at all of disappointment among the youth making aliyah to Eretz Yisrael, because it, the youth, in now going to Eretz Yisrael, burns all its bridges behind it and gives itself an account of the fact that the economic situation of the Jews in the lands of the Diaspora is becoming worse and worse from day to day.
How can one now speak of a possible disappointment among the youth making aliyah to Eretz Yisrael, when it knows positively that in the Diaspora it is condemned to hunger and want, when it feels at every step that in the Diaspora it is absolutely superfluous and without ground under its feet.
One might have thought that hachshara, apart from physical preparation, had one more aspect in mind, namely the learning of a certain trade.
Each of us who observes the life of the various hachshara kibbutzim can boldly assert that not one of the members who are in the various hachshara kibbutzim has yet learned any trade whatsoever, because the kibbutzim are so arranged that they lack the most elementary tools a craftsman needs, and even the proper teaching staff and instructors are lacking. One more argument that speaks against the idea of hachshara must be firmly stressed — that is the question of work.
Each of us knows that in the country [Poland] a monstrous unemployment prevails among Jews, a colossal lack of occupation, and how, under such conditions, can one think of full employment for all those young people who are sown and scattered in various hachshara kibbutzim throughout the whole country. It is therefore no wonder that in many hachshara points only a third of the members are steadily employed, whereas two thirds are idle.
If we take into account the circumstance that the average earnings of a halutz are considerably lower than the earnings of an ordinary worker, it turns out that the employed halutz must, out of his more than modest earnings, support two more persons.
It is therefore no wonder that in most hachshara points the youth, under such conditions, becomes swollen from hunger and want, and various illnesses prevail among them which undermine the young organisms.
A superficial observation can establish without further ado that almost every halutz who leaves the kibbutz is physically broken.
We should like to draw attention to one more aspect which, in our opinion, stands out prominently against the idea of hachshara, namely the climatic conditions in which hachshara takes place. The climatic conditions of Poland have nothing whatsoever in common with the climatic conditions of Eretz Yisrael.
Since hachshara lasts almost a year, it turns out that every halutz spends on hachshara the long Polish winter, which does not exist at all in Eretz Yisrael.
It is a well-known thing that the properties of the human organism are strictly individual; that means, in this case, that when a halutz easily gets through the winter in Poland, this is absolutely no proof that he will with the same ease endure the heat on the hot summer days in Eretz Yisrael.
Proceeding from this standpoint, the hardening and accustoming of the youth to cold is pointless, because, as is known, the climatic conditions in Eretz Yisrael are diametrically opposed to the climatic conditions in the lands of the Diaspora.
Summing up what has been said above, the question must be put: who actually needs hachshara, and in whose interests lies the continuation of a system that has gone completely bankrupt.
Willy-nilly, one must bring into this problem a political chord [note], which is forced[?] upon us by the ardent adherents of the hachshara system.
It is clear to every objective Zionist that the only ones who cling so passionately to the hachshara system are the left-wing groupings and their voluntary followers from the ranks of bourgeois Zionism. The impartial Zionists understand quite well that the moment the hachshara system is abolished and the distribution of the certificates is handed over into the hands of the various Zionist factions, there will cease the hegemony of the left-wing groupings, which have dominated all the bodies that deal with the distribution of the certificates.
The liquidation of the hachshara system as it has existed until now would, finally, have this further effect: that there would cease the Marranism [dissembling] which has seized a certain part of the Zionist youth that has bound its fate to Eretz Yisrael.
For it is an open secret [literally: "a secret for all of Brody"] that many young people who are preparing to make aliyah to Eretz Yisrael choose for their hachshara the kibbutzim of the left-wing groupings, because they believe that in this way it is easier to obtain certificates, although ideologically they absolutely do not agree with the ideology of the left-wing Zionists.
It is high time to remove the hachshara anachronism completely from Zionist life and to leave the function of distributing certificates to the separate Zionist factions, which will certainly carry out this function much better and more purposefully than the Palestine Offices, which are concentrated mostly in the main cities, far from the provinces, and quite often cannot check the moral qualifications of the candidates.
S. Żmucki.
Radio Corner

[Radio — music.]
The 150-year jubilee of "La Scala". An opera has been made of An-sky's "Dybbuk".
"La Scala" in Milan! It seems there is no educated person in the world who has not heard of this temple of art for music. Millions of music-lovers from the whole world long to hear, at least once in their lives, an opera at "La Scala" and to live through minutes of the highest artistic enthusiasm.
Now 150 years have passed of the glorious history of "La Scala", on whose boards the greatest singers, the greatest composers and conductors have appeared.
To have the privilege of singing at "La Scala" one must possess a wonderful voice and sing in such a way that it carries away and enraptures the spectator.
The Jewish people, too, has sent its singers to appear at "La Scala". These were: the great singer Margot Kaftal, who appeared in "Parsifal", Regina Pinkert and the world-famous Ada Sari. Of the Jewish male singers there appeared: Vinogradov, Hermann Jadlowker, Vittorio Weinberg and Hermann Sisberg[?].
For its 150-year jubilee "La Scala" is giving a whole series of operas, both from the old and from the new repertoire. Polish Radio has concluded an agreement with "La Scala", which will transmit 10 operas for Polish Radio.
There will be given: "Moses" by Rossini (22 February), a Palestrina concert (15 March), "The Dybbuk" by Rocca (27 March), "Isabeau" by Mascagni (10 April), "La Traviata" by Verdi (21 April), "Werther" by Massenet (29 April) and "Mefisto" ["Mefistofele"] by Boito (10 May).
For the Jewish radio listener a special significance will attach to the staging, for the first time, at Milan's "La Scala" of the opera "The Dybbuk" by Rocca. The composer Rocca created his opera on the basis of An-sky's mystical work. The opera "The Dybbuk" received the first prize at the international opera competition, and that is why it is being staged at "La Scala".
In this way, thanks to the wonderful invention of radio, we shall have the possibility of enjoying the greatest cultural values that humanity has created in the field of music.
Let the technicians explain in their dry language that radio is nothing more than waves, condensers and so on. But for a person who finds himself in a forsaken place somewhere in the provinces, the radio remains a wondrous revelation. One turn of the knob of the radio set is enough, and in a moment one is already in contact with the great bright world, with the most beautiful thing the musical world has created — with Milan's "La Scala".
Our Panorama

[Feuilleton — Sosnowiec, Katowice, Siewierz, Pilica.]
(An injustice passed over in silence. — Adherents of "Hakol Yodukha". — An armistice concluded. — Teeth in the Katowice mikveh. — Elijah the Prophet in Siewierz.)
We have committed a great injustice. At the time when Jewish Sosnowiec was in the heat of the elections, taking part in the holy war — we passed over in silence an event which, both in quantity and in quality, stands higher than
a Sosnowiec rabbinical seat...
The "lofty" affair was played out in the Aleksander [Hasidic] shtibl in Sosnowiec. The young fellows of that shtibl had cast envious eyes on the sharpness of other young fellows and decided to come up with some innovation — after all, there is no purpose in being a "sharp one" and going along with the older Hasidim, who show their Hasidism [only] when kehilla elections come round; no, that is not the way — one must create something, accomplish something. And "I toiled and I found": the young fellows held a meeting, at which, over a little glass of ts"kh[?] [apparently l"kh — "lechayim"], it was resolved to introduce the new ordinance of singing every Sabbath
"Hakol Yodukha"...
As the devil would have it, the gabbai of that shtibl is an opponent of "Hakol Yodukha" and brings up to the prayer-desk only the "anti-Hakol-Yodukhas".
— What do the young men do?
— They do not react — [but] when the prayer leader begins to sing "El Adon" — they sing — "Hakol Yodukha"...
There arose a singing and a banging. The situation became serious. A split threatened, the danger grew great — what will people say? A split, of all things, on the eve of the kehilla elections? — So indeed the middle party[?] came, the moderate Hasidim, and by their power an armistice was concluded until after the elections; and since the situation on the Sosnowiec horizon is not yet clear, and one does not yet know for certain whether one will not again have to throw oneself into the election cauldron, the matter of "Hakol Yodukha" too has been put off to a more favourable "conjuncture"...
———
In Katowice everything is done in the modern manner. Even one Hasid knocking out another's teeth does not happen as in "Konsovke"[?], in a primitive way, in public in the beit midrash or in the shtibl; no, the Katowice Radomsk Hasidim are already "modernised", and when the gabbai wanted to knock out a few teeth of an opponent of his, he carried out the experiment in the bathing establishment ("mikveh" in the vernacular).
The professional association of the Katowice dentists — having learned that teeth had been found on the floor[?] of the Katowice mikveh — took an interest in the matter and wanted to draw consequences, but when it was established that the teeth belong to a Radomsk Hasid and that the "dentist" is the gabbai of the shtibl, all fell hush and still.
———
Siewierz is doing "khorosho" [splendidly]; the Jews of Siewierz have entirely forgotten that in the world, and Siewierz included, there is a crisis; they have no mind for weekday follies, the vanities of this world, but from evening until morning, from early until late in the evening, the Jews of Siewierz stand with open mouths and with sticks in their hands and wait for the happy minute when there will be heard
the shofar of the Messiah...
For the Jews of Siewierz believe with perfect faith that the Messiah will show himself first in Siewierz. And the proof: the visit of Elijah the Prophet to the shtetl...
It happened last week. On a frosty early morning, when the Jews of Siewierz came in for the morning prayer, they found
— whom do you think?
— Elijah the Prophet...
Right next to the stove slept Elijah himself, and his little horse stood innocently in the women's section. At first the thing was a difficulty: why did Elijah quarter his little horse in the women's shul? That is surely a disgrace for the women... But about Elijah's deeds one must not ask questions; presumably he did it with due deliberation, and [held] that the "station" for his little horse must be in the women's section...
To the question: "Where is a Jew from?" the stranger did not answer; only when the covered wagon was already made ready to drive, Elijah went off into the mikveh; there the little horse drank its fill of mikveh water, and after that they drove on.
Well, does one need to prove any further that the stranger was Elijah the Prophet? So the Jews of Siewierz indeed stand at the crossroads and wait for the happy minute when there will be heard the symbol of the redemption — the shofar of the Messiah...
———
The report we have received from Pilica convinces us still more that the days of the redemption are drawing near, that the prophecy of "And it shall come to pass in the end of days" is being fulfilled. Let the Endeks make pogrom speeches in the Sejm, let the Polish Hitlerites think up plans how to wage war on Jews — we sing again the well-known little song: "Hulyet, hulyet, beyze vintn" ["Rage, rage, angry winds"]. We have no fear; since we have in our neighbourhood such brilliant heads as the "Mizrachi" leaders in Pilica, we can be sure that no evil will harm us. Never mind, the Mizrachists in Pilica have means enough to bring about a rapprochement between Jews and antisemites.
Now to the main point. Here is what they write to us from the holy community of Pilica:
The "Mizrachi" in Pilica arranged, in honour of the Fifteenth of Shevat, a celebration (a "bibka" in the vernacular), and among others the "Mizrachi" also invited the non-Jewish doctor, a great "lover of Israel", while the Jewish doctor, incidentally a Zionist, was not invited, for the "standpoint" of the Pilica "Mizrachi" is — to educate the nations of the world with commandments: let such an uncircumcised one indeed eat a fruit of the Land of Israel, then he will indeed love the people of Israel and will not draw up any reports for... uncleanliness.
— Bravo, Mizrachists of Pilica; a few more such "bibkas" and the hatred of the people of Israel will surely disappear...
Ben Amotz.
Home Notes. A Word about Punctuality.

[Będzin — "Home Notes" column / communal life.] Punctuality. There is no other word so popular among us, and no other word so profaned, laughed at and mocked, as the notion of punctuality among us Jews.
It is not the philological, phonetic — that is, abstract — meaning of the term that concerns us here, but its practical application in our daily communal life.
The nations of the world have fitted a proverb to us: "Żydowski zaraz — to pański poczekaj" [Polish: "A Jew's 'right away' is a lord's 'wait a while'"]. The same proverb exists in hundreds of variants, and everywhere it is meant to underline our attitude to the term "punctuality" — in the negative sense, naturally.
Everyone already knows that a Jewish assembly or meeting must begin two hours after the time stated in the invitation; among other nations that is out of the question.
For God's sake! Why should we not give ourselves an account of this and draw the consequences? Why can we not prevail upon ourselves to treat the practice of punctuality in our life, as all others do, with the necessary seriousness and respect?
Our communal life suffers enormously from it, and so do the people who have a connection with, a close attachment to, or an interest in the matter that is to be dealt with at the said assembly or meeting — they make sacrifices of time and patience entirely in vain and to no purpose.
Here, for example: the writer of these lines had last week no fewer than 13 meetings (read and write: thirteen), and he spent 18 hours waiting until the public should gather.
It is a crime to give up 18 hours to the idol of empty waiting until the public takes pity and comes. Why should it be so? Why can we not establish among ourselves that we come to every gathering — where we want to be — truly punctually, so that we need not make useless sacrifices of time and of patience?
After all, so small a thing is needed for it that it is truly painful that we do not grasp it.
One only has to be honest towards oneself and respectful towards the other person. Honest towards oneself: in that branch of communal, political, economic or cultural life in which one does not want to, or cannot, commit oneself to work, one should not turn anybody's head, but state clearly on the invitation, or to the one who presents it, the messenger or the chairman, that in this work he is not to be counted on and that he cannot come to the meeting. And respectful towards the other person: if he does commit himself to the work and is inclined[?] to be at the meeting, let him not regard himself as the great man for whom one may or must wait, but let him respect the other's time and the patience of the remaining persons, who do want to come on time.
Gentlemen, this punctuality is a trifle, and naturalizing it on our soil depends only on us, on all those "plain and everyday" people who come to meetings. We can carry it through in a very easy and simple way:
We are called to a meeting for 7.30, and the one who called it is not there (such cases happen among us more than often) — home, gentlemen, all of you; let those who summon learn to come first when they summon. The second time they will be more punctual. For the summoners and leaders of the institutions too we have the same advice: you call a meeting for eight, it is 8.30 and some have not come — do your part, gentlemen leaders, conduct the meeting without them, with those present, who did come; the remaining absentees — thrown out, struck off; pass over them to the order of the day. If they have understanding for the work, they will come punctually the second time. If not, if it does not interest them, one does not need them anyway.
So then, gentlemen, the invited and the summoners, let us pass to deeds in this direction, let us change our attitude to desecrated punctuality; it will then be comfortable for us, and above all it will be of use to the cause, the idea, the action that we wish to serve.
And one more thing, gentlemen, we must make clear to ourselves: if we manage to prevail upon ourselves to be, as said, honest with ourselves — not to want to turn the other fellow's head when the proposed work does not interest us at all — and also to respect the other's time by coming punctually, then perhaps in time we shall be able to deal further blows to the devil of the negative Jewish traits in communal life; perhaps we shall wean ourselves from making a din as loud as among no other nation, and also from talking so much over every trifle, and so on.
But that is the music of the future; for the time being one thing concerns us:
— Let punctuality be observed. Let us not have to waste 18 useless hours, and let us also not have to disperse with nothing.
So then: war on unpunctuality.
Sz. Chazan.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion (Terumah)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Terumah
Parsha
—o—
1) "You shall take My offering" (25:1)
Earlier it says: "that they take for Me an offering", which Rashi explains: "let them set apart for Me from their money" — they should give charity from their own money. But giving oneself is still too little; one must also take from others, collect for a good cause, and not consider one's duty done with what one gives out of one's own pocket. After you have given yourselves — "you shall take My offering": you are to take from others.
"Honour the Lord with your wealth [me-honcha]" — "read not me-honcha but mi-gronecha [with your throat]". Not only "from your wealth", from your property, shall you give charity, but also "from your throat" (calling aloud): you shall also call upon others and rouse them to give. Ketav Sofer.
• • •
In Berdichev there was a rich man, a miser, who never wanted to give a single grosz to charity. Once Rabbi Levi Yitzchak was going round collecting money for a charitable cause, and he came in to the miserly rich man. The rich man honours him as befits such a guest. Later the rich man asks the rebbe what he has come for. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak does not answer, but stands up and goes away... The rich man takes fright and runs after the rebbe to ask what on earth his visit and his not answering mean. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak says to him:
— I am going about collecting charity, but to you I did not want to speak, because "just as it is a mitzvah to say a thing that will be heeded, so it is a mitzvah not to say a thing that will not be heeded" (when one knows that the other will not obey, it is a mitzvah not to speak to him). But if I do not come to you, I shall not be fulfilling the "mitzvah of not saying"; so I came to you, and knowing that in any case you would give me nothing, I did not speak to you — and thus I have fulfilled the "mitzvah of not saying a thing that will not be heeded"...
This gripped the rich man, and this time he did give Rabbi Levi Yitzchak a donation. Says Rabbi Levi Yitzchak:
— Now I have already fulfilled the first half as well, "a mitzvah to say a thing that will be heeded", because as soon as I spoke to you, you did give me... Da'at Zekenim.
—o—
2) Terumah.
In Slonim there was a Jew, a Torah scholar, by the name of Reb Avremele. He was a frequent visitor at the home of Rabbi Eizel of Slonim.
All of a sudden this Reb Avremele became a rebbe. Reb Eizel meets him and asks him:
— You, a rebbe?
— Jews have made me their rebbe.
— But how does one suddenly become a holy man, a saint, just like that?
— That is the power of Jews — answers Reb Avreml — if they pick themselves a man and travel to him, call him rebbe, they draw holiness down upon him. We see this with terumah. A plain grain of wheat — and if a Jew calls it "terumah" it becomes holy to God; a plain grosz — and if a Jew makes it terumah it becomes holy.
Reb Eizel smiles:
— You have only just become a rebbe and you have already forgotten your learning. You have forgotten the Mishnah, that "a deaf-mute, a fool and a minor who set aside terumah — their terumah is not terumah". That if a fool makes a plain grain of wheat, or a plain grosz, into terumah, it does not yet become holy thereby... Mi-Dor Dor.
—o—
3) "From every man whose heart [libo] moves him" (ibid.).
In the Torah it is said many times "levavo" (which sounds rather like a plural form). With terumah, however, it has to be "whose l i b o [heart] moves him": he should have only one heart when giving terumah, not two hearts — one that pulls towards giving and one that pulls towards not giving.. Ha-Torah veha-Mitzvah.
—o—
4) "You shall take My offering."
"M y offering" — because, after all, everything is Mine — says God — the offering that you give for Me is also Mine, just as all your money is Mine: "Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord". Kiflayim le-Tushiyah.
• • •
The Maggid of Kelm once came to ask a donation of a rich man, a miser. The swinish [?] rich man did not want to give the maggid a single prutah. Says the maggid:
— You know, you will now remain a rich man for ever...
The rich man asks him how he knows that. He answers:
— The matter is simple: a poor man, when he drops a grosz into the mud, will bend down and pick the grosz up. A rich man, however, will not trouble himself to pick up a grosz out of filthy mud. The Master of the Universe is, after all, a rich man — "Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold" — and the bit of money He has dropped down to you is surely worth no more to Him than a grosz is to a rich man. Now that He has dropped a grosz into such mud as you are, He will never take it out again...
• • •
Reb Abishl of Frankfurt was once a rich man, and he distributed his fortune to charity. One of those close to him argued with him:
— Terumah is to be given one part in forty, tithe — one in ten. "And he who spends lavishly should not spend more than a fifth": more than a fifth of one's fortune one is no longer permitted to give away to charity. So how is it that you act against the law?
Reb Abishl answers:
— It is indeed a law. But of charity it is said "the more charity, the more life", so it is a matter of saving life [pikuach nefesh]: every grosz of charity brings life, and saving life overrides the Sabbath — so it certainly overrides the law of "he who spends lavishly should not spend more than a fifth". Imrei Tzaddikim.
—o—
5) "Within and without shall you overlay it" (ibid., 11)
"Within and without shall you overlay it" — Rava said: any Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside is no Torah scholar. Tractate Yoma 72b.
• • •
The "Chovot ha-Levavot" says: "He who is pious only outwardly, and at home, when no one sees, does all that is evil [?] — that man is in fact serving idolatry".
• • •
"I will give heed to the way of integrity — when will You come to me? — I will walk in the integrity of my heart w i t h i n  m y  h o u s e".
The whole task of the pious Jew is that also w i t h i n  h i s  h o u s e, in the home, when no one sees, he should likewise be one who walks in the integrity of his heart... Orach Chaim.
—o—
6) "And you shall make a menorah of pure gold" (ibid., 31)
The menorah, which symbolises the Torah, was placed opposite the table, which symbolises wealth. Two eternal opponents... The menorah stood on the right, on the south side, and the table on the north side, on the left.
"A wise man's heart is at h i s  r i g h t, and a fool's heart at h i s  l e f t"... Midrash Aggadah.
—o—
7) "And into the ark you shall put the Testimony" (ibid., 21)
The Torah is called "testimony" [edut]. King David too calls the Torah thus: "and My testimony that I shall teach them" (Psalms 132), because just as when giving testimony one may not read intentions into it, but must take it literally, so also the Torah. One may not study any hidden intentions into it. Sefer ha-Ikkarim.
Avrom Is Tired. (A Novella)

[Literature — a novella.] By Roza Jakubowicz.
(A novella).

Avrom and his son come out of the tax office; there two witnesses have signed the report on Avrom Kahane's poverty — the "akt ubóstwa" [Polish: certificate of poverty]. He ought to be content, Avrom: rid at last of his debts to the "urząd" [the office], which, without any material participation, had been a partner in his turnover — which had grown ever more paltry — and in his "dochód" [income], which had come to equal almost nothing. But Avrom Kahane feels wounded in his pride for the first time in his life: how so, is he really already a "rich" [?] pauper. He feels himself to be one. How easy it is to become a pauper, one from whom the tax office no longer has anything to take

But soon comes the practical side: what, after all, is he to do next? Along the quiet street an empty droshky drives by. Around the wheels, it seems to Avrom, he sees shimmering the white-and-red seals with the white eagle. He still sees the dark-blue ribbon in the lapel of the office chief's [naczelnik's] jacket.

They both stand, father and son, before the gate of the tax office; both feel all the same — old. Yet the son says to the father:

— Don't take it to heart, father; you'll see, you will yet work your way back to something.

Avrom's eyelids redden as though he had been weeping, although he too has never granted his eyes any weeping. With what? — he cries out, with his small animal-ness in his human tone, — with empty hands? When you, children, robbers, don't want to be men of business, and I am without strength, without goods and without money to trade with.

Avrom Kahane's outcry, "with what", rang so loud because it came from an overburdened spirit in which more than one sorrow had coiled like snakes. First of all, that his sons go their own separate way and do not want to be his heirs. And then the trouble that they do not actually have anything of the kind to inherit from him. Avrom Kahane has nothing with which to go to the table, nothing to trade with.

"To trade" — the one thing on which all his efforts to keep up the household had rested — is slipping out [?] from under his feet. He feels like a man whose foot has been taken off: how will he walk on?

Women go by, laden with market baskets of greens and provisions; Binem and his father come out onto the "exchange" [the merchants' street bourse]; here Jews stroll to and fro with sullen faces, avoiding looking at one another; they do not want to see their own failure mirrored in the other man's bankruptcy.

— I'm going, father, says Binem.

— Wait, I'm going too. The father needs to talk himself out before his son. Oy, Binyomin, the father says: the houses, the estates, the businesses that we had — where has it all gone?

Binem walks with his father but does not listen to him; there, at the end of the street, leaning against the wall, stands a group of unemployed men with their hands in their pockets. Binem looks as though he wanted, with his gaze, to draw fingerprints out of empty workers' pockets: what kind of movements do the hands make there, hands condemned to do nothing at all, and which through that passivity have nothing to carry to the mouth.

Avrom talks on as if to himself. All my years I toiled diligently — he finds a consolation in the fact that he did not stand aloof from events, only that the results depended on God. God sent a war, which burned down my business; then there was the German, who did not let one live freely; now the tax office. And so everything slipped out of my hands. Oy, Binyomin, the houses, the estates, the factories.

Out of habit he touches his breast pocket, where in the wallet there once lay Russian roubles and German marks, and now — only a single protest [a protested bill of exchange], which no longer has any force.

— What did I fail to do? — he spreads out his hands and knocks against the leather buttons of Binem's jacket; he snatches his hands back and folds them on his belly, remembering that one may fold one's hands like this only at a funeral. But he stays in that position.

— No one helped me, no wife, no children.

Binem does not answer. What should he have helped with? Trading together with his father? Back then, when he was studying and believed that with learning and knowledge he would conquer his world and make everyone happy. Now, diploma in hand, he stands at the crossroads. He does not know what to do. But what does father want of him?

— I'm going — he buttons himself up. Of course; how long is he to walk around like this with his father. But he adds: in the evening I'll come home.

Avrom wants to follow him, but soon loses sight of him. Avrom walks alone. He grows narrower, his back rounder, his chest hollowed [?], his beard thinner; even the shape of his gaiter-boots has changed. Only the eyes are the same big ones, looking about on all sides.

Is he then quite alone in the whole world, an accursed man? And he, dumb beast, had thought that God was leading him by the right hand, that God was watching over his business.

He had served so faithfully, toiled like a bee, worked all his days for wife and children — which is equal to giving charity — and here it is, poverty, against which all his generations had armoured themselves with thousands of locks, and against which he too, Avrom, defended himself in vain.

And is it not strange, he thinks: a man must endure his lot, fine. God has the statute of letting man suffer. But could He not have arranged for the troubles to be spread over all times, rather than bidding man drain the measure of troubles all at once? First God lets one enjoy seven fat years, and then, in one's older years, He takes from a man his health, his wife, his money, everything. At the worst time He presents His bill of exchange. Is God, blessed be He, harder than the tax office, which does, after all, spread the debt out in instalments?

Avrom draws up the balance: wife dead, fortune lost, the children taken from him, and yet his gait grows more erect. He has not fallen. Formerly, when he used to meet a ragged man in the street, he, Avrom Kahane, in his fine clothing, would fall in his own eyes in the face of the other's bitter plight; but now he, Avrom, can pride himself on his decline in the face of the one who is better off.

He sees himself in a back street, where [?], at the rubble [?] that is carted out of the town, former embroiderers are working? On rail trolleys, over rails, dust-carts go to and fro...

He too will hire himself out for work, be it what it may; work one must, after all, as long as one lives. He will not be ashamed; altogether he is losing his connection to people.

Like a fallen leaf in empty space, so a coldness draws him into itself, a congealment from which he will never thaw. He will be well in it; the emptiness will bring him closer to his dead wife, who also has nothing any more. He will live for himself, avoid meeting those who have something. The dead love rest.

The morning winds chase the dust from the plaster of the houses and from people's clothes and drive it back to where it came from. And why does he stop — am I angry at Binem? When he goes away from me he must, after all, begin to do something, just as I began; let Avrom only remember: did he, Avrom, not go by other paths? Than his father. His father, R' Pinkhesl, did not go at all, only sat, sat all his days over holy books. He could sit deep in the armchair; in the cash-box there were, in any case, still the jingling coins. But he, Avrom, worked and worked and was left with nothing. And now Binem has to begin — but where is Binem going? Both, fathers and sons, are obliged to work, and where is it written that only the fathers must. Eli, his brother-in-law, departed this world because he could not "must" provide a living, and they, Eli's orphaned daughters, can. The rotten shavings [?] fall off the machine, or, as Eli used to say: the waves of water hew away from the mountain, which stays standing, and they flow on.

Let the children take the reins into their hands; let them go with empty hands to work, or there where Kive is urging them to go — to the Palestinian reality, with bare arms in the eastern sun, towards the day of tomorrow.
Important Rulings of the Supreme Court

[Law — Supreme Court rulings.]
Bus concessions.
Upon conviction for a crime against the internal or external (espionage) security of the state, one immediately loses the concession for a bus.

Tenant protection
In the case of rebuilding a house, the agreement with a tenant can be dissolved — if [printed "ווי"] the house-owner places at the disposal of the tenant concerned another suitable dwelling and at the same time also reimburses him the removal costs. The dispute as to whether the premises offered are suitable is decided by the court. Before that the tenant has no duty to move out.

Fire insurance fund ("fayerkase")
An attachment ("zayentshe" — Polish zajęcie) may be laid on the sum received from the fire insurance fund only in the case where the debtor does not put up another building on the site of the one that burned down.

Fictitious agreements
A creditor can prove that the debtor has fictitiously transferred or encumbered his property not merely with written documents but even also with witnesses, and[?] [this] even if the said circumstance arose before the debt itself arose.

Bills of exchange of minors.
A bill of exchange (veksl) of a minor has no validity, even when the debt is called in only at the time when the debtor is already of full age.
The Jewish Queen of Yemen (7)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas; installment 7.]
Sh. Berg.

When Abu Karib died, he left three sons: Hassan, Amru and Yusuf. Hassan was the eldest, so he became king. Amru let himself be talked round by wicked men, and he murdered Hassan and seized the throne. Later Amru repented of his crime and put his murderous counsellors to death. But he found no peace, soon fell ill and died young.

Now Yusuf should have taken the throne. But a sheikh, an idol-worshipper, snatched the throne. He was a terrible tyrant. He did every kind of evil and oppressed the people harshly.

Yusuf was afraid that the wicked ruler would kill him — he was, after all, the heir to the throne — so he ran away and worked in a field far from the capital.

Once a band of robbers fell upon the field and wanted to carry off the grain together with the oxen. The labourers scattered in great terror; only Yusuf stayed, and with the ploughshare he beat the robbers and drove them off. The ruler heard of his heroism, wanted to know who he was, and sent a detachment of soldiers after him. They brought him to the palace and led him into the bath-chamber, where the ruler was washing his body in a tub of rose-water.

The ruler recognised him and said that now he would settle accounts with him. That meant death, and just as he was about to say his final confession [vidui], he caught sight of a small sword beside the tub, snatched it and, quick as lightning, plunged it into the ruler's heart. The rose-water turned red with the villain's blood, and Yusuf leapt out through the window; with the bloody sword he ran to the market-place and shouted:

— He is dead, the cruel one! I have killed him! He will torment you no more.

The people stormed with joy, brought him to the palace, seated him on the throne, danced and shouted: — Long live the king!...

— Seven years I have been sitting on the throne, — Yusuf said to Penina, — and I have not yet had one quiet day; wars all the time.

After Yusuf had finished his story, the guests danced the whole night; the wedding celebration lasted a whole week. Yusuf and Penina were the happiest people in the world. But their happiness did not last long.

For half a year Yusuf Dhu Nuwas [printed "De Nuwas"] and Penina were the happiest couple in the world. He did not go off to war, the land was at rest, and Penina thought her happiness would be everlasting. But it did not last long. One afternoon, [as] Yusuf and Penina [sat] in the shade-tent, a general came in, bowed and said that he wished to speak with the king. Yusuf went over to him. They talked quietly for a while, and soon Yusuf turned terribly pale and trembled with agitation. And before Penina could ask him what was the matter, he ran out with the general. She went out after them; but she no longer saw them.

Soon there was a great commotion. From every side came hosts of soldiers, horsemen and foot-soldiers, horses, camels, wagons with weapons and packs of food. The army marched past, and Penina did not see Yusuf; only towards evening did Yusuf come, armed from head to foot. She fell upon his neck and wept:

— Yusuf, my dear one, my king, are you leaving me already? What is it?

He tried to calm her, saying it was nothing, but she begged him so hard to hide nothing from her — she wanted to share with him his joy and his sorrow — that he told her the truth. As soon as he became king, he said, he wanted all his subjects to convert to Judaism. Many sheikhs with their tribes obeyed him. But there were some who did not obey. He was very severe with them; with the Christians, however, he was more severe still. He took revenge on them for the torments that the Christians inflict on Jews in their countries.

Penina heard this, shook her head in displeasure and sighed. He asked her why she was sighing, and she told him that a Jewish king ought to do only good to his Christian subjects. He should be a model for the Christian rulers, so that they would be good to their Jewish subjects.

He fell into thought and said that perhaps she was right, but it was too late — he had already done it, and more besides: seeking to take revenge on the Christians, he had always attacked the Christian merchants from Byzantium and Abyssinia who travelled through his land on the way to India, and killed them; out of fear the Christians stopped travelling through Yemen.

This vexed many sheikhs, because the land lost income through the fact that many merchants avoided it. The king of Abyssinia was greatly angered that he was disrupting his country's trade and that he had killed Christians. But he was afraid to start anything with him. Some time ago two Jews were killed in Najran [printed "Nagran"], a Christian land, so he set out with an army to take revenge for the Jewish blood that had been shed. For some time he besieged Najran, and when the town could no longer endure the hunger, the ruler came out with three hundred notable men and begged for mercy. But he would not hear them out, and his soldiers slaughtered them on the spot. Then he entered the town and forced everyone to become Jews.

Będzin
The Citizens' Committee at the Magistrate Has Begun the Campaign to Combat Begging.
The Citizens' Committee at the local magistrate, whose task is to support the poor population, has first of all — in order to obtain material support from the public — undertaken the campaign to combat begging in the town.

A Week after the Wedding He Mortally Wounded His Wife with an Axe

[Będzin — crime, family tragedy.]
An extraordinary family tragedy took place last Sunday in a Christian family in Będzin.
On Sunday the 4th of this month there took place in the local church the wedding (ślub) of the 30-year-old Mizera with the 23-year-old Walentek from Czeladź. After coming back from the church Mizera declared to her husband that she would not live with him, because she has a lover (kochanek).
The news threw the husband off balance, and he set about destroying everything that was to be found in the dwelling of his mother-in-law.
Mizera paid no heed to all this, and on the same day she left her husband and went off to her lover.
Last Sunday the husband came to the dwelling of his mother-in-law, where he also met his “faithful” wife; the husband and also her mother pleaded with her that she should cast off her lover. When Mizera refused the request, the husband seized an axe, with which he dealt her several blows on the head.
Afterwards the husband went off to the police station (komisariat), where he declared that he had killed his wife.
The woman's condition is hopeless.

[Będzin — banks, cooperatives.]
After a break of two years, a general meeting of the local Discount Bank took place on Sunday in the session hall of the City Council.
The meeting, for which the management of the bank and also the members had been preparing for weeks — was, according to the preparations[?], supposed to be a very stormy one; apparently for that reason the director of the Audit Union (Rewizjons-Verband) himself, the auditor Mr. Michelson, came down; but in the end it turned out that it was only “a storm in a glass of water”: there were some members who got a little off their chests, and everything remained as before.

Mr. Michelson appeals to those assembled to help with the further development of the bank.
After the balance-sheet report by Mr. Herman Pinkus a discussion developed, in which the bank's leadership was criticised for presenting the unsatisfactory balance sheet.

When neighbours quarrel...
[Będzin — from daily life; a short feuilleton.] „When thieves quarrel, one learns of the theft“ — and when neighbours quarrel it is even worse: it may yet come to a divorce between a young couple.
We say this with regard to a story that happened last week on Pańska Street.
On the said street two young women neighbours fell out over a little coal shed. And they quarrelled so long that they began to throw at each other the „sins“ of their girlhood. When this theme of girlhood pozoruzhe[?] [doubtful word — apparently „escapades“/„disgraces“] had been exhausted, they began to recount what each knows about the other, and out poured a whole list of true, fresh, wriggling sins of married women[?], from Krynica, Olkusz[?] and above all from Ustroń.
What is interesting is that the „neutral“ listeners to this most interesting and piquant dialogue were the two husbands. They stood there, poor things, and listened to how they were being made fools of.
The finale of the affair is this:
One of the husbands, probably the cleverer one, heard out the whole list of „accusations“ and dismissed it all with a smile. And the second took this „foolishness“ so much to heart that he is thinking of a divorce.
It will not end in a divorce — family, relatives and friends will not allow it — but meanwhile the young wife has great heartache from it all.
— Neighbours, live in peace, for if you quarrel people will learn your secrets, and that really does not pay.

In today's issue we bring the report that the „Agudat HaRabbanim“ [Union of Rabbis] has called upon the rabbis in Sosnowiec, and also the kehilla representatives, to go to a din-Torah with Rabbi Englard concerning the Sosnowiec rabbinate.
Interesting are the replies which each one of those called upon wrote to the „Agudat HaRabbanim“.
Rabbi Hager, in his reply, cited factual proofs and witnesses that Rabbi Englard rejected the peace proposal which was put to him by the Rabbi of Będzin. If Rabbi Englard withdraws [„tsuriktsirn“, reading doubtful] from the courts, then — writes Rabbi Hager — one can talk about a din-Torah.
In the reply of the Koziegłowy rabbi, Rabbi Frommer, he asks: why did the „Agudat HaRabbanim“ not intervene when Rabbi Frommer was persecuted and humiliated in Zawiercie?
The parnas [kehilla board member] of the Koziegłowy [rabbi's] side, Mr. Emanuel Drzewiencki[?], replied: „Even if Joshua son of Nun should rise in the resurrection of the dead, I too shall not act otherwise than as I have committed myself.“
— If the „Agudat HaRabbanim“ had lived in Sosnowiec for even one year, you would then have become acquainted with the actual situation, as the truth is — so replied the parnas of List 11, Mr. Josef Grochowina.

150 children wait for support from the Jewish public.
[Będzin — relief; TOZ.] The feeding campaign for schoolchildren, organised by „TOZ“ [the Society for Safeguarding the Health of the Jewish Population], is in full swing. One's own children who are employed in businesses must be registered with the sick fund
[Social insurance — sick fund.] According to the law on social insurance, one must register with the sick fund [Kasa Chorych] everyone who is employed in a shop, workshop or manufacture, even if this is a son, daughter or other relative of the owner.
The law regards a son or a daughter who works in a shop at the parents' just the same as an employee. The fact that the son, daughter or female relative takes no salary, but only eats and lives together with the parents — does not change the state of affairs.
Every merchant or shopkeeper who permanently employs a son or daughter in his shop must register them with the sick fund and pay monthly the social insurance sum (sick fund, ZUPU [the white-collar workers' insurance institution], etc.)

The Rabbinate Question in Dąbrowa.

Last Sabbath Jewish Dąbrowa made the acquaintance of the candidate for the Dąbrowa rabbinate who is supported by the parnasim of the Kromołów side. The candidate is a son-in-law of the Kromołów Rebbe and the son of the Rabbi of Opoczno.
The rabbi-candidate possesses rabbinical virtues, but is a weak speaker. The rabbinical candidates up to now made a greater impression with their sermons than the Kromołów candidate.
Altogether the rabbinate struggle in Dąbrowa has got into a tangle. On one side efforts are being made that the ruling of the rabbinical court, which the son-in-law of the deceased rabbi obtained, should not be altered, and in exactly the opposite direction works the Dąbrowa "Aguda", which aims at having the court's ruling concerning the Dąbrowa rabbinate revised.
There is also a third side, actually the right side, which for the time being keeps itself in "reserve" and does not yet say its decisive word. That is the opinion of the kehilla, the elected parnasim, in whose hands lies the "key" to the rabbinical seat in Dąbrowa...
As we are informed, a second competition for rabbis will most probably be opened, because the candidates up to now do not meet the proper qualifications for the office of rabbi in Dąbrowa.

R' Chanoch Jungster, of blessed memory

At the age of 63 there passed away this week, after a short illness, the former moreh-tzedek (rabbinical decisor) in Katarzyna, of late a resident of Będzin, R' Henech Jungster, of blessed memory.
On Monday towards evening the deceased travelled to his son-in-law, the moreh-tzedek of Katarzyna, Rabbi R' Yehonatan Stark. There R' Henech suffered a stroke of paralysis, and the next morning he passed away.
The deceased was a respected man, well-liked among people, and was the pride of the Sochaczew Hasidim in Będzin. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
The Unemployed Are Exempt from the Dwelling Tax

[Poland — taxes.]
The Ministry of Finance has now issued a special circular which exempts the unemployed from paying the premises tax (podatek lokalowy).
From now on, dwellings of 3 rooms (or 2 rooms with a kitchen) that are inhabited by unemployed persons will not fall under the law on the premises tax.
The circular points out at the same time, however, that only those unemployed who do not keep subtenants are exempted. An unemployed person who wishes to be exempted from the premises tax must hold an unemployment card or a certificate that he is already unemployed. In the applications one must also state that one has no subtenants.
The circular also points out that in dwellings of unemployed persons where the subtenants are unemployed as well, the tax offices may exempt them too from the premises tax. For this a card must be presented showing that the subtenant is also unemployed.

[Upper Silesia — regional column; Katowice, Zionism, crime.]
A festive "Keren Hayesod" academy.
Count Pusłowski ends his speech with "Next year in Jerusalem".
(L. T.) A festive "Keren Hayesod" academy [gala assembly] took place in Katowice.
Jewish Katowice of all strata filled the hall to the brim; on the handsomely decorated platform the presidium seats are taken by the poet Leib Jaffe, Count Ksawery Pusłowski, both Katowice rabbis and others.
After the Polish and the Jewish anthems have been played, the academy is opened, in Polish and Hebrew, by Rabbi Chameides. In warm words he greets the Polish count, the representative of the old liberal Poland; in Hebrew the rabbi greets the director of the Jerusalem head office of "Keren Hayesod", the esteemed and dear guest, Mr. L. Jaffe.
After a substantial introduction by Rabbi Chameides, which made a deep and strong impression, a fine speech is given by Count Pusłowski, who recalls the situation of the Polish people, the times of bondage, its heroic attempts at liberation, and then passes on to the heroic exertions of our halutzim [pioneers], whom he compares to the historical Jewish heroes.
After explaining the great significance of the Zionist idea, the count ends his enthusiastic speech with the old "Next year in Jerusalem". His address made a colossal impression on the listeners.
Then the poet L. Jaffe speaks; he begins in Hebrew, recalls the historic Katowice Zionist conference with Dr. Pinsker [1884], Mickiewicz's admiration for the old Jewish dream of revival.
This part of the address Rabbi Chameides at once reads out in Polish translation; then the speaker continues his speech in Yiddish.
The poet, well known to and beloved by us all, paints a splendid picture of the Land of Israel, of the effect of Zionism and the Land of Israel on the whole Jewish people; recalling the Jewish catastrophe in Germany, he says that the Jews there are like the Indian pariahs — only no German Gandhi has been found who would fast for them.
The speaker calls in ardent words for an all-out effort for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel, so that we shall not be too late.
Rabbi Chameides closes the academy, expressing the hope that Poland, as a great power, will be true to her old traditions in supporting the Jewish efforts.
