"Jus Primae Noctis"

[Article — Nazi Germany; the status of women.] By Sh. Rotenberg.

It has not been established whether there really existed in the Middle Ages a law on the "right to the first night", under which every peasant maiden had, on her wedding night, first to give herself to the lord of the manor; but it is a fact that such a custom prevailed in various countries during feudal rule. And even if there were no historical proofs of the existence of such a custom, plain reason would simply oblige us to invent it, for it is surely clear: if the lord was master over the life and death of his serfs, whom he regarded as an inventory with which one may do whatever one likes at any time — then who and what could have held him back from committing a sexual excess upon a pretty maiden who took his fancy?

Of that dark epoch every cultured person speaks with disgust and anger. That time was regarded as one that had vanished for all generations, one that would never again be repeated and would remain only as an ugly stain of shame on the pages of human history.

But who would have believed a few years ago (nowadays one can believe anything) that in the year 1934 a "scholar" would come from a country in the very heart of Europe and propose to reintroduce the "jus primae noctis"?

It is not hard to guess that this highly "cultured" and "civilised" country, from which the author of the "humanitarian" project hails, is bloody Nazi Germany. The Hitler lads have dug up some dubious "man of science" by the name of Hartleben, who proposes in his book "The Great Ages of Mankind" to put the above-mentioned law into practice, with the aim of obtaining a pure Aryan type. This pseudo-scholar writes that the nature of the woman and of the future child depends on the man to whom she gives up her maidenhood. Therefore a law on the "right to the first night" must be introduced, under which every maiden will first have to give herself to a special pure Aryan designated by the government.

That is the leitmotif of the book.

The twentieth century stands under the sign of the emancipation of women. Serfdom was abolished long ago, rape is severely punished everywhere, but one year of Hitler's rule suffices to come out with such a barbaric bill, the mere thought of which profanes the whole human race. For long years woman has been waging a hard struggle for her equal rights with man; every truly civilised person already understands today how foolish it is to regard woman as some inferior creature that is backward compared with man. Science established long ago that in certain respects woman stands even higher than man. And suddenly Hitlerites come and want, with their Prussian soldier's boot, to kick mankind, and women in particular, into the medieval quagmire of the lowest sexual perversion. Even the present-day representative of the Hitlerite intellectual elite, the psychopath Hanns Heinz Ewers, whose morbid imagination thought up an "Alraune" and "The Sorcerer's Apprentice", would surely not have been capable of devising such a brilliant vision as a "jus primae noctis" in the year 1934. On Guard / Cultural Work Among the Jewish Artisans

[Będzin — artisans; article.]
Little attention has so far been given to cultural work among Jewish artisans. It is a very neglected field, and cultural work could be conducted precisely on a large scale. All that is required is an attitude, an understanding of this problem on the part of the artisans' activists.
Especially now, when the forms of organisation are beginning to take an entirely different shape. Precisely the Jewish artisan, who[?], as a result of his consciousness, has from his earliest youth been possessed by the wish to become a productive person, so that with his work he should not merely satisfy his material egoism but also thereby create a benefit for those — for whom he works — this is a proof of cultural elevation.
But the professional organisations of the Jewish artisan have almost always occupied themselves exclusively with professional questions. Seldom has there been a lecture on a cultural subject arranged by an artisans' organisation. Let us take a town like Będzin, where the Jewish artisans' movement is relatively well organised in the various guilds, and yet one hears very little about cultural work, at the very least for the large membership.
The inner need of the Jewish artisan to raise himself culturally, too, to an appropriate level — we must note with regret — has not only not been cultivated, but even his professional organisations have taken no interest in it. The argument of being weighed down by cares cannot hold here. As an example may serve the Jewish worker, who, although he is no less preoccupied with his existence than the Jewish artisan, nevertheless his organisations have conducted cultural activity.
Nor can the particularly hard present moment of the Jewish artisan be taken into account here; on the contrary, precisely now, in his embitterment over the bad material situation, this must be made complete[?] for him through a broad cultural education.
It may also be that if the Jewish artisan masses, which are a popular movement, had been appropriately educated culturally, this would have greatly eased the — to a certain degree crude — forms of their economic struggle. One need only have the courage to tear the artisan out of the narrow circle of his daily worries and awaken in him the feeling of cultural needs. That this will succeed — of that we are sure, if the artisan will only for one moment give himself an account of the fact that in government circles too he is regarded, in the cultural respect, as second-rate. As an example may serve the fact that, according to the new Industrial Law, intellectuals will be represented in the Chambers of Crafts although they are not artisans. This cultural work must be begun with full force; if the work is conducted with earnest devotion, what has been lost can be won back in the course of a short time.
Let the Jewish artisans' activists think seriously about the matter. Of the assistance of the Jewish masses they can be sure.
1492—1933 / (Conversations)

[Article — Nazi Germany and the Jews; the expulsion from Spain compared with the „expulsion from Germany“.]
By Avraham Tiktin.
If in the 19th century a notice had appeared in a newspaper that a European state had decided to repeat in its country the expulsion from Spain, everyone would have said that this is nonsense, that this will never happen. Why? Simply because today is not the fifteenth but the nineteenth century. No state, be it ever so antisemitically disposed, will allow itself to adopt such a barbaric means; and if a state should cast off its shame and issue such a decree, the cultured world would raise such a protest that that state would be forced to withdraw its decision.
In the twentieth century an expulsion has been carried out before the eyes of the whole world — true, not in the form in which it took place in Spain in the year 1492, by a decree that within 4 months all Jews must leave the country, with the right to take their goods and chattels with them, but in a no less extreme and cruel form. The state has decreed to take away from all its citizens who supposedly belong to the Jewish race, without distinction of faith, the possibility of making a living — to exclude them from social intercourse, to degrade in them their human dignity, to embitter their existence through decrees[?] and persecutions, and by such means to bring it about that they should be forced to leave Germany, just as they were once forced to leave Spain.
The causes that brought about the expulsion from Germany stand, from the humane point of view, much lower than the causes that brought about the expulsion from Spain. The Spanish government explained the expulsion by saying that the Jews in Spain support the Marranos in quietly remaining with the Jewish faith, but that when Spain becomes free of Jews, the Marranos will remain proper Christians. Those causes, for all their groundlessness, bore in that era, from the Catholic and political viewpoint, a spiritual character. The causes that brought about the expulsion from Germany bear a purely egoistic-bestial character; they find their explanation solely in the power of the stronger over the weaker, in the force of violence over justice: I do not want to have you here — that is their plain meaning. The fig leaf of the race theory, with which they want to cover the disgrace, is too transparent for one not to see the naked reality that lies beneath it.
And which state was it that found the courage to cast off its shame and carry out an expulsion in the twentieth century? Germany! That very Germany which twenty years ago, through its lust for conquest, called forth against itself the hatred of almost the whole world; that very Germany which in the course of the World War did not refrain from any means whatsoever — from poison gases, from flame-throwers, from bombs, from submarines — in order to annihilate everyone who came under its hand, making no distinction between soldier and civilian, between citizens of belligerent and of neutral states, between man, woman and child. That very Germany which, out of hatred and revenge, turned the occupied French provinces into a desolate wilderness; that very Germany which possesses in its country not even a full one percent of Jews, and yet the egoism, the envy is so great that it cannot bear to watch how that handful of Jews, ardent German citizens and patriots, with the help of their honed[?] intellect received by inheritance, with the help of diligence, ability and energy, acquired a prosperous position in the country. Having at the same time the audacity to say that the Jewish race stands lower than the German, at a time when the facts, the reality, the Jewish economic and cultural level in Germany, which so pricks the Germans' eyes, prove to the whole world exactly the opposite.
Professor Mommsen[?] wrote in his time: „The harm which the Bismarck period brought the German people is far greater than the benefit it brought it; the gain in power and prestige are doubtful and transient values, which may be lost again in the next world storm, whereas the bending of the personality, of the German ego-spirit[?], is a fact that can in no way be made good again“.
Reality has confirmed Mommsen's[?] prophecy sooner than could have been reckoned. For two generations in succession, nationalism, chauvinism and militarism were systematically instilled and implanted in the hearts of the youth in the German schools and universities; the people were persuaded and talked into believing at every opportunity that right lies in might, that the weak must submit to the strong, that such is the law of nature in all organic life, and that therefore one must gather the necessary forces in order to rule the world and take in it the place of the so-called lower races — and lower races are all those who do not belong to the German descent, who are therefore condemned by nature to perish. One must multiply greatly, have many children; from seven children upward one received a premium from the Kaiser — and as a result there grew up hosts of millions of unintelligent, morally crippled proletarians, whose mouths must[?] now be stopped with something. Militarism was apotheosized into an art, the art of war, and in war everything is permitted, in war there is no pity.
Everyone knows Count Moltke's theory, which reflects the general national-German standpoint: „A lasting peace is only a dream, and not even a beautiful one. War is one of the elements in God's ordained[?] world order. Without wars the world would stand still in its development and dissolve in materialism“.
The same Moltke wrote in his book on the French war of 1870 that Prussia provoked the war with Austria in the year 1866 with the aim of establishing Prussian hegemony in Germany. In other words: Prussian and Austrian Germans killed one another for the sake of purely Hohenzollern, dynastic ambitions.
Today it stands under a question mark whether Germany would find itself in its present plumage[?] and would have sunk morally so low in the eyes of the cultured world if, in the 19th century, instead of under the Hohenzollern hegemony it had fallen under the Habsburg hegemony.
The question arises: for what, and for what purpose, did the German people sacrifice its youth on the fields of Sadowa?
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tisa)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat [Ki] Tisa
The Portion
—o—
a) “That there be no plague among them when you number them” (Ex. 30:12)
That is why God ordered that an equal half-shekel be taken from every Jew, and “the rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less” — all alike — because “that there be no plague when you number them”; for if a larger tax were fixed for a rich man and a smaller one for a poor man, there would at once have been a plague: this one would have shouted that he is a poor man and cannot give even a single penny, and that one would have pointed out that his neighbour is as rich as Korah and can give a great deal... Therefore an equal half-shekel was fixed for everyone. Matok MiDvash.
—o—
b) “This they shall give, everyone who passes among those who are numbered” (ibid., 13)
Charity is to be given by “everyone who transgresses the commands” [a pun on ha-over al ha-pekudim] — the transgressors, who want to redeem their sins with charity. Likutim.
—o—
c) “Half a shekel” (ibid.)
The measure of charity was fixed at half a shekel in order to hint that however much one gives — one is always giving only a half... Charity is in truth[?] one of “these things that have no fixed measure”; however much one gives, it still does not mean that one has already fulfilled the commandment in utter perfection... Ktav Sofer.
—o—
d) “And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath” (Ex. 31:16)
The Targum of Yonatan ben Uziel says on this verse: “And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to make the delights of the Sabbath” — the commandment is: to make the Sabbath a delight with dainties and delicacies... Likewise in Yevamot 93a, on the saying in the Gemara “that you may learn to fear the Lord your God — these are Sabbaths and festivals”, Rashi says: “Learn from this a warning[?] not to do away with the delight of the Sabbath”. The Rashba, in his responsa, no. 122[?], rules as a matter of law that it is a commandment, like all the commandments of the Torah, to make the Sabbath a delight...
• • •
The author of “Degel Machaneh Ephraim” [R' Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov] was at first a poor man. The Sabbath in his home was poor: two small loaves and two candles in clay candlesticks. Once he had become revealed, the Sabbath in his home was already rich: meat, fish, challahs and silver candlesticks. When the “Degel” once came home from prayers, he sees his wife standing and beaming with pleasure at the richly laid Sabbath table, at the silver candlesticks, and he says to her:
— For you it is bright now, and for me it was bright before...
• • •
The “Degel's” brother behaved differently: Rabbi Baruch of Mezhibozh [Międzybóż]. He was fond of wealth, so he travelled about after money through towns and townlets in order to be able to keep up a rich house. Once, passing through, he came to his brother; at that time candles in clay candlesticks were still burning in his home on the Sabbath. Rabbi Baruch says to him:
— Brother, it is high time you had silver candlesticks in your home.
— Brother! Brother! — the “Degel” answered him — better that the silver candlesticks should be somewhere far from home and I at home, than the candlesticks at home and I far from home...
• • •
“Rabbi Yochanan said: If Israel were to keep two Sabbaths properly, they would be redeemed at once” — (Shabbat 118).
Why exactly two Sabbaths? And secondly: in Midrash Rabbah on Exodus (25)[?] Rabbi Yochanan actually says that the redemption comes for the sake of keeping o n e Sabbath.
But by “two Sabbaths” both parts of the Sabbath are meant: the part that belongs to God — doing no work, resting; and the part that belongs to man — making the Sabbath a delight. If Jews kept not only the second part but also the first part, not only held to the Sabbath in matters of pleasure but also kept the Sabbath from work — the Messiah would have come... Sefer Yanchenu[?].
Purim — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Purim (the “Oneg Shabbat” column)

[Oneg Shabbat — Purim.]
“A hundred and eighty days” (Scroll of Esther 1:4)
On this the Vilna Gaon gave a wonderful reckoning:
The Midrash (section 2) says that Ahasuerus showed his guests six treasuries every day. Another aggadic midrash [printed: “agudah”] says that Ahasuerus inherited 1,080 [tatar"f] treasuries from Nebuchadnezzar. So, when he wanted to show them 1,080 treasuries, and showed six treasuries a day — he must after all have needed a hundred and eighty days... Yalkut Gershuni.
—o—
“Esther had not made known her people” (2:10)
Esther knew that if she disclosed who she was, Ahasuerus would raise up her family, make them ministers, and this would arouse envy among the gentiles. Jews never have any joy from their relatives who are close to the throne, from their exalted ministers. It arouses envy and hatred among the gentiles. Yalkut.
—o—
“And sending portions one to another” (9:19)
When the Malbim was rabbi in Bucharest he had many enemies among the reformers, with whom he waged a war. Once they played a prank[?] on him and at Purim sent him, as mishloach manot, a little pig made of sugar. When the Malbim saw it, he said:
— I know that the Jews of Bucharest love me dearly, but I did not know that they love me so much that they are even ready to give away to me t h e  v e r y  m o r s e l  f r o m  t h e i r  m o u t h s... Daat Zekenim.
—o—
“And Harbonah, too, be remembered for good.”
When the Russian antisemitic writer Ivan Sergeyevich Aksakov died — who had preached antisemitism in his newspaper “Rus”, and only once, at the end of his years, in a time of pogroms, let fall a good word about Jews in the “Moskovskiye Vedomosti” and called for the pogroms to be stopped — the Vilna town preacher [shtot-maggid], R' Yaakov, eulogised him:
Such a people are we Jews: every year they say [thus printed] “And Harbonah, too, be remembered for good”, although Harbonah was “of the same counsel” to destroy the Jews; but because he later blurted out one useful word, “Behold the gallows” — we have been mentioning him for good year after year.. Such a grateful people are we.
Eli HaLevi.

The Soviet radio technicians have now completed a loudspeaker which is the largest in the world. The voice of the loudspeaker can be heard within a radius of 50 kilometres.
This loudspeaker is a real giant, weighing over 1000 kilos. The Soviets have, of course, set up this instrument for propaganda purposes. An aeroplane will fly with this loudspeaker over the small towns, and the peasants of the surrounding villages will suddenly hear fiery sermons carried through the air.

Penalties for violating the radio regulations.
In the event that the radio inspectors establish that the radio installation is not registered at the post office, or that the radio installation does not correspond to the conditions under which the licence was issued, the police draw up a report and criminal-administrative proceedings are conducted against the owner of the radio set. For violating the radio regulations a fine of 3000 zł. and arrest of 3 months are provided. The radio set may also be confiscated and compensation demanded amounting to a 6 months' fee.

The man who speaks “with the wind”.
Mister Frank Carty[?], as leader of a scientific expedition, set out together with three more Englishmen for New Guinea with the aim of exploring the course of the Ramu River. Mr. Carty[?] was recently in the Papuan jungle, where the people go about completely naked and the woman is the property of every man.
The only contact with the civilised world for Mr. Carty[?] was the radio set which he had taken along with him. The English expedition travelled for the whole time of its dangerous journey in a motor boat. This boat, which moved by itself, the Papuans regarded as sorcery from heaven. On top of that, when the sounds of music were suddenly heard from the radio loudspeaker, the Papuans crowned Mr. Carty[?] as the greatest god and called him “Yan”, which means the “master, he who speaks with the wind”.
To the radio set the wild Papuans paid the greatest honour, as the voice of their god. How astonished the Englishman was when, on a certain day, the Papuans began to bow before the motor boat and the radio set and drummed[?] on the “tom-tom” — in this way the man-eaters were warning of a sudden flood of the Ramu River which was soon to occur.
Thanks to this warning from the savages, the English expedition was saved from certain death; for half an hour later enormous masses of water suddenly came rushing in, and the whole expedition would have perished in the roaring waves of the river.
What Is One to Do?

[Feuilleton — humoresque.] By B. Kovner.

(A monologue of a father who has three daughters.)

A Jew pours out his heart:
— I am nothing more than a sinful father. Had I not sinned, I would not have been a father. My wife — may it not befall you — died. She left me three daughters, fine, healthy girls like oak trees.
All of them are blonde, and all of them have blue eyes, and all of them have dimples in their cheeks, and all of them can sing a little and play the piano a little — girls of today.
Naturally they have a sea of young men. Day and night my house is full of young men; it looks as if a conference of young men were being held in my house. Among the young men you will find graduates, such as have not graduated, and such as attend university, and such as have not a grosz.
My three daughters dig them up as if from under the ground and bring them into the house. Meanwhile they eat at my place, nibble at my place, bang on the piano, let the radio run, and there is singing and dancing.
If I stay in the house while they gather, they are not pleased, my daughters: I am spoiling their pleasure, they say; so they send me off to the cinema or to the theatre, so long as I get out of the house and they can give the orders there. And since I reckon that from among all these young men some three bridegrooms will stay put, so that I can marry them off, the daughters, and shake them off my shoulders, I do as they wish and leave them alone — let them stand on their heads!
And if I do not want to go, because the dinner dishes have not yet been washed, the daughters shout at me: Father, go![?] It is none of your business, we will wash the dishes ourselves; don't forget to take the key along; you needn't hurry to come home.
“I don't need a key,” I say, “when I come home you will still be up, of that I am sure.”
And I go off without a key. Where I am going — I don't know; I have nowhere to go; in the cinema I sleep.
So I wander about the streets, look into the shop windows, study the prices. Sometimes I meet an acquaintance in the street, I stand and talk with him, and I find out that other fathers are in even worse trouble than I am; to their daughters no young men come at all.
In just this way I roam about the streets until eleven or twelve o'clock at night and I come back home, and lo — at my place it is still merry. The house is not to be recognised: full of cigarette smoke, the table is covered with ash, with scraps of paper, with matches, the little pillows from the beds lie on the floor, the ashtrays are full of nutshells with brown sweet-wrappers, with gnawed apples, with plum stones, with whatever you like; and my daughters twist strangely[?] with their bodies, they look like screwdrivers, they are great artists at these things, they are the greatest twirlers.
I look at my daughters, and my heart is torn for them: how they turn a whole world upside down in order to get bridegrooms! They dress up, they paint themselves, they twirl, they sing, they dance, they kiss, they let themselves be kissed — but it still comes to no practical end... And the daughters grow older, paler, more worn out. Such revels, you should know, do not add to one's health. The girls become nervous, afterwards cannot close an eye, toss a whole night on their beds, and there is sighing, and often I even hear a quiet weeping out of a dream...
That is how it is, as you hear, almost every night of the week: they neither get fresh air, nor eat on time, nor sleep on time. By day they work and by night they cook and tidy up the house — five rooms; and often they wash out their things and iron them, and all this has to be done before the young people gather.
So all three of them work like bees; the work burns under their hands.
But the real troubles begin only at two o'clock after midnight, when the gang goes home. Then a war breaks out among my daughters: one accuses the other of wanting to take away from her her “przyjaciel” [Polish: boyfriend]. The other swears it is not so. But the first, the elder, does not believe her: “It isn't true, what you say; it isn't true! You danced with him the whole night and did not let go of him for one minute and kept cuddling up to him every moment — I am not blind, I have eyes, I see.”
And I, the father, must listen and keep silent; I may not interfere; after all I was not at home. Often they tear each other by the hair and call each other all sorts of names... The elder one screams at the top of her voice: “You will not take Benye[?] away from me, unless after my death!”
The younger one joins in: “And when you took Leon away from your girlfriend, from Pola[?], was that all right? Only from you one mustn't take anything away... What do you need two for, while others are to have nothing?”
The elder becomes even more irritated and cries out in a voice not her own: “It's a lie! It's a lie! Leon hates her, he loves me, he has told me so a hundred times. I did not take him away from my girlfriend!”
In short, the whole house is turned upside down! And you ask: what, who and whom? Not one of the young fellows is in earnest, it does not even enter their left sidelock to think of getting married, since they cannot marry at all, even if they wanted to; not one of them works or earns; they are all dying for a grosz, idlers, an empty gang, without money and without sense. They come to my daughters exactly as they go to other houses, to other daughters, just like that — to dance, sing, tell silly jokes, talk about the cinema stars.
And do not think, my friend, that only my daughters are like this. Not at all! Almost all the girls here are like this. Some are cleverer, some more foolish, and some more foolish still.
Meanwhile there is trouble: they grow older with every day, and to the wedding canopy it is still a long way.
Give me, sir [“panie”], a piece of advice: what is one to do?
Who knows whether I shall yet live to have joy from them?

[Purim — the humour page "Der Greger".]
DER GREGER [The Purim Rattle]
(in place of "Kokh-lefl" ["The Cooking Spoon" — the paper's regular humour column])
Compiled in honour of Purim by Ben Amotz.

Esther, the Woman.
Do not be surprised that of all the heroes of the Megillah I have picked precisely a woman, Esther.
Today is already Shushan Purim, and still one feels like playing about a little with the fair sex. By the way: were it not for Esther we would have had no Purim and no Megillah at all. They would have slaughtered that handful of Jews in Shushan, and basta.
And had there been no Purim, we would not have gulped down the hamantaschen with the kreplach, and there would have been no Purim feast.
In short, for today's holiday we have only Esther to thank, that is to say, woman; so I really do want to dedicate the Purim feuilleton to woman.
What exactly is a woman?
I already regret having taken on such a hard question; go and explain what exactly a woman is.
But I wriggled out of the situation.
I myself indeed cannot interpret the word "woman", so I turned to competent persons and asked them to state their opinion about it.
Listen to what they answered me.
The head of the kehilla, Elazar Rubinlicht — A woman is like the shochtim [ritual slaughterers]: however much money you give them, it is still too little.
Dr. Weinzieher — Were it not for a woman, the "orphanage" would already belong to the magistrate [the municipality].
Dr. Perl — I have never yet met any bad proletarian women.
Dr. Tarasheiski[?] — A woman is like a "budynek" [Polish: a building]: everything depends on the foundation ["fundament" — colloquially also: the behind].
The "Muza" players [the drama circle] — A woman is like one of our performances: nobody understands it.
The Sosnowiec shtadlanim [lobbyists/intercessors] — A woman is like an army contract: you never know into whose hands she will fall.
Presumably even now you still do not know what exactly a woman is.
There is one more word to be said about woman, and then you would know everything. But I have to put it off until next Purim...
Yosef.

"Yes" and "No"

[Purim — political satire.]
These two words have played an important part in Germany, because with these two words it was decided whom to elect to the Reichstag.
These two words also play a very important part here with us in Poland.
If, for instance, one were to ask the 30 million Polish citizens who wants a little loan, 29,999,999 votes would answer "yes" and 1 vote "no".
(That one will also have to be photographed!..)
To the question: can one believe in Hitler's readiness for peace? — 29,999,998 votes will answer "no" and 2 will abstain from voting.
Should new taxes be introduced? — 30 million citizens will answer: "No".
Does one need the tax-assessment commissions? — 99 per cent of the population will answer "no" and 1 per cent (the assessors) "yes".
Does the kehilla satisfy the needs of the Jewish population? — all Jews will answer: "No", and the seat-squeezers [the chair-warmers of the kehilla] — "yes".

Stormy Sittings of the New Będzin „Parliament“...

[Będzin — kehilla; the sittings of the new community council on the 1934 budget.]
Declarations of political organisations. — Not a mikveh but a bath-house. — Presidium of the council against the budget. — The fallen in Austria honoured. — The new board will open the coffers[?] of the hidden cash. — A sharp incident over the Żupowicz[?] affair. — „Mizrachi“ goes together with the „Agudah“. — Instead of a 10 per cent reduction only 7½.
On Sunday afternoon the kehilla council, which for 2 years had not been admitted to power, held its first sitting, at which the budget for the year 1934 was dealt with.
Compared with the council sittings up to now, the sitting bore a different character in the outward sense — it is only a change of scenery. The „gallery“ seats are not taken by the little yeshiva lads with their tucked-away sidelocks, but by the „masses of the people“, for whom the greater part of the parnasim and dozors [board members] „care“ only for the benefit of their interests; inwardly, on the other hand — the same hubbub[?], the same debates[?], the same heatedness, the same chaos and the same — „witticisms“ and barbed quips...
At the beginning a certain earnestness was noticeable, the mood — a tense one, more correctly — a sensational one, for Landner's speech of accusation addressed to his party comrades, against the presidium of the board, was after all the most interesting number for the audience. The „J'accuse“ ought, after all, to have come from another side. But little by little the earnestness vanished, tempers became heated, the gallery „united“ with the parnasim, there arose a confusion of minds, a tumult, a banging, and in just such a mood the first spectacle ended...
———
The sitting is opened by the president, Mr. Y. M. Kurland, who greets the new parnasim. We are proceeding — says Mr. Kurland — to consider the budget in all seriousness, and therefore it is desirable that every item be considered calmly and to the point.
After the reading of the minutes there are read out
Declarations.
The first declaration is read by parnas Feiner (Left Poalei Zion), in which the draft budget is criticised as being, in his opinion, a clerical one that does not answer the needs of the broad masses of the people. We do not need — he says — a mikveh, but a bath-house according to the newest hygienic installations.
In the name of „Hitachdut“ parnas Rozinker reads a declaration in which it is stressed that he will vote against the budget, which is not [drawn up] in the light of Eretz Israel in upbuilding.
With a sharp criticism of the board there comes forward the vice-president, Mr. Landner, who says that the present budget hardly differs from the Agudah budgets up to now — the same system. The present kehilla board — says Mr. L. — combats, just like the Agudah, the bringing-in of outside meat, which causes meat to be dear; the new board is also introducing national assimilation: in the internal kehilla correspondence — says Mr. L. —
the Yiddish language is avoided,
in the budget not a single złoty has been allotted for Hebrew courses, above all for the children who learn in the general elementary [„powszechne“] schools, in the nests of assimilation.
President Rubinlicht takes the floor and says: instead of the vice-president Mr. Landner giving programmatic directions, he comes with accusations. It is a well-known thing that a sound building must first of all have a sound foundation; when 5 months ago we took over the kehilla's economy, we found a ruin, rotten from the sole of the foot to the head,
120 thousand zł. of debts,
the whole inventory of the community [„gmina“] — sequestrated, and the most urgent work of the presidium was only to hold back the waves of destruction. That has partly succeeded, and little by little we are proceeding to build up kehilla life. In the new budget there are three items, and if they are realised, that will be a sufficient satisfaction for us. These are: the kimcha [Passover-flour] campaign, which this year will no longer be conducted by the old, beggarly system, but will be covered from the community treasury; then the coal campaign, and completing the mikveh.
The reproach concerning the Yiddish language — hit me hard, but so the local supervisory authority demands of us.
Parnas Chaim Welner reads a Hebrew declaration in the name of „Mizrachi“ and „Torah va-Avodah“. Mr. Welner is for the budget; as regards the raising of the etat [the community tax] — he says — it will not fall as a burden on the poor masses.
Parnas Kleinman speaks out against the raising of the etat and proposes that the sitting be adjourned and that a budget committee be elected.
In the name of the Small Traders' Association parnas A. Y. Rechnitz declares that the raising of the etat is the outcome of the fact that the poverty among the Jewish masses is great, and so the community needs to have the necessary relief fund.
Dozor Hampel criticises the draft budget, and in particular the item of salaries for the rabbinate — which has — he says — enough side incomes, [and] takes payment for every religious function.
From his criticism of the rabbinate Mr. Hampel gallops off to Vienna, speaks with fervour of the heroic struggles of the Austrian revolutionaries, and he succeeds —
The fallen heroes are honoured by rising.
Parnas H. Ehrlich polemicises with the left-wing parnasim over their combating of religion — you — says Mr. Ehrlich — need not, on that account, come into the community, which is a religious institution. Passing over to the budget, Mr. Ehrlich points out that at the time when the subsidy for the Talmud Torah has been reduced by 1,500 zł., a sum of 5000 zł. has been allotted for a secular school which is to combat religion (interjection by Mr. Liwer: your „Agudah“ comrades did, after all, vote for the secular school).
Vice-president Landner is not content with his first appearance but continues his accusations. This time he dwells on the new kehilla activity, which consists of no more than carrying out the role of bailiffs [„executors“].
In Mr. Rubinlicht's reply he shatters, with the force of figures — the accusations of Mr. Landner.
The floor is given to the vice-president Mr. A. Liwer, who speaks with pathos of the former demoralisation that reigned in the kehilla in general and of the plans of rehabilitation for the future in particular. The Jewish masses — cries out Mr. Liwer — should not be frightened of the high etat, for our motto is: not to take etat from those who cannot give, but we want to take from the
Rich men with cold hearts
from those who pay for no communal or philanthropic institution whatsoever.
Then come the votes on the motions that were submitted; Kleinman's motion [printed "Kleimans"] is rejected.
Londner's motion concerning the Yiddish language is adopted in the following wording: "The board is called upon to intervene with the Jewish National Council regarding the circular (okólnik) of the local authority that the kehilla's correspondence be conducted in Polish; until an answer comes from the National Council, the kehilla's correspondence shall be conducted in Yiddish or Polish.
After the general criticism of the budget, which lasted no less than 4 hours, they finally proceed to the order of the day — to the budget itself.
Mr. Londner explains the position of the board regarding the reduction of the rabbinate salaries, and he calls on the council to vote for the reduction.
Councillor (parnas) Rozenblum submits a motion that, on account of the side incomes, the salaries of the rabbi and the dayanim (morei hora'ah) be struck out.
Councillor Welner cannot tolerate that the rabbinate salary was reduced by 10 per cent and the other officials by 5 per cent. He is in favour of the salary of all officials, the rabbinate among them, being reduced by 7 and a half per cent.
Councillor Rozinker makes a declaration that he will not vote for the rabbinate item.
Councillor Fajner is in favour of the rabbinate salaries being given for the benefit of an artisans' school.
A sharp incident breaks out when Mr. Liwer takes the floor and polemicises with the councillor Mr. Ryński, who speaks out against the reduction of the rabbinate salaries. The incident breaks out when Mr. Liwer censures the Rabbi, who sent the board a letter in which the Rabbi declares that "by the power of the holy Torah and
by the power of the government
he will not allow Cantor Żupowicz to lead prayers in the Będzin synagogue". Messrs. Ryński, Kurland and Piekarski shout that Mr. Liwer is interpreting the contents tendentiously. Mr. Liwer shouts still louder: let the letter be read. A tremendous tumult arises. Mr. Rubinlicht, who brings the letter, backs up Mr. Liwer's words, but Mr. Kurland keeps to his first opinion, that the Rabbi did not mean to threaten.
Speaking further against the reduction are Councillor Szenberg and the dozor (board member) Skoczylas. For the reduction — Councillor Herszlewicz.
At the vote Mr. Kurland can no longer control the situation, and the sitting is conducted forcefully by Mr. Rubinlicht.
The motion of Mr. Welner is adopted, that the reduction for all officials shall amount to 7 and a half per cent, with the amendment of Mr. Londner that the reduction does not apply to officials who earn up to 150 zł.
At 11 o'clock the sitting was closed.
The second sitting
which took place on Monday evening, was "rich in content" — in... demagogy, wisecracking and, above all, in "speeches". Every councillor, and the board members too, fulfilled the commandment of... talking. And not merely talked, but "all my bones shall say": they soared in the upper worlds, wrestled with the Sitra Achra, lamented the ruin of religion, split hairs over the laws of "Choshen Mishpat" and the Shulchan Aruch, and when that was still too little, they threatened with the Angel of Death...
And for what? For what did they squander 4 hours? — All because, of the 600 zł budgeted for rent for the premises of the beit din, half was to be struck out...
After the heated and passionate discussion of the question, the motion was rejected with the help of the "Mizrachi" votes.
At the sitting it came to a sharp exchange of views between the president of the board, Mr. Rubinlicht, and the president of the council, Mr. Kurland. The cause of it was Mr. Kurland, who displays too much "neutrality" in favour of the Agudah side.
At the item — premises for the rabbinate — the matter of the side incomes that the rabbinate has came up once again. In this connection some not very pretty stories were told, which are supposed to have occurred in matters of divorces (gittin). And the motion of Councillor Fajner is adopted, who says that the rabbinate is obliged to perform all
religious functions free of charge
for the poor, against a certificate from the board.
At the further items of the office, Councillor Rozinker moves to hang up in the premises of the kehilla
Herzl's picture
Councillor Ryński proposes the picture of the "Chofetz Chaim" of blessed memory — Councillor Kisner wants Jabotinsky's picture. Karl Marx and others are also mentioned. Mr. Londner's motion is adopted, that in the kehilla there should be pictures of the leading Jewish personalities.
At 2 at night the sitting is closed.
On Tuesday evening there took place
The third sitting.
which did not differ from the previous sittings; more correctly, the chaos was greater. The "gallery" was numerously attended, and those who could no longer get into the hall stormed the entrance door and often disturbed the course of the sitting; only with the help of the police was order restored to a certain degree.
Before the start of the sitting the chairman, Mr. Kurland, appeals that the incidents at the previous sittings should serve as a lesson, that the councillors should not use any drastic expressions and should treat the budget matters seriously.
At the item of expenses for the synagogue there came up again
The cantorate question.
Councillor (parnas) Goldsztajn is for striking out the vacant post (wakat) of a cantor amounting to 4,000 zł., and for the conductor and choir 1,500 zł., because such an atmosphere now prevails in the synagogue that engaging any cantor whatsoever may lead to further quarrels.
After a rather long discussion of the question, the proposal of Mr. Landner is adopted, that the sum of 4 thousand be reduced to 3,000, and for the choir 1,200 zł.
The same discussion developed over the salary of the beit-midrash cantor, for whom the board had budgeted, at the cantor's request, a sum of 500 zł. But the majority of the councillors — for the most part those who never stop shedding crocodile tears that the situation on the Jewish street is so bitter — were „consistent“ and raised the salary to 850 zł. The „providers“ even voted against Mr. Landner's proposal that the increase be given on condition that the cantor renounce his side incomes.
A fierce struggle was fought out over the item for the purchase of books for the beit midrash. In the discussion it became clear that: a) the large quantity of books of the beit midrash had been taken away by young men from various shtiblekh... and b) the Agudah representatives, who wanted the sum to be increased, did not come off with due honour when it was pointed out to them that the former Agudah rulers had budgeted for this purpose no more and no less than one złoty... Finally, after the storm and personal insults, the board's proposal remained — 150 zł.
At the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) item, Councillor Kisner brings in an
interpellation concerning the shochet Makower,
who committed a not very nice deed which brought damage to the kehilla treasury. Mr. K. proposes, as a fine, to reduce his salary by 25 per cent.
Councillor Herszlewicz demands that the vacant post of 2,400 zł. for a fourth shochet be struck out. Councillor Rozynker expresses himself in the same sense.
In the discussion Mr. Liwer delivers an hour-long speech about the sadly notorious shochtim affair in Będzin, characterises the negative attitude of the shochtim towards the kehilla and also towards the rabbinate, the wheeling and dealing to install 2 young little shochtim, and so on and so forth.
In the vote all the proposals brought in fall, and the item remains according to the board's draft.
Owing to the late hour (the clock shows 3...) the „spectacle“ is broken off.
—
The sum total.
The general sum total of the „nights of vigil“ is that hundreds of hours were taken away from people and used up on personal abuse and insults; for the kehilla council brought forth nothing at all of substance at the three sittings: all the items of the budget sections that were fixed went through according to the board's draft, with the exception that the reduction of the rabbinate salaries was lessened by 2½ per cent, and... the fallen revolutionaries in Austria were honoured.
To the Jewish Population of Będzin (Keren HaYesod appeal; local news)

[Będzin — Keren HaYesod; appeal.] Brothers!
We come to you, Jews of Będzin, with the same constant faith, with the same trust in you, at a moment of difficulties and disturbances, when the people is filled with deep worry and uneasy expectation. We are setting to work — to the campaign for Keren HaYesod. Precisely at the present time, when the Jewish people is struggling hard for its existence, in the time of the calamity in Germany, we come to you with tidings of comfort and encouragement.
The Land of Israel is today the only creative reality in Jewish life, the lighthouse that shows the way in our forlornness. The Jewish home is in a state of economic flowering; immigration has grown strongly. New agricultural settlements are arising; thousands of our brothers who have come from Germany are settling in the country; private capital streams in unceasingly and takes up new positions. All this was made possible mainly thanks to the national capital, which created the elementary preconditions for our work of upbuilding, which strengthened the absorptive capacity of the country, which trod out a path for private initiative. Now we see that our achievement would have been far greater had the answer of the Jewish people been different and had our means been greater.
Never yet has Keren HaYesod been so desperately necessary for the upbuilding of the country as at the present moment. Precisely now, when tens of thousands of our brothers in the lands of the Exile are knocking at the gates of the Land of Israel, when the impoverished masses of the people, the middle class and the artisans are striving towards the Land of Israel, when Jewish youth is straining towards pioneering deeds, it is necessary to broaden and strengthen many times over the economic and cultural foundations of our work of upbuilding, in order to make a broad immigration into the country possible.
We begin our work at a time of a hard political trial. To all the attacks on our movement we have one answer: to increase our efforts, to consolidate our positions, to create new ones; this will also strengthen our political struggle and protest. No temporary political disturbances can halt our work for the Land of Israel, nor will they weaken the unbroken courage and[?] readiness for sacrifice[?] of the Jewish people.
Our funds must remain outside the struggle of the parties. They have stood, and must continue to stand, above party quarrels and differences of opinion. The funds are that force which unites all parts of the Jewish people. All who are faithful to Zionism, all who ache and care for our work, must guard and strengthen their prestige and power.
Beginning this year's campaign for Keren HaYesod, we turn to you, Jews of Będzin:
Fulfil your duty to Keren HaYesod!
Polish Jewry, which is closely bound to the Land of Israel, which has created valuable, lasting achievements in the Land of Israel, which has won itself a name by its devotion to Keren HaYesod, will now, even more than ever, know how to appreciate the significance of Keren HaYesod for the further upbuilding of the country and will fulfil the historic task of our generation. Not a single proud and faithful Jew may be missing from the roll of honour of those who are building the Jewish land and the Jewish future.
Keren HaYesod Patronage in Będzin.
Sz. Fürstenberg, J. Gutman, L. Rubinlicht, Dr. S. Weinzieher, Eng. G. Weinzieher.

[Sosnowiec — rabbinate; investigation.]
On Friday Rabbi Frommer [„Fromer“; the Koziegłowy rabbi] was summoned to the investigating judge for an examination concerning a din-torah [rabbinical arbitration] which a certain Młynarski had had before the rabbi 2 years ago. Terrible Catastrophe in the Upper Silesian Coal Mines

[Upper Silesia — mine disaster.] On Wednesday at about 6 in the evening a terrible catastrophe occurred in the Upper Silesian coal mine "Karsten-Centrum", which lies on the Polish-German border. Two gigantic blocks of rock broke away and buried 11 workers. A feverish rescue operation then began. By means of knocking signals on a water pipe it was established that several of the buried men are still alive. At about 2 at night the rescuers succeeded in digging out 3 workers, but all 3 were already dead.
The feverish rescue operation is still going on without a break. The buried men are 800 metres under the ground. It is hard to foresee when the rescue crews will be able to get through to them. Around the site of the catastrophe stand the family members of the victims, and their weeping rises to the heavens. Over the towers of the coal mine hang black flags as a sign of mourning.

After the greetings from the ladies Ratman[?] (Sosnowiec), Margulies (Zawiercie) and Weksler (Częstochowa), there follow 2 lectures rich in content, on the WIZO movement and on the significance of the Jewish woman in the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. The Jewish Residents of Gzichów Ask for Protection. Jews with Bruised Heads Come to Ask the Kehilla Representatives for Help.

We have already written several times about the hooligan deeds that occur in the evening hours on Gzichowska Street in Będzin. Almost every evening the Jewish residents there are attacked, and to this day the proper police guard, which should keep order, has not been posted on that little street.
This week the attacks on peaceful Jews have again intensified; they were beaten by Hitler's comrades, who have their nest on that little street.
In the office of the kehilla the names were registered of: Yechezkel Szwarcbaum, Avraham Sztajnbok, Moshe Erlich, Leib Kuperberg and others, who were attacked by a group of hooligans at the said place.

Help "Beit Lechem" Carry Out the Passover Campaign.

This week we had the opportunity to become acquainted with the activity of the "Beit Lechem" society in Będzin. On the list of those registered to receive support for Passover we unfortunately also found, among others, a number of respectable families who only recently were themselves handsome givers...
— Does the society possess the capital needed for the Passover campaign? To our question the president, Mr. Bolimowski, declares that there is a deficit in the treasury of "Beit Lechem". The relief campaign for Passover — he says — depends on the support of the Jewish public.
It is therefore to be hoped that not a single person who has the means will refuse to help, so that "Beit Lechem" may this year too carry out its traditional relief campaign for Passover.
Conference on the Question of the Summer Timetable for the Trains in Zagłębie.

At the railway station in Sosnowiec a conference took place on the question of the summer timetable. The conference was conducted under the chairmanship of the special delegate of the Ministry of Railways, Mr. Diakiewicz[?]. Representatives of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, the school inspector and the interested circles also took part.
At the conference the question was dealt with first of all that a train should run from Katowice in the time between 1 and 1.30, after midnight. The question was also raised that the early-morning trains to Katowice, which are full of school youth and officials, should stop at the stations for more than 3 minutes, which is too little.
The representative of the Ministry of Railways promised that all the proposals put forward at the conference will be settled favourably.

The total sum of the ordinary and the extraordinary budget amounts to 1 million 166 thousand zł. A not inconsiderable sum in a time of crisis. In any case, the budget has been reduced, compared with last year, by 284,000 zł.

Which Taxes Must Be Paid This Month?

[Taxes — Ministry of Finance notice.] The Ministry of Finance draws the attention of the payers of the direct taxes to the following:
By the 15th of March the monthly instalment on account of the turnover tax for the year 1934 must be paid in.
This instalment amounts to as much as the tax comes to on the turnover that was achieved in the month of February in the commercial enterprises of the 1st and 2nd category and industrial enterprises of the 1st to the 5th category, and which keep proper commercial books.

Today's children...
The 16-year-old Jadwiga Zygmund and the 18-year-old Duda threw themselves under a train beyond Poznań and were killed.

Miss Zygmund and Duda fell in love and decided to marry. Since Duda's father was against it, the enamoured couple went off to Poznań. The parents reported this to the police, who sent out wanted notices after them.
