Institutions and Society

[Sosnowiec — institutions and society; boycott of German goods; old-age home; Linat haCholim.]
The founding of the Anti-Hitler Committee in Sosnowiec. — The "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] must be rescued. — The disrupted work and the tasks of "Linat haCholim".
The days of Chol haMoed were, as every year, used this time too for public deeds. Here and there consultations took place, general meetings and report meetings.
An account was taken of the state of affairs, so that one realised clearly what the situation looks like, and the practical upshot of it all is that one may no longer remain indifferent to all this; one must stand on guard and protect the interests of the people. The interests of the community.
At the district conference of the Anti-Hitler Committee in Zagłębie various resolutions were passed, among them also that committees be created in Zagłębie wherever they do not yet exist. It goes without saying that it is unheard of that until now there should not be committees everywhere; regrettably, however, it is a fact that they do not yet exist everywhere, and one must set about establishing them by all possible means. But it is still too little, we say, that such a committee will be created in Sosnowiec and the holiest promises will be made, while tomorrow everything will be forgotten, the hall will stand empty, and those who until now do business with the Hitler Germans will go on doing theirs with a quiet conscience, and, as until now, there will be no reaction to all of it later either. So what is the "firm" needed for? What for all the hullabaloo and noise? We do not need a paper committee for form's sake, just so that Sosnowiec may be counted among the towns that possess committees.
One must therefore see to it that the committees that have arisen perform for the people and fulfil their tasks; if not, then what is the point of the drumming and the ringing of bells? It is ridiculous to make a comedy of oneself. On the other hand, a town like Sosnowiec may by no means remain without a committee, which must, without any excuse, take upon itself the fulfilment of the necessary tasks. And in Sosnowiec there is much, much work for this committee, for in no town in Poland does one trade so openly and so freely in German goods as is done, to our shame, in Sosnowiec. And this committee, which has yet to come into being, must take upon itself the duty and the responsibility of rooting out the shameful deeds committed by our own brothers merely with the intent of filling their pockets, who do not reckon at all with the fact that they are disgracing Jewish pride.
Jewish and democratic Sosnowiec must, in its own name and in the name of Jewish self-respect, give a worthy answer to these disgracers and not allow Jewish Sosnowiec to be continually disgraced in this way merely because there are grown-up egoists who reckon with nothing and with no one.
That is the task that lies upon those who are to bring the necessary committee into being.
*
How long is it altogether since the building of the Sosnowiec "Moshav Zkenim" was shown [i.e. inaugurated]? It seems only yesterday. Just a short while ago it took place, and we admired the beautiful building, the aesthetic and hygienic execution, the devotion of those who put so much strength and effort into the institution — and yet we already have to cry out now that the institution is in danger of being closed. Is this not a disgrace for Jewish Sosnowiec? That already now, when everything is still so fresh and it seems that the young couple has only just begun to run the household, and already, already everything vanishes — regrettably that is a fact, a true and a sad one. The patrons, those who devoted themselves body and soul to the institution all their days, are already growing tired of doing so, seeing that the proper subsidies are lacking and that the town treats this necessary institution with a world-wide apathy, as if it did not exist at all.
It is unheard of that at a time when such a prestigious building stands, one so necessary for the town, it should be treated with such coldness. One certainly cannot demand that the institution be carried on the shoulders of a few individuals who have committed themselves to the necessary work.
Everywhere, in all towns and townlets, in all countries, a "Moshav Zkenim" belongs to the whole town, and as a municipal institution it must be maintained by the town. It must be subsidised both by the Magistrate [municipality] and by the Jewish community.
The town as such must see to it that its old people, whose lot it is to live out their last few years there, can stay quietly and modestly in the building especially designed for this purpose until their last breath, and that these helpless old people should not have to tremble lest, God forbid, they be driven out of there.
And if they are dispersed, where will they go? Where will they then have a place to lay down their heads and rest their old bones? Does one take account of this sad situation? Does one really not understand what a catastrophe that would be for these helpless old people?
And if yes, if we understand it, if we look a little deeper — what is achieved by it? What are we doing to maintain the institution?
But let us be honest and sincere and tell the truth as it is, and then one must admit that nobody dwells on the question and the matter interests nobody at all, so that, perhaps unintentionally, it is being let fall asleep.
And therefore a duty, a holy duty, lies upon our public workers, with the kehilla representation at their head, that measures be adopted to create a fund for the institution. One must not forget that such an institution may not depend on chance, i.e. by chance there will be money in the till — there will be something to get through the day with; and by chance there will be no money — the old people will, God forbid, have to go hungry.
Such an institution may not live on chance; it must have a budget fixed in advance, and the revenues must flow in regularly every month; otherwise one cannot run an old-age home.
Let our public workers understand this, and let them, with this awareness, energetically set about reorganising the necessary work, so that one should not once again have to start storming that there is a danger of locks being hung on the institution's gates.
••
"Linat haCholim" too held its general meeting during Chol haMoed, and as usual the so-called "[—] heads" [i.e. the notables] stayed at home.
There too we hear the cry of woe that the institution is treated with apathy and cannot progress properly, in spite of there being so much urgent work, and that the ambulatorium [outpatient clinic] must be enlarged. It seems that precisely this branch is so necessary for the whole town without exception, and yet so little interest is taken in it. Sosnowiec is no longer the almost village-like settlement of the past, so that the ambulatorium always has enough work and needs new instruments and proper equipment — so why should the town remain cold towards this very institution? One must take an interest in it, so that it can play a decisive role in everyday life.
It is interesting that complaints were made at the meeting that the institution suffers, apart from the municipal apathy, also from its competing "little shops". It is characteristic that the suburbs too have their own Linat haCholims, which act on their own, so that as soon as [printed "gur", for "nor"] a celebration takes place in town, everyone runs around with plates and collection boxes; the public does not know which is the true institution and treats all of them together with the greatest light-mindedness, so that the prestige has fallen to the "highest" degree, and it is no wonder either. One must not allow there to be "little shops" with one and the same name and one and the same aim, and the blame must unconditionally be ascribed to the Sosnowiec "Linat haCholim", which as an institution ought not to have tolerated this abnormal phenomenon.
And if proper order is to be introduced, all the Linat haCholims must be concentrated in one place, and only the Sosnowiec institution shall have the right to collect money, where strict discipline and order shall also prevail; only then can proper order be created. Otherwise it is a pity to appeal to the inhabitants, who cannot tell which institution is the "genuine" one and which the "false" one, the imitation.
A duty lies upon the management of the Sosnowiec "Linat haCholim" to bring order into this harmful phenomenon and to root out the abnormal growth.
Dr. Papuri.
The Participation of the Jews of Będzin in the Polish Freedom Struggles

Moshe Feinkind [Mosze Fajnkind].
(On the 140th anniversary of Kościuszko's Uprising.)
The Jews of Będzin have a very[?] fine patriotic past, having taken part in all the Polish freedom struggles.
Belonging in former times to the Kraków Voivodeship and being also close to the royal residence, the „Kraków patriotism“ had, in all likelihood, a great influence on the Jews of Będzin, who always showed themselves to be loyal children of the Polish soil.
This fine tradition passed on to the latest generations too.
One need only leaf through the yellowed pages of the historical records, which are found among us and scattered in the archives and have not yet seen the light of day, and one truly obtains a fine picture of the Jews of Będzin, who inscribed their names in golden letters in the history of Poland's liberation.
It is not my task today, within the framework of a newspaper article, to relate here all the details connected with Będzin's participation in the historic struggles for Poland's freedom. For, I must admit, I have not managed to exhaust and discover everything. And readers will have to content themselves with the following short sketches, which will give „very little“ [sic], at least a small picture of the sacrifices the Jews of Będzin made in those days when the town was threatened with the danger of being conquered by the enemy.
* * *
We shall proceed in order.
When Stefan Batory — who was very well disposed towards the Jews of Będzin, permitting them for the first time to live in the „makom“, i.e. in the town proper, and to conduct business and trade alongside the Christians — died (1586[?]), a part of the szlachta, led by the Zborowski family, strove, to spite the Zamoyskis, to hand the Polish throne to the young Austrian Archduke Maximilian, a brother of the Austrian Emperor Rudolf II.
A great struggle then flared up between the magnates Zamoyski and Zborowski over the Polish throne. The royal election (elekcja), held outside Warsaw, was surrounded by two armed armies belonging to the two sides. Each side elected its protégé king. Thus the so-called „Black Front“ (Zamoyski's party) elected Sigismund (Vasa) as king, while the so-called „General Circle“[?] (Zborowski's party) elected the Austrian Maximilian.
Maximilian hurried and came with a large army to Kraków to take the Polish throne by force; while besieging the whole Kraków area (1587), Będzin was then threatened by an attack of Maximilian's soldiery. The walls surrounding the town had to be strengthened and repaired against the enemy; the burgrave Miszczkowski had no money, so the rabbi of the time, R' Natan Meitelis (Matteles!), hastily collected among the Jews a sum of 50 gold ducats, and with this money the burgrave Miszczkowski, to whom the castle belonged at the time, repaired the fortress walls; and when Maximilian's army set about besieging and conquering the town, it was — thanks to the Jews — a truly hard piece of work.
Incidentally, I wish to note that, as far as I know, the present-day generations who also bear his name, Meitlis (corrected), and live in Zagłębie to this day, are said to descend from that patriotic Będzin rabbi.
* * *
We also have information about a second instance of Będzin patriotism.
It took place at the time of Kościuszko's revolution (1794).
Kościuszko, the greatest Polish national hero, at the time when he solemnly assumed command of the uprising against Catherine II on the Kraków Market Square (Rynek), simultaneously turned, in the Old Synagogue in Kazimierz, to the Jews, asking that they too take part in the freedom struggle against the enemy and support him for the freedom of all.
After Kraków came[?] the neighbouring town of Będzin, again the first, where the Jews responded to Kościuszko's appeal.
Rabbi R' Yaakov Natan set about agitating among the Jews to enlist in the revolutionary formations; he also collected money and in person spied on the Russian positions for the benefit of Kościuszko's troops.
The „anonymous rabbi“, as R' Yaakov Natan was called in Polish circles, did not keep silent afterwards either, even after the suppression of the unfortunate revolution, and when the Prussians had occupied the Będzin district, they rendered him harmless by putting him in prison in Schlossberg.
Only when, thanks to Napoleon's victory at Friedland, the Poland occupied by the Germans and others became, under the Treaty of Tilsit (July 1807), a free duchy under the rule of the Saxon King Frederick Augustus, did the „anonymous rabbi“ and great Polish patriot manage to free himself from his dark captivity.
But hardly had R' Yaakov Natan tasted freedom than he went on working for the Polish national army, which operated together with Napoleon's army against the Austrians etc. (1807—9).
Because of his self-sacrificing life and struggle against Poland's enemies, folk imagination wove around him a wreath of legends, namely that R' Yaakov Natan went about in rags and tatters, giving everything away to the poor without distinction[?] of faith, that he was a miracle-worker, etc.
That R' Yaakov Natan was something of a mysterious person — there can be no two opinions about that.
Whether he was a rabbi or a rebbe in Będzin — that can indeed be put under a big question mark.
(Conclusion follows.)
Jewish Politics Is a Desert

In the present hard times, when all the blackest clouds have gathered over our heads and it looks as if the Jewish people stands before a terrible catastrophe — at such a time we ought to have singled out from among us the best people of our milieu, to be our advocates (melitzei-yosher), defenders and guardians against all evil.
Such representatives we do not have — for where could we get them?
In former years, in the ghetto, the Jewish shtadlan and politics-maker used to come down from above, with a mandate [?] from the ruling authority, which had come to know him through various speculative business dealings. Today, however, we must after all choose our politicians ourselves. And from where are we to choose them?
Among the nations of the world, local public work is a stage on the way to general politics. If a man appears in the community with intelligence, with energy, with a public sense, perhaps also with strong elbows, he begins to receive mandates in the local representative bodies, from which he already strolls over into general state politics.
It is just like a craftsman who tries out his worker by first giving him a simple piece of work, and if that succeeds, gives him more complicated, responsible jobs.
With us, however, it is not so. In our local milieu there still dominate, first and foremost, forces that have scant connection with the wider world: religion and philanthropy.
A great part of the Jewish intelligent forces is occupied with maintaining the Torah among Jews: people study themselves en masse, organise campaigns and societies to support the poor Torah scholars. All this is very fine; the Torah is indeed a guarantee for the survival of the Jewish people in the future; Orthodoxy, it is said, is the reservoir of the best forces of the Jewish people. But to draw from this reservoir already now, for Jewish politics — that cannot be done.
A very large place in Jewish life is taken up by philanthropy, charity (tzedakah). The specific living conditions of a separate community, a community within a community, created the necessity for a peculiar self-protection, developed the Jewish feeling of compassion and called into being the broad network of charity societies, which did not let the Jew go under in the life of exile.
But charity is not politics; it possesses neither the psyche nor the means of politics. And even if it conducts itself according to all the rules of democracy, with public accountability and the strictest internal discipline, it can at most rise only to political forms — its substance is something quite different. And just as no cabinet-maker can come out of a tailor's workshop, so no politician is reared in a charity society.
And these two parts of our communal life take up with us the lion's share of our intelligence, acumen and public-mindedness. Perhaps because they are still the strongest weapons for our protection in exile; and the influence of this psyche, of this mentality, is quite strong in our communal life.
Of course, the last few decades of the surrounding political life have politicised the Jewish community too, and have reared cadres of people who engage in real politics, internal and external; but the characteristic features of the main factors of our public life are noticeable here as well.
Just as pious Jews splintered the Jewish congregation into many study-houses and minyanim in order to have as many gabbai posts and aliyot as possible; just as little societies of every kind used to spring up among us like mushrooms after rain; just as the individualism of the Jewish rabbi, scholar, rich man, strongman (takif), tax-farmer (baal-takse) and the like used to dominate the whole of ghetto life — so too in the newly arisen Jewish world politics we are splintered into dozens of little parties and little groups, and our whole thinking apparatus functions in a very narrow, parochial [?] way, regardless of the democratic forms to which we try to adapt ourselves.
And as a result we have remained utterly without leaders, without politicians.
For a certain time we complained that our best, most intelligent, most disciplined and best-trained forces were being given over to the Zionist movement, which is indeed very important, but still not everything; and to fight for our existence, for our political rights, we no longer have any representatives. Now the plague of the exile mentality has spread into Zionism itself — apparently because it has become real and answers concrete questions of life — there too things have been brought to chaos, to personal tearing and friction, which completely stifle the ideal itself.
But worse still is our local political struggle. Here there is complete bankruptcy along the whole front. The hundreds of thousands of Jews who must form the political representatives out of their own midst have created their economic organisations with explicitly philanthropic aims — to help and rescue the individual. Just as the sick man turns to the Linat ha-Tzedek for medicine, so the man who has suffered materially turns to his association for an intervention, advice, substantial financial help; and in exactly this philanthropic direction flows the whole of our trouble-laden politics. Whether it rescues one individual or a thousand [?] individuals, it is no more than charity — both in its essence [?] and in its forms and means.
And this very philanthropic psyche spreads over all the branches of our public activity. One sends a representative to a kehilla, and he receives one directive: to obtain [?] a subsidy for this or that society, for this or that community, for patents [trade licences], for [—] [?], for Sabbath observance — quietly. Of course, every parnas will pay his dues to those who sent him; but as for reforming, secularising the whole policy of the kehilla — there is not enough understanding for that even among the most progressive of our representatives.
And as the tasks, so their bearers. Had one wished to realise ideas of broader scope in the kehilla, one might perhaps have had to look for suitable persons for that; but to carry out these petty-bourgeois demands one can be the capable fellow [?] oneself — and indeed one sends nobody, one goes oneself.
So it is in the city council, too, and so in the Sejm.
People once racked their brains over what one must fight against: the plight of Judaism (tzarat ha-yahadut) or the plight of the Jews (tzarat ha-yehudim). Today we know of neither, only of the plight of the Jew — the need [?] of the individual Jew: philanthropy.
Only this do the masses demand, and only this do the leaders promise — they promise and do not give, because they have not grown up to politics at all.
In the present hard times we ought to have had leaders of Jewish grand politics, but our little circles and little kloyzes have reared for us charity gabbaim, modern [?] strongmen and shtadlanim.
Jewish politics is a terrible desert, where we drag ourselves about without a goal, and none of the leaders knows the way to a fruitful [?] free life.
P. K.
Social Insurance. — Registration Rules.

[General — social insurance, workers' rights.] Registration rules.
The insurance institution [Ubezpieczalnia Społeczna, the social-insurance fund] accepts registrations of newly hired workers from the enterprises and also from the workers themselves. As regards the formal side of registration, it must be established that the duty to register lies indeed with the employer; on the other hand, the worker too has the right to register himself, especially in cases where the employer wants to wriggle out of the duty for one reason or another.
A registration made by the worker himself gives the worker the same insurance rights as registration by the employer; it does not, however, release the employer from his own particular duty to register the worker, and the prescribed fine of 5 hundred złoty is imposed in any case when the duty is not carried out.
On this occasion it is also worth pointing out the difference between simply not wanting to register a hired worker and forcing him to give up his right to belong to the insurance institution, threatening him, for example, with removal from his post if he should nevertheless insist on being insured with the insurance institution.
Whereas in the first case the law provides only a fine of up to 500 zł., for the second offence it threatens arrest of up to 3 months.
Speaking of the duty to report, it must also be added that every employer who sets up a new enterprise or takes on workers for the first time is obliged at the same time to report the enterprise to the insurance institution.
———
In all cases where the law provides for fines, when the fine cannot be collected owing to poverty, the fine is commuted to arrest.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

The "Modrzejowska Lane"...
— What's new?
— How are things going?
— Have they come to a settlement?
These very questions were put to me as soon as I had set foot on Sosnowiec ground, last Sunday afternoon.
Having no idea whatever what it was about, and seeing the melancholy faces of those who put these questions to me, the thought occurred to me: what has happened here? Perhaps the [Zionist] Actions Committee has moved its session from Jerusalem to Sosnowiec? Or maybe the League of Nations' mixed commission for minority rights has come to Sosnowiec to put an end to the "7-year war"? Or what do I know? Can one say what may happen in these abnormal times on an ordinary Sunday in Sosnowiec, in the already world-famous town?...
Later, coming into the "heart" of the "Modrzejowska" [ulica Modrzejowska, the main Jewish street of Sosnowiec], the hard question was answered for me.
It became clear to me that a rich Jewish woman had died in the town. And it is over the deceased that there is such tumult and noise in Modrzejowska Lane...
The lane looks like a concentration camp: everyone is out in the street and everyone is talking and telling stories; big and small, young and old are "busy" with this inheritance
— It's already at 8 thousand...
— 8,500.
Suddenly the news bursts through the "packed crowd":
— They've already come to terms.
— Really? How much?
— Ten thousand five hundred...
The inheritance enters a new phase; little groups form in the street, big ones and small ones, and undisturbed by the policeman people stand there and pleasantly tell little stories... well-known little stories about Sosnowiec "big-heartedness"... and contemplating the general picture in the street, I gain "respect" for the town of Sosnowiec, merely because it possesses
— Modrzejowska Street...
The street is the seal proving that Sosnowiec is truly a big city. For example, New York is famous for its — Broadway lane, Paris for the "Pletzl", London — for Whitechapel, Warsaw — for the Nalewki, Łódź — for Bałuty, and Sosnowiec
— for the Modrzejowska...
A trifle, the "Modrzejowska"? It is the inner essence, the content, the whole substance of Sosnowiec's Jewish social life. In the street rabbis are decided upon, discussions are held on all general and Jewish questions, a "stock-exchange rate" for a plot of land is quoted, even the kehilla budget is decided in the street. Therefore our opinion is that Sosnowiec should be proud of its "Pletzl"
— "the Modrzejowska Lane"...

What Are We?...
...Again voices are heard in the Jewish street, again bad tidings arrive from Hitler-land: how our brothers there are tortured and bestially murdered only because they are Jews, their goods and possessions are plundered because they are "half-humans".
And the people of Israel is again called upon to use its only weapon
— Boycott!
And from the headquarters in Warsaw emissaries were sent out to encourage "the people" not to buy any German goods made with Jewish blood, not to have any dealings with those who spit in our faces, with those who want to sell us goods produced with the money that the barbarians robbed by force from our helpless brothers.
And they came, the public emissaries, to Zagłębie too, to talk things over with the Jews of Zagłębie, especially with the Jews of Sosnowiec, about the great danger that threatens us if Hitler stays in power. The delegate, editor Wolkowicz, depicts the sad prospects awaiting us at the end of days... also the bitter present, and he comes to the conclusion that we are on the brink of destruction; but suddenly I hear beneath me a Mephistophelian laugh.
— Ha? What are you laughing at? — we ask angrily, at such a serious moment?
— I'm laughing at this, — he says, — that you emissaries of the people always come with sermons to "the people", and the few you leave in peace... Why — he cries out — are the merchants who to this day do business with the Hitler gang not put in the pillory? Just last week a Będzin iron merchant (his name is in the possession of the editors) bought a large consignment of German steel-works products; but he is not the only criminal, many in number are here [?] in Zagłębie; like beasts of prey they swoop over the heads of the Jewish victims and sate their lusts
— with goods stained with Jewish blood...
Reflecting on this [?], I recall the question of Adv. Wartgłas [?], who asks in his article about the German boycott:
— "Are we human beings, or simply a gang of fences [?], chasing after the profit it can get from the murderers by buying stolen goods from them"?
Dear readers, give an answer;
— What are we?...

The Foundation Is Missing...
In the new premises of the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec.
A buzzing as of bees. The assembled merchants [—] and puzzle over a very important problem
— the ten-groszy coins...
All the questions that stand at the summit of the world no longer exist in these premises; the only worry that occupies [?] the minds of the hundreds of members is just how to solve the question
— of the ten-groszy coins.
Now the chairman of the association takes the floor and reports on the new decree of the industrial law, on the new tax law and on other calamities lying in wait for the heads of the Jewish merchant class.
After the report the speaker turns to the assembly, asking them to put questions to him about the new laws.
And in the hall there was indeed one single person who put a question to the speaker, a question truly very characteristic, which can serve as an illustration of what interests the Jewish "kupiec" [merchant]...
The question itself; "Why did Gimpel pay one złoty for an appeal and Todros a whole one and a half złoty"?
Well, if someone asks one must answer — the chairman answered that, firstly, Reb Todros is not a member of the association, and secondly the association has to maintain premises, a secretariat, etc.
The answer did not entirely satisfy me, because the chairman ought to have explained to this "what's-this" questioner that the association must also think about making the Jewish merchant, who possesses commercial abilities, more conscious. In organizational matters he is still quite backward
— the foundation is missing...
Who Is to Blame?

(Around the [question?] of the newly adopted law).
The press sharply criticizes the Central Craftsmen's Union and its leaders and reproaches them that they are to blame for the industry law that has just been adopted.
The position of the Central Craftsmen's Union was, after all, clearly defined by the resolutions adopted and afterwards printed in the press — resolutions adopted already a year ago at the 4th Craftsmen's Congress as well as at the district conferences in the voivodeship towns; so the question arises: why did the press keep silent then, when there was still time to change the position, and sound the alarm now, when it is already too late? The sharpest criticism is voiced against the qualification certificates for craftsmen, which have already been in force since 1927. That the craftsmen are supporters of these qualification certificates is no news, because new workshops keep springing up whose owners do not hold these certificates of competence, and thereby they do harm to the trade group concerned.
On the other hand, [the law] brings the so-called compulsory economic craftsmen's associations, which can be introduced at the demand of 10 persons who wish to create a voluntary economic organization; it will have to approach the Union of Chambers of Crafts with a proposal that the Union submit to the Ministry to convert the voluntary organization into a compulsory organization. On this question the Chambers of Crafts of the individual voivodeships will have their say, as will the guilds of the trades concerned, and if the trade in question realizes that belonging to the compulsory organization will bring harm to that trade, it will have the possibility to oppose it. We must acknowledge the truth that the leaders of the Centrale were throughout against introducing compulsory associations. They strongly warned against this experiment, but they had to reckon with the voices of the organized masses.
At the Kielce craftsmen's convention last year, comrades Rosner, attorney Herszberg and others declared in the name of the executive that they were against compulsory guilds, but they were supported only by individuals, and against their will it was adopted almost unanimously by 100 delegates to approach the government about introducing compulsory guilds.
At the 4th Craftsmen's Congress, too, the leaders of the Central Craftsmen's Union in Warsaw sharply opposed adopting a resolution demanding compulsory guilds, and only thanks to the Galician delegates did the congress adopt almost unanimously the resolution demanding the introduction of compulsory guilds.
The Jewish craftsman has nothing to lose; his impoverishment is so great that he has no strength to help himself, therefore he demands a law that should help him. The Jewish craftsman is being pushed out of his positions, his independence is a fiction; the Jewish craftsman is in the great majority dependent on the merchant: when the merchant wants, he gives him work and dictates him a price. In the shoe trade, for example, the Jewish shoemaker and the uppers-stitcher (kamashn-shtefer) are today so degraded and enslaved that it is an ideal to earn one gulden [złoty] a week.
In the tailoring trade the independent tailor is gradually being liquidated; his place is taken by the chałupnik [home-worker], who works with his family somewhere in an attic room, for the worst wages and under the worst conditions. On the day he works he barely earns enough to eat. The merchant, having no obligation to provide for his chałupnik, tries to procure as many such [?] as possible, although he has work for each of them for only one day a week; but it pays him, because in this way he can push down the price. From this one can see that the situation of the craftsmen is so sad that their freedom is a freedom to die of hunger.
This cry of woe was heard at craftsmen's conventions, and when the Galician craftsmen, who stand culturally higher than ours, threw out the slogan of compulsory organizations, they found favourable ground. They had lived over a hundred years under compulsory co-operatives together with Christians, and even in impoverished Galicia they had bread; only since 1927, since free guilds were introduced among them too, have they been dying of hunger together with us — so they argued.
We are, however, categorical opponents of creating these organizations together with the Endeks [National Democrats], and this we clearly provided for in the resolution of the 4th Craftsmen's Congress, because we demand our rights as Jews.
Therefore we reject the merchants' claims against us that we are to blame for it. For the law applies to merchants too, and on their behalf the Chambers of Commerce as well as the merchants' organizations had their say.
H. L. Goldsztejn.
Bibliographical Notes

Handbook of Modern Perfumery and Cosmetics Manufacture, by Dr. S. Rotsztejn, 184 pages, large book format, 5 tables, „Technochem“ [?] publishing house, Vilna 1934.
At a moment when the Yiddish book is going through a very severe crisis, one must certainly welcome the fact that Dr. Rotsztejn has now published a technical book in the Yiddish language, which is based on scientific, theoretical and practical foundations.
Abroad such books are published by the thousands; there are special, large publishing houses there which deal exclusively with publishing popular technical books. Here, however, this field has been completely neglected.
Dr. Rotsztejn's handbook is written in a clear, popular Yiddish and is so well edited that it enables anyone — even those who have no knowledge whatsoever of chemistry — to start immediately the manufacture of the most varied cosmetic and perfumery articles, on a small or large scale.
The book is divided into 2 parts;
In the first part the author describes precisely all the raw and auxiliary materials needed in modern perfumery and cosmetics manufacture. This is truly very important, so that in practical work the beginner should not handle the raw materials blindly and mechanically, but with exact knowledge and understanding of their most important properties. Only in this way is it possible to combine the most varied materials consciously and to work with success.
In the second, practical part of the book the author has given the newest, [?] recipes for the most varied perfumery and cosmetic articles, such as: many kinds of perfumes, eaux de Cologne, hair and face waters, toothpastes, soaps, powders and mouthwashes, face and hygienic powders, creams, make-up, nail varnishes, cosmetic bath salts and many others.
The main thing, however, is the fact that the practical execution of the recipes is set out so clearly and precisely that anyone who can merely read Yiddish will certainly be able to produce all these articles.
It is evident that the author has put much diligence, knowledge and practical experience into his handbook, and one must admit that he has succeeded in creating a first-class popular technical book.
After the text some tables, very important from the practical point of view, and various explanations are appended.
In the hard struggle for work, for a piece of bread, Dr. Rotsztejn's handbook can bring help to very many people. Cosmetic and perfumery articles are nowadays no longer a luxury, but mass products, which spread more and more with every day. Making these articles — even only in the form of home manufacture — can give new livelihood opportunities to many thousands of Jewish families.
It is therefore to be hoped that the handbook will have the success it deserves and will penetrate the broadest strata of the Jewish population, giving it a chance for productivization and at the same time for good livelihood opportunities.
Eng. L. Rozenszajn [?].
(Lecturer in chemistry at the Vilna Jewish Technikum).
New circulars and laws

[Poland — new circulars and laws.]
Signboard tax.
Because doubts have arisen, the Ministry of the Interior explains that the signboards of shops in which only tobacco products (bearing the state emblem) are sold are also subject to the tax on signboards and advertisements.
—o—
General duty to be vaccinated against smallpox.
In Dz. U. [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] No. 13 a law has been published under which all children born must be vaccinated against smallpox for the first time before the end of their first year, and for the second time before the end of their 7th year. Adults too may be made subject to the smallpox-vaccination duty if it turns out that they have not been vaccinated a second time.
Both the vaccination itself and the issuing of the corresponding certificates are free of charge.
Violation of this provision is punishable by a fine of up to 200 zł. or arrest of up to 14 days.
—o—
Stamp duty on applications for permits to transport the dead.
Under an ordinance of the Minister of Social Welfare, applications for permits to transport the dead must be paid with a stamp to the amount of 40 zł. If it concerns moving the body to another grave in the same cemetery, 60 zł. must be paid.
On the other hand, for permits to exhume a body from a grave and transport the deceased abroad (Eretz Israel), a stamp duty of 80 zł. is charged on the applications.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shemini)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemini
The Portion
—o—
a) "Draw near to the altar" (Lev. 9:7)
"For Aaron was ashamed and afraid to approach. Moses said to him: Why are you ashamed? For this you were chosen." Rashi.
Moses said to Aaron: Why are you ashamed? Already you feel shame? For this you were chosen — that is why you are a leader: so that you should endure disgrace and contempt. For this you were chosen: this is the reward of a leader — shame and slights... Rabbi Yechiel Meir of Gostynin.
* * *
"We are sated with contempt" (Ps. 123:3) — a rabbi's lot is to have his fill of contempt... Rabbi Yaakov Weissfrat[?] of Kraśnik.
* * *
The Gemara says: "Whoever rises to greatness is forgiven all his sins." The question arises: why should a leader who rises to greatness be forgiven his sins?
But in Berakhot 12 the Gemara says that shame wipes away sins: "Whoever commits a transgression and is ashamed of it is forgiven all his sins." And one who rises to greatness is exposed to such humiliations that all his sins are forgiven him on account of the shame... Imrei Chen.
—o—
b) "And Moses diligently inquired for the goat of the sin-offering, and behold, it was burnt" (Lev. 10:16)
"Half of the Torah in words: darosh on this side and darash on that side."
When the Torah is divided — darosh on this side and darash on that side — one interprets the Torah this way and the other interprets it the opposite way, then "behold, it was burnt": thereby, God forbid, the Torah is burnt. That is our sin, that "darosh darash Moshe" — when one interprets the Torah thus, the other interprets it the opposite way... R. Yosef Kahanowicz[?].
—o—
c) "And when Moses heard that, it was good in his eyes" (ibid., 20)
Once Rabbi Natan David of Szydłowiec came to the Rabbi of Sanz (Nowy Sącz) for Parashat Shemini. At the "tish" the Rabbi of Sanz honoured the Szydłowiec rabbi with "saying Torah". But the Szydłowiec rabbi did not want to say Torah in the presence of his master, and on the other hand he did not want to refuse either, so he said this Torah:
— "And Moses heard, and it was good in his eyes": Moses preferred that Aaron should say Torah and he should listen, rather than that he should say Torah and Aaron listen... Mishenet Moshe.
—o—
d) "These are the beasts which ye shall eat" (Lev. 11:2)
The "Noda BiYehuda" once met the Baal Shem Tov. A fowl about which there was a ritual question was brought before the "Noda BiYehuda". The Besht sniffed at the fowl and said: it is kosher. Afterwards the "Noda BiYehuda" began to study the question, and it indeed turned out to be kosher. The "Noda BiYehuda" asked him: How did you know that the fowl was kosher? The Besht answered: I looked at the fowl, sniffed it as well, and saw that no spirit of impurity rests upon it, so I knew that it was kosher...
To this the "Noda BiYehuda" said: Now the saying in Shabbat 138b is explained to me: "A woman will in future take a loaf of terumah and go round the synagogues and study houses to know whether it is impure or pure." The question arises: why will she have to bring the loaf of terumah into the study house? Will it not be enough for her to come merely to ask a question? What does one see[?] from a loaf of terumah? But just before, the Gemara says "The Torah will in future be forgotten in Israel": the Torah will be forgotten, there will be no rabbis, only rebbes. So people will bring the loaf of terumah to the rebbes to look at it and sniff it, [to know] which spirit rests upon it, a spirit of purity or a spirit of impurity... Parashat Mordechai.
—o—
e) "And the stork" (ibid., 19)
Well, a man being a hasid — says a misnagdic jest — can still be tolerated; but a h-a-s-i-d-a [stork / female hasid], a Jewish woman who plays the hasid — she already belongs among the unclean birds..
—o—
f) "Every beast which divideth the hoof, and is not cloven-footed" (ibid., 26)
On this Rashi says: "Such as the camel, whose hoof is split above but joined below."
So the camel counts as one that divides the hoof. The question arises: above (11:4) the verse says explicitly: "the camel, because he cheweth the cud but divideth not the hoof."
A wonder! R. Shmuel Stacir[?].
—o—
Avot, Chapter One.
g) "Love work and hate lordship [rabbanut]" (Mishnah 10)
Because usually, when a craftsman rises even a little, he at once has a craving for rabbanut, for authority, for being a gabbai.. Ezor Eliyahu.
—o—
h) "Not study is the main thing but deed" (17)
Rabbi Mordechai of Nadwórna used to say: "Happy is he who comes here with his learning in his hand (Pesachim 50a)" — not merely his learning in his mouth but in his h-a-n-d: he must have realised his learning with his hands, not merely preached it...
He also used to say: "Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah?" (Chullin 139b) — one can be a Haman from the Torah: to be ostensibly a Torah Jew, to have studied Torah, but in good deeds — to be a Haman... a wicked villain... Tiferet Mordechai.
* * *
In the blessing of the new month we say "a life in which there is fear of Heaven and fear of sin" and further: "a life in which there will be in us love of Torah and fear of Heaven" — why fear of Heaven once again?
Fear of Heaven a second time together with love of Torah, because usually one who is a ben-Torah thinks that thereby he has already fulfilled his duty, and it is precisely he who lacks fear of Heaven...
Devarim Nechmadim.
Paris Invites Jewish Merchants.

A conversation with the French Minister-President [Prime Minister]. From our correspondent Z. Haber (Paris).
"When people talk anywhere in the world about Paris, everyone tells of the thousands of amusements that are to be seen[?] here, of the hundreds of venues, of Montmartre, Montparnasse and many other parts of our city, which all people go to look at when they come to Paris. But it occurs to no one that we do not, after all, live off these places of amusement — that we are a people that works hard and bitterly and has created an industry that takes up the competitive struggle with all, all the greatest industrial states of the whole world."
Thus the French Minister-President Lebrun complained to me when he recently received me in his chancellery.
— You, as a representative of Jewish newspapers, can after all have a practical effect. Jews are not in the world merely for amusement. Jews are, after all, a practical people of trade and industry. You can tell them that we invite them to us, to Paris.
On 9 May this year we open the great Paris Fair, which lasts fifteen days. Here at the fair they shall see that we manufacture and supply everything that people could possibly need. In the last thirty years we have developed so strongly that there is nothing in the world in which we are not better and cheaper than all competitors in the four corners of the earth.
How far we have risen in our production you can see from the fact that in the year 1904 there were barely 497 exhibitors at our fair, and now more than eight thousand exhibitors from French industry will come to us, and besides that many exhibitors from 33 other countries. Last year more than two million buyers from the whole world came to our fair.
We are making all preparations for our present fair. On all railways one gets large discounts; on the French railways fifty per cent.
Let Jewish merchants come to us; we will provide them with guides and interpreters who will show them everything, and we will advise them in all matters.
They can buy and sell here, they can obtain new connections with our colonies; we will be of help to everyone in all that concerns trade[?], and we will be glad to see them here — they will surely not regret it.
A Happy Passover Was Not Meant To Be

(From the local tales.)
Sosnowiec is a town of "rich happenings"[?], of many events and sensations. It is already a foregone thing that every eve of a holiday something must happen. Last Passover eve such an incident took place in Sosnowiec.
Not everyone knows the young woman S., and not everyone knows the story of how she acquired herself, by force, a bit of a husband, and with what tricks she led him to the wedding canopy. She is truly, people say, a capable woman, for she managed to take a young man who is younger than she by no more and no less than 15 years, and to lure him into the sack. It did not help at all that the groom's parents held their ground and protested against[?] the match. One fine bright day she snatched the groom, went off with him to Będzin and held the wedding there.
Only some time after the wedding did the groom learn the bride's exact age. Without powder, without rouge and without dye he saw her true figure. Her "artificial" (sztuczne) teeth and the padding[?] meant to give her a fine figure suddenly opened his eyes, and he began to work out a plan to take to his heels. He hit upon a ruse and one day declared to her: know, my little wife, I am going to Palestine. Here there is nothing to do and nothing to take up. I will go first and afterwards bring you over.
The "young" wife lost her wits precisely here: she untied her knipl [savings bundle], gave her husband as much money as he wanted and joyfully saw him off to the train.
Time passed, and the husband vanished like a stone into water; there was already a rumour that he had married a girl there. But she did not despair, and when she finally received a letter from the Land of Israel she taunted her enemies. The letter to her was full of love, and it said that the husband longed for her and hoped that already by Passover she would be a queen and be together with him in the Land of Israel. He only asked her, at the same time, for a small favour — that meanwhile, until he had settled in better in Palestine, she should send him a little more money. He gave her to understand in the letter that the Land of Israel is a country with a dear currency, and therefore one needs somewhat more money to make a living.
The "young" wife again untied her knipl and sent money, not heeding the advice of her relatives that the husband only meant to swindle her out of her money.
She prepared for the journey to Palestine, made an effort to look better and prettier. But in vain, poor thing, was her effort. A few days before Passover she again received a letter from her husband. But instead of the entry[?] papers she had expected, she took out of the envelope with trembling hands some incomprehensible letter written in script letters[?] with many little dots.
She immediately ran off with the letter to her relatives, and when they explained to her that this was a get [bill of divorce], she felt faint and swooned.
Now it became clear to her that her husband had long since married in the Land of Israel — right after his departure.
A happy Passover was not meant to be.
P. Poliar.
Wonders of Technology

A machine that imitates 2000 sounds.
In one of the halls of the Polish Radio [Polskie Radio] a machine has now been set up which makes a very strange impression. This machine consists of a three-legged stand on which hang a drum with screws[?] and a cylinder with a handle for turning, and over all of it is spread a piece of linen on which there are a box of sand, a box covered with leather, several slats[?], several strips of linen and paper, and other wooden or iron implements.
Busy around this extraordinary machine the whole time was its inventor, namely the Italian Count Mazaglia Cutelli [Mazzaglia Cutelli?], who gives quite detailed and interesting explanations about his invention.
With the help of this machine, he says, one can imitate more than 2000 different sounds, noises and other audio effects that occur in nature.
One must know that the radio microphone, which picks up sounds like an ear and converts them into electric current, does not react to every sound exactly as a human ear does. It often turns out that the microphone reacts in exactly the opposite way to the human ear. Thus, for example, the microphone does not tolerate the sound of a kiss. In our ear the sound of a kiss rings very discreet and delicate, whereas the microphone renders the sound of a kiss in the loudspeaker or earphones[?] in the form of a bomb explosion. That is the reason why in sound films one does not hear the sound of a kiss. Film heroes are strictly forbidden to kiss loudly, because in the cinema it would resound like a clap of thunder.
— Besides, says Count Cutelli, one cannot after all bring all the sounds and noises that occur in nature into the studio in front of the microphone. For this very purpose he invented his apparatus, which is to imitate natural sounds, creating the complete illusion of natural sounds.
Count Cutelli gives some sort of turn to his apparatus, and suddenly the loudspeaker produces the distinct booming of cannons; right away the noise of an aeroplane is heard. All at once one hears the sea roaring, and immediately afterwards a crash, as if a great wall had collapsed. The noises keep changing[?] like this without pause. One hears a train arriving at the station, a revolver shot and the rattle of a machine gun. All at once one hears the gallop of horses. Suddenly the noise of a snowstorm bursts in, the wind whistles terrifyingly and soon turns into a hurricane; presently one hears the rhythmic marching of soldiers, treading as if in thick mud.
These, more or less, are only a few of the numerous acoustic effects that the inventor gets out of his machine.
The biggest American film magnates have already taken an interest in his invention and have bought it. Now the Americans will no longer need to travel with the microphone in an aeroplane or a train in order to capture the required sounds or noises. Count Cutelli's machine will do all that for them.
The Polish Radio too has acquired such an original machine, and now we shall have all kinds of acoustic effects over the radio, which will create the most complete illusion of reality.
Perished for the Sanctification of the Name

[Serialized story — the 1919 Ukrainian pogroms; continuation.]
H. Akerman.

(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919).

But for Hanna his words went in one ear and out the other. She told him openly that his words were wasted; she would not convert. Not for his sake and not for anything else in the world.
And when Shcherbatov [Szczerbatow] received such an unhappy answer from Hanna, he still did not lose hope; he went to the Harnsteins' house to talk to them about it. He had chosen precisely a time when Harnstein was due to pay him a great deal of money for the lease [the "arenda"]. And he reckoned that when Harnstein laid down so many thousands before him and he, the squire, would refuse to take them and would moreover tell him that he wanted to make him a gift of the whole forest, Harnstein would surely seize upon the "match".
But when Chaim Harnstein heard from Shcherbatov what he wanted, he politely "begged off all the bad dreams" onto him [?] and told him plainly and simply that he was indeed his squire, but he did not want to hear such talk from him any more.
Shcherbatov had not expected such an ending and left the Harnsteins' in a murderous rage, slamming the door. And the very next day he let Harnstein know that he was taking the forest away from him and that he could keep his "match-bride" [?]. In the Harnstein house they were very glad that the squire had got so angry, and they gladly forgave him the forest.
True, it was from that forest that Harnstein had made his wealth, but once it had come to such a thing, it was a fine, clean atonement. So many Jews — they thought — live without forests; God will help them too in another way. Their only daughter and their faith were dearer to them than anything, and the Harnsteins indeed promptly brought Hanna home from Proskurov [Płoskirów] and began preparing to give up the forest.
But Hanna did not leave Shcherbatov's mind, and although the last time he had left the Harnsteins' house with a bang of the door and the next day had threatened them that he was taking the forest away, he nevertheless came once more to the Harnsteins' house, again with the same talk: he would compensate them; if only they would agree that Hanna should become his wife. And if they did not want her to convert, he agreed to live with her without her converting. And he demanded once and for all that they give him an answer at once.
Of course they did not give Shcherbatov an answer on the spot; they put him off a little until later. Meanwhile the Harnsteins went and sent their daughter away to Kiev; so that Shcherbatov could not again find out through the postal clerk where Hanna was, the parents corresponded with her under a false name, through a false address.
And so several months went by; Shcherbatov did not stop coming to the Harnsteins' house to ask after their daughter, and kept offering Harnstein all sorts of favours he was ready to do for him. He would give him back the forest, [a line appears to be missing in print] they would not get rid of Shcherbatov so quickly — they told him that if what he said was really true, that he loved Hanna so much that he could not live without her, then let him convert to Judaism and become a Jew, and then they would allow their daughter to marry him.
Shcherbatov had not expected such an answer. Hanna converting — no, but he converting — yes. That he could not understand, just as Chaim had not wanted or not been able to go [that way] [?]. So he no longer came to their house, and in his heart a great anger flared up against "the Jews", for having blocked his way to his happiness.
The Harnsteins meanwhile thanked God that the squire had taken offence and no longer crossed their threshold. Then the Harnsteins thought that the best thing would be simply to find a match for Hanna and marry her off. Then the squire would see that the matter was lost and would leave them alone entirely. And since Reb Chaim Harnstein was a [a line appears to be missing in print] [...de]cided for a while to give up business altogether. He thought: first he would make a match for Hanna, then he would sell everything off in Bilovka [?] and move to a bigger town, and there he would again take up business.
But it was evidently not destined for the Harnsteins to lead their only daughter to the wedding canopy.
At that time the bloody pogroms all over Ukraine began to be heard of, and they cast great terror and fear upon the whole Jewish population. From all the towns and shtetls across Ukraine dark tidings began to arrive. Here there was a pogrom, there Jews were killed. And like a forest fire the terror began to spread over all the settlements of the Kiev guberniya; in that guberniya the pogromists raged more than anywhere, in that guberniya was the nest of all the "batkos" [gang atamans] and of all the wild and dark plagues that brought siege [?] and devastation upon many Jewish shtetls.
(To be continued)
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

(Friday, 28 Nisan 5694 — piątek 13 kwietnia 1934)
Będzin
Hooligan attack causes terrible panic among the Jewish merchants on the Old Market.
On the eve of the holiday of the second days [the last days] of Passover, before candle-lighting, a terrible panic broke out among the Jewish merchants on the Old Market. It happened because of a hooligan attack on old Mordechai Kalman Adlerflügel, who, on his way from the mikveh, was attacked on Kościelna Street by several young hooligans; one of them dealt Adlerflügel a blow in the face and left him bleeding heavily. When the hooligan was detained by Mr. L. Rozenblum, a tumultuous crowd gathered, threatening with knives and irons if the attacker were not freed; the throng of Jews and Christians kept growing, tempers became as strained as during a pogrom. Terror broke out especially when a friend of the attacker tore out a young tree, with which he threw himself on the Jews.
Only the police, when they arrived, restored calm.
—o—
New complaint by the young petty shochtim to the Ministry of Religious Affairs.
Last Monday the kehilla administration received from the Starostwo a demand that within 7 days the administration give an explanation concerning the complaint which the petty shochtim Gerlic and Radoszycki submitted to the Ministry of Religious Affairs.
So that readers may be informed about the abilities of the petty shochtim, who write complaints constantly (the wags of the generation call them "little denunciations"), we give the content of the complaint in a faithful translation.
"To the Ministry of Religious Affairs, Warsaw.
P e t i t i o n.
Some time ago we turned to the Ministry of Religious Affairs with a petition in which we pointed out the wrongs done to us by the Jewish community in Będzin. Now too we are forced to turn again with a petition to the Ministry of Religious Affairs, because our sufferings still continue. The Jewish community uses a great many schemes, so that the former shochet Moshe Frajberg, who does not hold office (?) ["piastuje"] in the Jewish community, is nevertheless paid the whole pension. We, on the other hand, who fulfil our functions, receive no pensions at all. Now, because the community is setting up a commission about it, all this is being done so that we should not receive any pensions. We live in hunger, therefore we beg very much, with supplications, that the Ministry settle our petition in the nearest time.
We were forced to write the petition by hand, because we find ourselves in a very critical situation.
Israel Icchak Gerlic."
—o—
Shops of 1 and 2 rooms are exempt from paying the surcharge for the Labour Fund.
In reply to the inquiry of the Association of House and Plot Owners in Będzin, the tax office has explained that shops of one and two rooms are exempt from the surcharge [podatek] for the Labour Fund ("Fundusz Pracy").
—o—
House owners must submit lists of rent income.
During the months of April and May of this year all house owners must submit the lists of rent collected in the period from 1 "Stitsher" [sic; probably styczeń, January] 1934 to 31 March 1934 from premises of more than three rooms, and pay half a percent to the Labour Fund
—o—
The shochtim summon the presidium of the kehilla administration to a Din Torah.
This week the "dollar-shochtim" Radoszycki and Gerlic summoned the kehilla presidium to a Din Torah [rabbinical court case] before the Będzin rabbinate.
In this connection the presidium replied that according to the Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat, Laws of Judges, siman 9, the Din Torah cannot take place before the Będzin rabbinate.
—o—
Until the 15th of this month is the last date [printed "te min"] for paying the first instalment of the ryczałt for 1934.
We have been asked by the local tax office to point out that the payment deadline for the first instalment of the ryczałt [lump-sum] tax for 1934 ends on the 15th of this month. Against those who do not pay the tax by that date, distraints will already be carried out on the 16th of this month, which will cause great costs; therefore everyone, in his own interest, must pay the ryczałt tax by the proper date.
—o—
The question of a fourth moreh hora'ah becomes topical; the hat is already there...
Several weeks ago it was murmured in town that negotiations were being conducted about the kehilla taking on a fourth moreh hora'ah [rabbinical decisor]; later the matter went quiet, as if it had never been spoken of at all. But, as we are informed, the question is already topical, and this week a rabbinical hat ["kapelusz"] was brought from Kraków for the candidate...
—o—
Extraordinary meeting of craftsmen.
On Saturday night an extraordinary general meeting took place in the Jewish Craftsmen's Association (Podgórska 4), devoted especially to the new Industry Law.
Chairman Grosman opens the meeting, attended by 260 craftsmen, and declares that the board could not [printed "bekant"] remain indifferent to the question of the new law, which also concerns the Jewish craftsman. A longer lecture on the new Industry Law is given by Mr. A. Klejman, who lists a series of points of the new law, a large part of which hits the Jewish craftsman in obtaining qualification certificates in future.
Mr. Klejman dwells at length on the new elections to the Chambers of Crafts, which are to take place shortly, in which the Jewish craftsmen's organisations will have to fight for their existence.
Mr. Zylbergold criticises the old Industry Law, which led to the degradation of all craftsmen.
Then it is announced that every craftsman can sign up for a loan of 100 to 1000 zł. The money has been allotted from state credits of the "Bank Gosp. Krajowego".
The delegate of the Anti-Hitler Committee, Mr. Jedwabny, appeals to all craftsmen not to buy any German products.
In conclusion the following resolutions are adopted: The craftsmen of Będzin assembled in the Jewish Craftsmen's Association demand that the board be on guard during the introduction of the new Industry Law and use[?] ["tsitirn"] every possibility so that the broad Jewish masses of craftsmen should not suffer especially from it.
The board calls on all master craftsmen to send their apprentices to evening supplementary courses at the Magistrat, because when taking an examination one must present a certificate from vocational supplementary courses.
The board calls for all journeymen and apprentices to be registered in the guilds specially created at the association; otherwise the masters face heavy fines under the new law.
The assembled craftsmen of Będzin express to the board their recognition for its activity so far, and [for having] successfully defended its members.

Sosnowiec: Stormy Debate on Sunday Rest at the Chamber of Commerce / The Birth Pangs of the Kehilla Budget — The Budget Meeting Postponed Again / On the 24th of This Month — Convention of Small Traders' Organisations / Carter of the Lamprecht Firm 'Simulates' a Bandit Attack / Finding No Place of Rest, She Came to the District Court / The Ranks of the Anti-Hitler Committee Strengthened

This week a meeting of the Commerce Commission took place at the local Chamber of Commerce. Among other things the meeting dealt with the proposal submitted some time ago by the Będzin Merchants' Association on easing the decree of Sunday rest.
The vice-chairman of the commission, Mr. Rubinlicht, reported on the proposal, arguing that the Jewish merchant, who bears all the state's burdens, keeps his business closed 2 days, and in the winter months two and a half days, a week.
The proposal provoked a storm among the representatives of the Polish Merchants' Association in Sosnowiec, and their chairman, Mr. Kucharski, put forward a counter-proposal: to turn to the authorities so that the police should watch whether Sunday rest is kept according to the regulations.
Mr. Rubinlicht again takes the floor to answer Mr. Kucharski.
We — says Mr. Rubinlicht — stand on the position that every law must be observed by all citizens without exception; but if it happens that a Jewish shopkeeper somewhat transgresses the Sunday-rest law, I will make you understand it, gentlemen, with the following example:
We see that fish want to swallow one another, whereas the wildest beasts live among themselves in peace. That is because — says Mr. Rubinlicht — the fish are cramped in the water, and no other place to live exists for them, but wild beasts have at their disposal huge forests and fields, and therefore they live among themselves contentedly.
The parable made Mr. Kucharski boil, and he shouted at Rubinlicht — "So you compare us to wild beasts?"
— "I am not comparing you to any beasts" — explains Mr. Rubinlicht — "I used the parable only as an argument that the Jewish merchant is like a fish in water..."
The chairman of the commission, seeing that the discussion was taking on a stormy character, removed the proposal from the agenda.

Who Gets the Lump-Sum Tax and Who Doesn't?

[Taxes — the ryczałt.] A large proportion of merchants are having their ryczałt withdrawn.
In setting this year's ryczałt [lump-sum turnover tax] „agramaw“[?] for the retail merchants, a great many misunderstandings arise and great difficulties are created, from which many merchants suffer.
A very considerable number of merchants have been refused the ryczałt this year, although there was no ground for it. The only reason is surely that some officials do not interpret [—] the law properly.
Paragraph 5, point 2 states that the ryczałt will not be granted to those merchants who in the years 1932 or 1933 had a turnover larger by 50 per cent than the average turnover for the years 1930—31.
On the basis of this paragraph a great many merchants are now receiving notices from the urząd [tax office] that they will not be given the ryczałt, but that this year they will have to pay zaliczki [advance payments], and afterwards their turnover for 1934 will be assessed.
If, for example, a merchant had a turnover of 35 thousand zł. in 1930 and 25 thousand zł. in 1931, together 60 thousand zł., that means the average was 30 thousand zł., on which the ryczałt is due. If, however, the tax office says it has information that in 1932 or in 1933 the merchant had a turnover in one year amounting to 45 thousand zł., that is, 50 per cent more than the average turnover, then in such cases no ryczałt is due. That is the meaning of par. 5, point 2 of the law.
This point covers not only merchants whose turnover was assessed, but also those who had the ryczałt in past years, although their turnover for the previous years was not assessed, but the office possesses its own information that last year the turnover was larger by 50 per cent than the average turnover for the years 1930—1931. In that case the ryczałt is no longer recognised.
The merchants are mostly mistaken in thinking that the office goes by the turnover according to the ryczałt of past years. That is, if one paid a tax on a 20 thousand zł. ryczałt and the average turnover in 1930—21 [sic, for 1930—31] was 25 thousand zł., they think there is no reason to withdraw the ryczałt. But the office is within its rights, in the sense of par. 5, point 2, not to go by the ryczałt turnover of the previous years, but may rely on its own information about the turnover.
We point out that merchants who have been refused the ryczałt can apply to the office and ask on what grounds they were refused and on the basis of which sums a different, larger turnover was set for them, and then an appeal can be lodged by 1 May of this year.

Theatre Notes

[Theatre — review.] "Din Toyre" ("The Rabbinical Trial"), a play after Urke Nachalnik; staging: R. Shoshe; produced by M. Lampe; music: Beygelman.
The play was adapted for the stage from Urke Nachalnik's story "Din Toyre".
In "Din Toyre" Urke Nachalnik leads us into the kingdom of the underworld, where the characters are mostly thieves, pimps, prostitutes and plain criminals. This society has its own jargon, way of life, morals and ethics.
The underworld regards the "din toyre" as the highest and holiest thing; everyone must submit to its verdict, and woe to those who try to be defiant.
The tribunal usually consists of the deserving members of this very "neter"[?] society, which has absolute trust in the "objectivity" and "purity of conscience" of the judges it has chosen.
In this case it is a "din toyre" between two underworld heroes over a girl.
In the play, as in Urke Nachalnik's stories in general, there are rather weak traces of artistry. These are mostly badly made reportages, which have rather scant connection with true literature.
Urke Nachalnik did not delve into his heroes; with him they are passive types, fatalists who make peace with their fate. — Once you have fallen into the swamp you will never again pull yourself out — that is the credo of Nachalnik's heroes.
Instead of a critical analysis of the causes that brought about the sad condition of his heroes, who are mostly victims of the ruling order, Nachalnik sees in every misfortune God's punishment; when he looks for work and does not get it because of his red prison passport, he accepts it with love.
A true artist would surely have created something of value from such material. Of Urke Nachalnik's "Din Toyre" there remains only the picture of the prostitutes' "auntie" with red garters and the rotten smell of a pimp-and-brothel atmosphere.
It is truly regrettable that such talented actors as Lampe, Shoshana, Landoy and Gotlib, whom it would really be worth seeing in purely artistic plays, stoop to concoctions of such a genre as "Din Toyre".
A pleasant refreshment was brought at the end by the fragments from Sholem Aleichem's "Tevye the Dairyman". Here Lampe found himself in his true role, and he proved to be a brilliant interpreter of Sholem Aleichem's Tevye. The fine diction and wonderful mimicry, the subtle nuances of movement bear witness that we are dealing with an actor of high artistic culture.
Sh. R.

A Hasidic Landlord Takes His Tenant's Last Possessions.

Last Tuesday a group of Jewish residents of the Old Market in Będzin came to us at the editorial office and related the following.
In the house of a Hasidic landlord, a long-standing gabbai of the Chevra Kadisha, lives a Jewish iron-monger[?], a poor man who has come down in the world and is in a very critical situation, who owes the landlord 18 zł. for water[?] (for the shop). The tenant turned with a request to the magistrate[?] that the 18 zł. be remitted to him, but in the meantime the landlord got in first and obtained a judgment (wyrok) for a sum of 80 zł. He was not content with the mere judgment, however, but carried out his holy purpose in every detail.
On Tuesday, when the tenant and his wife, already elderly people, were sitting in their wretched little shop, the Ger Hasid came in, accompanied by a bailiff (komornik), to the impoverished tenant to carry out the distraint (zajęcie). In his own person he took down from the walls the whole little bit of merchandise that was to be found there, put it into a box and ordered it to be sealed.
When it happens — the informants say — that merciless bailiffs take from a Jew his last goods and chattels, we cry out; how much more painful it is when, at the hands of a Jewish public figure, a Jewish family is utterly ruined for the sake of a few złoty.
The Debts to the Sickness Fund and to “ZUPU” in Instalments.

In Dziennik Ustaw no. 29 the decree has already been published concerning payment in instalments of the sums owed to the Sickness Fund (Kasa Chorych), ZUPU and other social contributions.
All contributions whose due date fell before 1 July 1533 [sic, for 1933] can now be paid in instalments.
All interest that accrued because of arrears over the whole period up to 30 September 1933 is entirely remitted. Only for the insurance of white-collar workers and for accidents at work are the interest and penalties not remitted but reduced to 6 percent a year.
If one has a mortgage, one will pay off the debt of all social contributions over 10 years, beginning on 1 July 1934, calculated at 4½ perc. from 1 October 1933 onward.
Those who have no mortgage security will pay over 3 years, beginning on 1 July 1934, and will pay six percent a year for the period from 1 October 1934 [sic; probably 1933].
To make use of these payment facilities one must apply to the appropriate institutions: the Sickness Fund, ZUPU, etc.

On the Elections to the Zagłębie Town Councils

[Zagłębie — municipal elections.]
Any day now the ordinance on the elections to the town councils, which will take place on 27 May, is to be published in Zagłębie.
During the next [?] 20 days the voters' register will be finally [?] compiled and checked, and then come a further 16 days for submitting and confirming the candidate lists.
In this connection the Jewish street must at last get down to concrete election work. There is no more time for fooling around. Every day that the parties and organisations let slip, they can thereby do harm to themselves and to the Jewish population.
The new statute [?] and the new electoral ordinance now create an entirely different situation. First of all, each town will no longer form one electoral district but many districts; consequently one will have to submit not one list for the whole town but as many lists as the town has districts.
The citizen votes as many times as the number of mandates his district gives; for example, one district elects 5 councillors. The number of the list is "1" and 5 candidates figure on the list: the citizen hands in a ballot on which "1" is written, i.e. the number of the list, and in addition he must write down the names of the candidates from the district. He has a choice, however, not necessarily to write in 5 names: he can write one name 5 times, and not necessarily the name of the first candidate on the list, but even the 3rd or the 5th. He can also divide the 5 votes among two or three candidates from different lists. In this way the voter gets the possibility of choosing with his votes candidates from different lists, and not as until now, when he had to vote for the whole list if he had sympathy for even one of the candidates.
This possibility creates a very complicated and difficult situation for the parties. It threatens deep chaos and disorientation among the voters. Propaganda will therefore have to be doubled compared with former times.
It can easily happen that, if a certain person is popular in a certain district, he can beat all the other candidates, even if they are representatives of big election committees. After the elections the votes each list has received are counted separately in each electoral district; according to the proportion one calculates how many mandates the list receives in all, and only then is it determined, according to the votes cast for each person separately, who gets the first mandate, the second, and so on.
So much for the technical side of the coming elections. As the reader sees, the main role here will be played by the division of the electoral districts and the number of mandates allotted to each district: if Jewish streets are joined to an area where there are no Jews, the Jewish votes may be lost entirely ("nullified one in sixty"). The same will also happen if the Jewish votes are split [?] among many Jewish lists.
It is therefore expected that in each town only two Jewish lists will arise: a bourgeois one and a proletarian one.
Apprentices Need Be Insured Only Against Sickness

[Poland — social insurance and crafts.]
They are exempt from other insurances.
We draw attention to the fact that apprentices in craftsmen's workshops are exempt from contributions to the "Fundusz Pracy" (Labour Fund); they are also exempt from being insured in the unemployment fund. They must, however, be insured against sickness. They are counted in the group earning not more than 6 zł. a week. The contribution for insuring the apprentice against sickness is paid in full by the employer.
It must be noted, however, that only those are regarded as apprentices who go through learning the trade on the basis of an agreement which is registered and subject to all the provisions of the guild law. Apprentices must also be insured against accidents at work. On the other hand they are exempt from the pension (emerytal) insurance.
