The Collecting of Donations and Public Control.

A subject which is in fact not new; it has already been dealt with several times in the columns of our paper, and so it is perhaps already banal, tiresome — for after all one always wants to read the very newest, the very most important; otherwise the writer of the article has achieved nothing at all with his writing, otherwise he has said nothing new whatsoever, so that on that account the article becomes inferior and uninteresting.
It concerns the collecting of donations. As is known, collecting donations is among Jews one of the greatest mitzvot; from time immemorial this kind of thing was approached with a certain respect and reverence; the average Jew never refused to give a donation — on the contrary, people knew that by doing so one fulfils a sacred duty, and were glad to be able to take part in the mitzvah.
So it was years ago. Lately, however, a great demoralisation has set in in this field. This kind of donation has kept growing. As soon as anything at all happens, a little couple gets together and sets out into the town to collect money. We do not doubt the importance of collecting the money, nor would we wish to accuse anyone of the collected donations not reaching the right place; yet one may say boldly and with full responsibility that a tremendous disorder reigns in this field: anyone who wishes does it; much, very much money is collected about which nobody knows, and above all nobody has the possibility of knowing about it. It happens [?] that for one and the same family several couples go round, very [?] often, and one does not know of the other; besides that, the existing philanthropic institutions are exploited "properly" for the same person. It all depends, then, on the abilities and the cunning of the person: whether he knows how to work the matter; if he is fit for it as he should be, the respectable man is treated in a most respectable manner, so that he can rest for a certain time and not put his hand into cold water.
This pity for people oversteps every limit; one does not realise that one thereby turns the respectable into real beggars and idlers, and they stop thinking at all about earning a grosz in a respectable way. Such pity for people often means leading them to the very abyss, and they consequently become links [?] in the long chain of "respectable" beggars which we, with our own deeds, with our "feelings of pity", have helped to lengthen — this tree which has already grown to its full size and "splendour", and from which a considerable number of branches have already sprouted that bring the Jewish people neither honour nor glory.
Actually, those to blame for this first of all are the couples, the ones who go out after the donations; but what can one hold against people who are harnessed in the heat of the moment [?] and told to go and save lives? Of course, when it is a matter of saving people, it is one of the greatest mitzvot, and what happens afterwards they no longer know; these people do not have, and incidentally cannot have, the aim of radical help, which should aim not to let families fall, not to let them be broken, not to let them come, God forbid, to beggar's bread.
It is understandable that such people must be helped radically, so that they can go on living as citizens; but such an initiative is surely not for individuals, who have enough to do with themselves.
We have enough and more than enough philanthropic institutions whose work this ought to be, if they were healthy and understood their tasks. Yes, if they understood their tasks, they would not dare allow so much money to pass from the population into the hands of individuals. The philanthropic institutions ought in this case to stand on guard and protect the interests of the people, which helps the existence of the said institutions. They must understand that as soon as people have considerable philanthropic expenses outside the charitable institutions, it harms their interests, and they cannot, with the best will in the world, pay the monthly contribution at the level it ought to be, so that this or that institution can fulfil its obligations properly.
Moreover, it must also be taken into account that the money is extracted not, God forbid, from the big ones, from the so-called "carp-heads" [?], but solely from the masses, from those for whom it is not easy nowadays to keep up their budget. The mass, the middle class, is the hardest-pressed element. It has to wage a hard struggle for existence; it is he on whom all the burdens fall, both as citizen and as Jew. People call on him at every opportunity; he, the man of the people, although he does not give such large donations and taxes as the big man, as the industrialist, nevertheless gives proportionally more than the greatest rich man. It is, after all, a well-known rule that one drops straight in on the shopkeeper and the other average man, and one can have him at any minute — while to the big man one has no access at all. First, one does not come to him when it concerns ordinary, everyday donations and events; and secondly, if one does go to these "carp-heads", when one gets to them a precise, all-round investigation must first be carried out as to what the boss and director and president needs such a thing for, and if one can wriggle out of it (and one can wriggle out of it very often), it is settled on the spot and dropped; if not, there begins a business of going and adapting oneself to the time, but at the proper time he is, as usual, busy, and still one is not let in to see him; and meanwhile, meanwhile, at the expense of these rich men, one collects the necessary money from the average masses.
As for the average masses, they are divided: there are those who cannot and do not give, and those who could give and also do not hold with it. And to these two categories one does not go at all; there remains the one category that does take part in popular relief, and to them one goes at every opportunity for several reasons: first, because they give; second, because there is nobody else to go to; and third, because they are the easiest to reach and the quickest to get the donation out of.
These people mostly give beyond their strength; they give because one comes to them, they give because they do not want to withdraw from the relief, and they give because they cannot bring themselves to refuse — although they cannot and may not give the donation because of their weak material means.
The question therefore arises: may one call on people so often and wrest from them money which they give beyond their strength? We hold that this is a great crime. The mass does not know what is more important and what is less. One must not keep "assailing" people with tickets and badges and funds [keren] and all the other events just because one knows that the other has not the courage and the strength to refuse, although in truth he gives far beyond his means.
An unusual demoralisation reigns in the field of collecting money; very large sums are wrested, and all of it from the average people, who carry heavy burdens on their shoulders both as citizens and as Jews; and these masses are already so downtrodden, so pessimistically disposed, that very often one commits a crime when one comes to them for donations that are not of first-class importance.
Were we a people like all peoples, this demoralisation could not have arisen; it could never in life have been realised to that extent. Our feelings of pity, which we "understand" how to steer, are leading a large part of the people to the utter abyss.
It is high time to stop at this question and to consider it from all sides — and not merely consider it: it must be solved objectively and upheld, if we do not want to arrive at catastrophic failures, which the far-seeing eye already sees here and there.
It is superfluous to describe in what critical times we live, how hard it is to meet the everyday obligations; one must, however, realise that the situation is made worse by its becoming steadily more critical, so that it is not ruled out that tomorrow we may, God forbid, have to collect for bread for the one who only yesterday still helped another — and then what shall we do? From whom shall we take then, since no fresh rich men — we mean average ones — are growing up today? To whom shall we then turn for support, for help? When a people finds itself in such a difficult situation and has to carry so many obligations on its exhausted shoulders — at such a moment one must stop and reflect on all this. The collecting of donations for all kinds of purposes, the giving of money without knowing for what purpose and where it ends up, must be crystallised. At such a time one must not allow money to be drawn out of people unless one knows that it is a hundred percent necessary. One must reckon with the situation, with the possibilities.
If this phenomenon does not take on public forms, we are certain that it will lead to the mass completely losing its trust in everything, and then public life will go bankrupt, and there will be nobody to support anybody, nobody to help anybody.
The only way out, therefore, is that the collecting of donations, the going round with tickets, the undertaking of various events be placed under public management, and that the control be a responsible, authoritative one, in which the people will have trust and respect.
R. Les.
The "Datsh"

By Dr. Shazi
A "Datsh" [nickname for a German Jew, a "yekke"] has "quartered himself" in my home. And truly "quartered himself", for a guest, whom one must invite and beg to come — he is not; a member of the household, who comes as if to his own home — he is not either. Simply, the bitter fate of his non-Aryanness "according to the Ashkenaz rite" has carried him off to a foreign land, and at my place he seeks to push away his loneliness, his not being used to exile, and his longing for home, for the "mame veyger" [?; perhaps: mother's cradle], from which he has been torn for the first time.
He drops in, pours out his bitter heart, hears the news from the Jewish papers about Hitler's imminent downfall (if only it were true!) and somewhat refreshes his hope of soon being rid of exile.
Every evening he drinks a glass of tea at my place with a lot of sugar, eats a slice of bread with a lot of honey, and nibbles a few lumps of sugar just like that. The "Datsh" loves sweets like a child: but in other respects too he is really like a child, despite his 23 years of life and 8 semesters of philosophy at the "Kaiser-Wilhelm University in Berlin". And may "He Who lives forever" forgive me for joking with him sometimes.
— "Datsh", have you already heard about Leipzig?
— What exactly, an assassination attempt, a revolt?
— What, haven't you read that in Leipzig a cow flew over the market square and laid an egg?
— Ach, how "is that possible"? Did you really read it yourself? "Why, that is remarkable" (merkwürdig)!..
———
In my home he became convinced for the first time that what the world has only now confirmed — that the Germans are, at bottom, not at all of the highest level of culture — has been obvious to us Jews for many generations, and that in our folk literature the psyche of the German people, as it has now revealed itself after the Hitlerite disaster, has been known since time immemorial.
— Because — says he, my "Datsh" — even if Hitler now died an unnatural death and Nazism suffered complete defeat, it would still be impossible for Jews to live in Germany. The German people takes everything seriously [printed "ergst", probably for "ernst"] and is carried away by every new invention ["oystuekhtsn", doubtful reading]. Not much was needed for the German people to be inspired in a bestial manner by such novelties as, for instance, racial purity, "Jewish depravity", "Aryan kashrut", etc. etc.
— Well, say I, among us it is called "calf's enthusiasm" (kelberne hispayles).
— Ach, he catches on, that is a great truth, that is the right word, a thoroughly comprehensive concept... How did you say?
— Kelberne hispayles — "Kalb-Begeisterung" (calf-enthusiasm)!
— Ja wohl, ja wohl, "Kelbernes Peylos" [his garbling of "hispayles"].
He pulls out his notebook and writes down in Latin letters: "Kelbernes Peylos". In the same notebook there is already written, also in Latin letters:
On the hill
With green grass,
Stand a couple of Datshn
With the long whips,
High stomachs [?] they are,
Short clothes they wear;
Avinu Malkenu,
My heart is merry,
Merry we shall be —
Let them kiss us...
It took a month until he learned the little song from me by heart, and to this day he stumbles over the "Avinu Malkenu", which comes out of him as "Apini Mikhaylakh".
A German after all!...
It may be that this "Avinu Malkenu" is what has led him to study Hebrew so [reading doubtful] energetically. Every five minutes one hears:
"Nicht wahr, khalon — ein Fenster, bakhalon [?] — das Fenster"... (window — the window!) Truly a pity to see what Hitler the Führer has brought these Jewish "Datshn" to!
My Datsh is a gifted young man; he especially excels in the talent of imitating the antisemitic speeches of Hitler, Goebbels, Göring and Streicher, may their names be blotted out. Fear falls upon us when my Datsh plants himself in the Hitlerian pose and begins:
"... Und ich verspreche euch, meine nationalsozialistischen Parteigenossen, die jüdische Pest, das asiatische Gesindel... (here go off a dozen "compliment" epithets for the "kingdom of priests and holy nation", until a mortal terror falls upon those present!) von deutscher Erde und deutschem Volke mit Feuer und Schwert auszur..r..r..otten!!! (to root out!)"
Then he passes on to the lame-legged one [printed "nokhakh"], to Goebbels, may his name be blotted out: "...Ja, meine lieben Parteigenossen. Auch die Wanze ist ein Tier (the bedbug too is an animal!) und auch der Jude ist ein Mensch.. Aber ich verpflichte mich, diese asiatischen Parasiten... etc. auszur..r..r..otten"!..
And when he begins, imitating Göring's swinish voice, to depict the shame that seizes every German "Volksgenosse" when one sees [reading doubtful] walking about on German soil the lice-ridden Jew with thick "negro lips", robber's [?] eyes, Asiatic cheeks etc. etc. — a horror seizes us and we look at one another as after a nightmare, and sigh [?] with a heavy heart. With these imitations "my Datsh" carries us for a while into the hell of the twentieth century, which everyday life sometimes makes us forget.
More than once the thought occurs to me that these imitations of the Hitlerite antisemitic speeches could be the best means of calling our people to the all-Jewish action against [printed "about"] Hitler. As with Kobrin's sinful village lad Yankele Boyle while Khatsye the melamed talks to him about hell, — the hands and feet of every Jew who cheats on the boycott of Germany would tremble when he was told about Hitler's credo ("ani maamin")! "The Jewish plague, the criminal Asiatic parasite-rabble, to the very last, to root them out of the world!!" After such a "rooting out", the fire of hatred for Hitler would be kindled even in the worst Jew, and the "God of vengeance", our true God of retribution, would truly appear all the sooner..
The City-Council Elections in the Light of the New Law

On the basis of Articles 41 and 129 of the law of 23. 3. 1933 on the partial amendment of territorial self-government (Dz. U. 31), the election regulations for the city councils were published on 30 March of this year; they are binding from the day of publication throughout the country, except Upper Silesia.
According to the regulations the elections remain, as hitherto, "five-adjective", i.e. universal, equal, secret, direct, and the distribution of mandates proportional. Also unchanged is the provision that one may vote only in person.
The right to vote belongs to citizens who meet the conditions of the law of 23. 3., i.e. who on the day the elections are ordered have completed 24 years of age, have lived for a year (counted from the day the elections are ordered) within the territory of the city concerned, and have not lost their right to vote for the Sejm.
The passive right to vote (eligibility) belongs to every citizen who on the day the elections are ordered has completed 30 years of age, holds the right to vote in the city concerned and commands the Polish language in speech and writing.
Cities of over 5 thousand inhabitants are divided by the administrative authority into at least 3 electoral districts with a corresponding number of mandates.
Each district may be divided into obwody (sub-districts). In that case the voter has the right to vote in only one obwód.
The number of councillors is fixed according to the number of inhabitants as established at the last census. The number of deputies (substitutes) is the same as that of councillors.
The Electoral Commissions.
The elections are conducted by the main electoral commission and the district electoral commissions. If the districts are divided into obwody, obwód commissions must be created.
The main and district commissions consist of a chairman, his deputy, and 4 members and deputies.
The chairman, his deputy, 2 members and 2 deputies are nominated by the administrative authority; the remaining 2 members and 3 deputies — by the head of the self-government.
The obwód commissions consist of 5 members: a chairman, his deputy and 4 members, nominated by the main electoral commission.
According to the regulations, the members of the electoral commissions must hold the active right to vote.
Important is the provision that members of the main electoral commission cannot be candidates for councillor, whereas members of the district and obwód commissions cannot stand as candidates in their own district or obwód.
The Voters' Lists.
According to the provisions of the election regulations, the voters' lists are compiled by the heads of the self-governments on the basis of the residents' register; the whole formalism of the registration system of temporary and permanent registrations, as well as the way the register books are kept, will be of great importance in compiling the voters' rolls; in particular, the correctness of the first names and surnames in the register books will decide the question of the right to vote.
Within 16 days — and in larger cities (over 5000 inhabitants) 20 — the main electoral commission must publish: 1) the division of the city into districts and obwody, 2) the composition of the main electoral commission and of the district and obwód commissions, 3) the premises and office hours of the main and district electoral commissions, 4) the date and place where the voters' lists will be displayed, as well as the date and place for submitting complaints (reklamacje), 5) the deadline for submitting candidate lists, and 6) the number of voters entitled to submit candidate lists in each electoral district.
The announcement of the main electoral commission must stress that after the stated deadlines no complaints will be accepted, and that the right to vote will belong to persons who appear in the approved voters' list.
The regulations order that the voters' lists must be displayed for inspection by the voters for 7 days, 5 hours daily, of which 2 hours after 4 o'clock in the afternoon — on the premises of the district electoral commissions. Under the previous electoral ordinance the lists were displayed at the obwód commissions, which covered a larger number of voters than the present district commissions[?], of which there are barely a few in each city.
Only during those 7 days and only during office hours can every voter submit complaints orally or in writing. Sending complaints by post is excluded.
Of the highest importance are the provisions concerning complaints, and we shall therefore especially underline these points.
Complaints about not being entered in the voters' rolls must be settled by the district electoral commission at the latest by the third day after the complaint is submitted, and it must notify its decision to the person who complained.
Against this decision there is no appeal whatsoever. Every complainant must therefore substantiate his complaint precisely and support it with proper documents.
If a complaint is submitted demanding that someone be struck off the voters' lists, the commission must, on the second day after the complaints are submitted, i.e. the next day, notify in writing or orally the person whose right to vote has been questioned.
That person has the right to defend himself before the commission only during the second day after the notification, i.e. only the next day.
A chance absence from home, an error and the like can easily lead to the loss of the right to vote. Against these decisions too there is no appeal!
Candidate Lists.
At the latest by the 20th day, and in larger cities (over 5000 inhabitants) by the 30th day, candidate lists for each electoral district may be submitted to the main electoral commission.
The number of candidates may reach up to three times as many candidates as there are councillors foreseen in the district concerned.
The same candidate list cannot be submitted in several electoral districts.
Every candidate list must contain the number of the electoral district, the first name, surname and age of each candidate, and declarations by each candidate: 1) that he agrees to stand on the list concerned in that electoral district, 2) that he has the passive right to vote, 3) that he has acquainted himself with Articles 6, 8 and 9 of the law of 23 March[?] 1933.
(Art. 6: the duty to fill the office throughout the entire term; Art. 8: on loss of the mandate and penalties; Art. 9: prohibition of business connections with the city administration.)
If such a declaration is not attached, the candidate is struck off.
One may stand as a candidate on only one list and in only one electoral district.
The chairman of the main electoral commission has the right to summon every candidate in order to check whether he commands the Polish language in speech and writing. If the candidate does not report, the main electoral commission may strike him off the candidate list.
Every candidate list must be signed in their own hand by at least 2 percent of all voters in the district, or in the city if there are no districts. Each voter may sign only 1 list.
The chairman has the right to summon the voters who signed the list, to check whether the signatures are in their own hand, and to strike off the signatures of those who do not appear at his demand and within the stated time.
With the signature of every voter his address must be given.
The person who signed the list first is regarded as the list's plenipotentiary; the second is his deputy. When handing in the list, however, one may designate other persons as plenipotentiary and deputy.
Each list receives a number in order of submission.
In each electoral district there is a separate numbering.
This last provision makes the already complicated electoral method enormously[?] more burdensome.
A technical understanding between the election committees or parties is almost a vital necessity, because otherwise it could turn out that one party will have several numbers, i.e. a different number in each district, which will burden the campaigning and no doubt disorient the voter.
Therefore, regardless of the ideological and party side of the elections, there must already be created at least a technical committee of all trends and organisations without exception, since it is surely in everyone's interest to ease the work of campaigning and to enable the voter in general, and the man of the people in particular, to fulfil his civic duty.
(To be continued.)
Dr. R. Rechtman.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

So he lived — so he died...
The "people" mourns. Thousands, thousands in number accompanied with tears to his eternal rest a child of the people. No aristocrats' titles [„prutsim“ — grandees] did he cherish in his life, he did not sit day and night over the Gemara, he was not even a parnas of the kehilla. Just a folk type in the full sense of the word, always toiling at plain labour, grimy, coarse in appearance, a maker of quips at which a refined person might blush...
His real name was Mordechai, but among the people "Mordechai" was not popular; they knew him as Matusz the good brother, Matusz the benefactor, Matusz the fine lad, who was ready to sacrifice his life for all the common folk without distinction of nation — international; and when it comes to a Jew — then surely good...
And a sea of people flows, and they tell stories, stories of the kind that ought to be woven into the folk legends about the hidden ones, stories of the Lamed-vovniks [the 36 hidden righteous], whose everyday conduct was coarse, uncouth, but whose deeds were done quietly; without public thanks they visited the poor common folk, listened to their requests, to their sufferings, and afterwards, from their hard work, from their earnings as water-carriers, from cleaning soiled[?] pails, they brought help and warmth[?] to those who were in need of it...
— Recently — one man tells — I meet him, Matusz, running down the street, holding in his hands a big pot of milk. "Where are you running?" — I ask him. "Don't hold me up with your questions — says Matusz — I'm hurrying with the milk to a sick Jew..."
— Oh, I have a story — a second interrupts — I'll tell you a "finer" story: it was before Pesach. Matusz was passing a low little house on Zawale Street and saw through the window how a Jew, by the way a great Torah scholar, sat studying by a tallow candle.
Matusz went into the room and in his bass voice asked:
— Uncle, why are you studying by a candle? Have you no pity on your eyes?
— There's no help for it — the Jew answers — there is no possibility of having electric light shine in this little room.
— Good night to you — says Matusz, and out he went.
Next morning early Matusz came with a few workmen, carried out the necessary installation, and without even waiting for the family's blessings he quickly left. He did the little [good deed] and went off...
From minute to minute the number of mourners in the procession grows, and the number of good deeds. He was, after all, the only specimen of his kind in our town. He embodied in himself the raw material[?] of the highest quality — a third person speaks up, a Hasidic Jew of all people, who tells facts that ought to be a moral lesson for those who preach charity and morality, for those who give not a grosz as long as they are not sure that their names will be printed in the newspaper...
— Matusz — he says — took care of such sick people whom their closest family would not touch. Matusz comforted his poor tenants that they should not grieve: "God will help you — he told them — and you will pay the rent." Every Friday Matusz kept to it, as a pious Jew keeps to prayer, to send parcels of food products to the quiet needy. Matusz was — but why list the details? His last deed surely contains within it the whole Torah: he gave his young life as a sacrifice, just to save a Jewish soul. "Love thy neighbour as thyself — this is a great principle of the Torah"...
— So he lived and so he died...

The third verse...
The door of my flat opens and in comes a young man who hands me an appeal to sign the petition proclaimed by Ze'ev Jabotinsky.
The appeal points out the great wrongs being done to us, the just grievances, and whoever wants to put an end to these injustices should take part in the petition campaign.
But no sooner has the young man with the petition gone out — than a second comes in, an "anti-petitionist", who takes me "on his kapote"[?] and with various proofs and hints tries to convince me how "harmful the petition campaign is".
Hardly has the "anti-petitionist" gone out — when in comes the third party, the "third verse" of Rabbi Ishmael. You know, of course, what Rabbi Ishmael says: "When two verses contradict each other, the third comes and decides."
— We are living through — says "the third verse" — a "golden age". Once, in the good times of the Zionist élan, "the third verse" had to fulfil the duty of — giving to Zionist causes, since the whole activity consisted of builders and givers; but when "the two verses" fight each other, one wanting to tear the other out by the roots — then the word belongs to "the third verse", which decides — not for good but for bad; for however many faults the antisemites reckon up on our account, we can still pride ourselves on one virtue — "not giving", especially when the "people" is drilled not to give...
— Yes, truly a fine thing, [„khlebn as“ — doubtful reading, perhaps an oath, "as I live"?]
— "The third verse"...

He was ashamed...
... "Come, panie [sir], to today's Kaladny concert; you, proszę pana [please, sir], will certainly be pleased. You'll enjoy it — he's, I tell you, a 'świetny śpiewak' [an excellent singer], this Kaladny."
This "agitation speech" I happened to hear in a Będzin[?] barber's salon; the owner, while "working on" one of the customers, pressed him hard to come to the concert.
— "Jak on się nazywa, Kładny?" [What's his name, Kładny?]
— Nie Kładny, tylko Kaładny [Not Kładny, but Kaładny]; he is — I tell you, panie... a splendid singer.
— I've never heard of such a singer. I know almost all the Polish singers, comedians, even Dymsza, Krukowski too, but some Kaladny?!
— But he's not a Polish singer, he's a Jewish singer... — the owner of the barber's establishment explains to him.
— Ach tak! A "żydowski śpiewak" [Jewish singer], well then; with me you've already succeeded, but I'm almost certain that my wife won't want to go to a concert by a Jewish singer; owszem [indeed], as soon as a poster appears about a Polish performance, a concert or a "zagar"[?] of the cheap shmontses [silly jokes], she is among the first "devotees"...
— Tak, tak [yes, yes], I am przekonana [convinced] that so it is: not only your wife, but almost our whole so-called intelligentsia avoids everything that is Jewish. Na przykład [for example], in the "Klub Towarzyski" you will find newspapers in all seventy languages, except a Jewish one...
In the end the pan [gentleman] let himself be talked round and came to the concert.
After the concert the "agitator" asked him:
— Well, panie, — satisfied?..
— "I am ashamed" — the pan answered to himself, — that as a Jew I did not know there was such a Kaladny in the Jewish world!
— "I am ashamed"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Acharei Mot–Kedoshim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Acharei–Kedoshim
The Portion
—o—
a) "And he shall confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel... and put them upon the head of the goat" (Lev. 16:21)
The Midrash says about this that God takes all the sins of the Jews and lays them on the guardian angel (sar) of Esau. The angel argues: how shall I be able to bear all of Jacob's sins? So the Master of the Universe takes the sins upon His garment and atones for them.
God lays the Jewish sins on the angel of Esau. For it is thanks to him, thanks to the exile, that we are driven to crimes and sins... But the angel of Esau cannot bear all the Jewish sins, because there are sins for which he is not to blame — pride, for example. Is it because the Jew is in exile that he must be proud?... Therefore God must atone for these sins with His own garment — "His garment is righteousness [tzedakah]": God's garment is tzedakah, and tzedakah atones for everything, "redeem thy sins by charity."
R. Natan Adler.
—o—
b) "After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do" (Lev. 18:3)
After all, you do not do the very deeds of the land of Egypt, but "after the doings" — you merely ape them like monkeys. You only want to be "like all the nations," with the kaf of comparison — like them, imitating them. It is not, after all, a natural will to sin, but a craving to copy, to imitate...
"Neither shall ye walk in their ordinances" — do not do what among them, among the gentiles themselves, is a statute, merely a statute without a reason, in which they themselves see no sense... Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "Nor make to yourselves molten gods" (Lev. 19:4)
People apply this verse to those Hasidim who spend their days at little feasts and over little glasses of liquor. "Thou shalt make thee no molten gods" — do not make liquor your god, your rebbe...
—o—
d) "Thou shalt leave them for the poor and the stranger... Ye shall not steal" (ibid., 10–11)
Many "fine Jews" have an excuse for swindling and committing abuses in trade: after all, they give charity and thereby supposedly buy off their sins. But the Torah says "ye shall not steal" — even when "thou shalt leave them for the poor and the stranger." One must not steal even when one throws something of it to the poor... Tiferet Shlomo.
—o—
e) "Thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour, and not bear sin because of him" (ibid., 17)
Rebuke your fellow you may, but "and not bear sin upon him" — do not magnify his sin. For when speaking of another's sins, a person likes to blow them up, to make them big.
Kol Yehuda.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man" (ibid., 32)
With "hoary head" (seiva) the word "face" (pnei) comes first, and with "old man" (zaken) the "face" comes later. For by seiva is meant simply an old man; before him you are obliged to stand up without any arguments or objections. By zaken, on the other hand, is meant a Torah scholar, "one who has acquired wisdom," and before him you are not obliged to stand up beforehand, until you have understood by his "face" what sort of face he has — whether he truly is one who has acquired wisdom...
In jest. R. Avraham Shmuel Binyamin Sofer.
—o—
g) "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord" (ibid., 18)
If there are quarrels among Jews, the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not whole. "Love thy neighbour as thyself" — then it will be "I am the Lord"... Milei de-Shmaya.
• • •
"Love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord" — just as God loves His children although they are not pious, so you too love your fellow, although he has sinned against you... Ilana de-Chayei.
—o—
h) "But I have said unto you: Ye shall inherit their land, and I will give it unto you"
"Their land" — the Land of Israel is in fact their land. It belongs in fact to them, to the gentiles, who have defiled it... So it is, alas, because of our sins... Be'er Yitzchak.
—o—
i) "Ye shall separate between the clean beast and the unclean" (ibid., 25)
"And how much is there between most of it and half of it? — a hair's breadth." Rashi.
That's just it — the Rebbe R. Bunem used to say — the whole of Judaism stands on a hair's breadth. The way from the Garden of Eden to Gehenna is as thin as a hair... Beit Yaakov.
—o—
Avot.
j) "Anyone with whom people are pleased" (Avot 3:13)
The rabbi of Lisowisk[?] had to endure much persecution from opponents, quarrel-mongers. He wanted to resign from the rabbinate, because "anyone with whom people are not pleased, God is not pleased with him either," and since he knew[?] that people were not pleased with him, then presumably God was not pleased with him either, and so he was not fit to be a rabbi. He travelled to the Rabbi of Sanz[?] with this decision and wanted his approval, justifying his resolution with the said saying in the Mishnah of Avot.
The Rabbi of Sanz shouted at him:
— By "people" is not meant just quarrel-mongers... By "people" I am meant, and I am pleased with you — my spirit is pleased with you... Mekor Chayim.
A Man Has Died (a few words at Matek Winer's fresh grave)

[Obituary.] (A few words at Matek Winer's fresh grave)
Schopenhauer wrote that death says to everyone: "Because you are the product of that act which ought not to have taken place, and in order to atone for it you must die."
And indeed, every newborn creature carries with it, together with life, death as well. Since time immemorial, in every second of our existence, death cries out into the void of the world with its frosty breath that it, and it alone, is the mightiest dictator over the lives of all that exist, without distinction of class and station. Man has had to make peace with the thought that somewhere in the future lies a point in time when death will, with mathematical certainty, knock him into its skeleton arms. Day after day it devours with cold-blooded cruelty hundreds of thousands of quivering lives; it knows no mercy, the tears of the unfortunate do not move it; like an insatiable Moloch it gorges on lives and spits out annihilation.
Man has therefore become blunted to this "normal" phenomenon which is called death. And when someone dies — unless it is someone very close — one takes it with resigned indifference.
What, then, was the reason that, when it became known that Matek Winer was no longer alive, literally the whole town was shaken? What moved many thousands of people from all strata of the population, women and men, young and old, Jews and Christians, to stream like a stormy lava along all the roads and streets in order to pay him their last respects?
Because a man has died, a true man.
It seems no more than a man. But how hard it is to find one today — harder than searching for a diamond in a mountain of sand.
Man — that name was meant to serve as a symbol of the highest perfection among living creatures; he wished to embody in himself: "love of one's neighbour," "love thy neighbour as thyself," liberty, equality and fraternity! And what has come of it in reality? Gratuitous hatred, man is a wolf to man, oppression, class distinctions and Cain's murder.
Just like one of the Thirty-Six Righteous of folk legend, the deceased too lived from his hard toil, was content with little, always hurried to help those in need, looked after poor sick people, gave away his last with an outstretched hand — in a word, a man with a heart, who like a sensitive seismograph reacted to all the suffering and pain of those around him.
A man has died!
No more than a simple man of the people, who lived from his own work, without higher education, without a diploma, but for that very reason without that bitter falseness and empty pride of modern "homo sapiens."
He embodied in himself the naïveté and goodness of a child, the primitive openheartedness of a man of nature, but at the same time the heroism of a titan. After all, he was out of all danger; after all, he could have listened to the voice of the instinct of self-preservation, which surely warned him not to dance into the arms of death. But Matek Winer the man prevailed[?], and rushing to rescue another, he himself tragically perished.
That is why the mourning is so great and the grief so deep, and his memory will long live on in each of us, because
a man has died!
Sh. R.
New Circulars and Laws

Criticism in the press.
On the instruction[?] of the Prezes of the Council of Ministers [Prime Minister], all the ministers have sent to the bodies subordinate to them a circular saying that they must treat with the greatest attention the attacks appearing in the press concerning the activity of certain state or municipal organs of authority — offices, institutions, establishments — or, as the case may be, concerning officials of the institutions listed.
Concerning every such attack a strict investigation must be undertaken at once, and a proper clarification or correction must be sent immediately to the newspaper in question.
If it concerns an office, the correction is sent through the mediation of the starosta [district head]; if [printed: “in”] the press attack concerns an official, the intervention is carried out directly by the official attacked.
—o—
Regulations on the burial of the dead.
The Minister of Health Supervision has published in the Dz. U. [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] an ordinance which has regulated the rules on burying the dead and establishing the causes of death.
The said ordinance contains the following important rules: the dead may be driven or carried through the town only until 2 o'clock in the daytime; later no street funeral may any longer be held. The doctor who treated the deceased must issue a death certificate, even free of charge. Removing the dead from graves and transferring them elsewhere may take place only in the winter months.
Moshe Shloyme Becomes a “Grain Merchant”...

After the Będzin merchant, the owner of the little herring shop on Yatke [Jatki?] Street, had such a sweet dream — that he had already passed the examination and received a concession for his “trading enterprise” — he cannot close an eye a single night. He keeps pondering how one gets through this harsh decree.
This week, after lunch, Moshe Shloyme caught a nap.
In his sleep he dreamed on that he alone had indeed passed the examination, and of all the “merchants” who had gone to school with him not one had received a concession.
The signboards on the Old Market [Stary Rynek] and on Kołłątaja Street took on a sort of new look.
From the little shop with the 3 lumps of coal, 2 brooms and two bits of kindling[?] on Wale [Wały?] Street a new signboard looks out with the inscription: “Licensed grocery, proprietor Jan P–ski”, and by the door stands, poor thing, a hunchbacked, limping little Jew looking for an interest-free loan to send his concessionaire his “pension”.
Thus almost all the Jewish shops went over overnight to “-ski” and “-cki”.
Only on his own signboard stands his full[?] name: Moshe Shloyme Hoyuntsayg[?].
But what comes of it, that he already has a concession in his own name and needs no concessionaire, when there is no livelihood anyway?
Just yesterday they seized from him, for taxes [“poratkes”, i.e. podatki], his last little barrel of herring, and he was left in the empty shop with the concession.
His neighbours, on the other hand, have no concessions at all, and they have a livelihood in plenty — it really overflows with them...
Without thinking long, Moshe Shloyme scraped together a few złoty [“gilden”] and started going to the special courses for licensed grain merchants.
Besides the school, Moshe Shloyme also studied separately, attended all the lectures, not even skipping[?] the lecture “Bad breath”.
Every early morning he studied the grain exchange, so that of all the pupils he was the best.
In a lucky hour Moshe Shloyme passed the examination and received a concession for a grain shop.
In the emptied herring shop Moshe Shloyme installed an English scale, and with a straw in his mouth he began circling round the peasants' carts and, together with everyone, began buying grain.
Easily said — buying grain. And where[?] are the old grain dealers who have been running the trade for many years? There began a series of “into your father's father”, so that they even dug the great-great-grandfathers out of their graves and hit each other with them.
If the old dealers paid the peasant 17 groszy for a kilo of grain, Moshe Shloyme paid 17½ groszy; if they gave 17½, he gave 18 groszy.
With great toil and trouble Moshe Shloyme barely bought up 2 little korzec [grain measures] of grain over the day, and towards evening he went off to sell it to the wholesale buyers, so that tomorrow he would have something to trade with.
He comes in to the merchant — and feels faint. Instead of 18 groszy a kilo, as he paid the peasant, they give him only 16 groszy.
He thinks, of course, that they are cheating him; but he sees that all the dealers don't get any more either, and they are quite satisfied besides; they say that they had a fine livelihood that day...
Thrashed[?], Moshe Shloyme runs home and begins looking through the little books — perhaps he is running the trade badly. But he sees that he knows everything. That one should give the goy 18 groszy, sell oneself for 16 groszy and still be left with a nice couple of złoty profit — this theory he did not find in the little books, nor could his mind grasp it.
Next morning Moshe Shloyme no longer bought any grain, but circled round the carts and watched how others buy.
Watching like that, only then did he notice that all his learning was thrown away. All the examiners [printed “ekzamistn”] and professors may come to the market to learn the fundamentals of trade...
And indeed, what on earth is such a grain dealer to do when a peasant digs in his heels and insists on 18 groszy a kilo while it costs only 16 groszy? Not buy? But one needs a livelihood. For that there is a remedy: the peasant wants 18 gr. — here, have 18 gr., but in return one gives the regulator of the scale a little push. So that grain bought for 18 groszy can be sold for 16 and there is still some profit left.
A black, dismal dream on the heads of the teachers with the little books and the schools! — with such a greeting Moshe Shloyme went into his shop, tore up the concession and threw out the books. — — — — — — — —
The bitter dream was cut short by Moshe Shloyme's wife, who woke him, announcing that people had come to call him to a meeting about forming a united bloc for the town council elections.
H.[?]
Notes of the Times. — The Struggle against the Small Merchant.

16 years since Poland's liberation had to pass before big industry found a means to begin a struggle against the small merchant and, even more — against the small Jewish manufacturer.
And the means was indeed found.
The means is called anonymous trade and anonymous manufacture. That is: against all those merchants and manufacturers who work without patents [trade licences], big industry, with the help of the tax authorities, has launched the struggle.
And here it must be explained that all merchants' organisations are against the system of trading or manufacturing without patents. For that system is simply unfair competition and must lead to chaos.
But for big industry the struggle against the anonymous small and middle manufacturer is merely a cloak — "how to get rid of him altogether, once and for all. —
The methods of the struggle against the so-called anonymous trade have taken on such forms as are liable to break the existence of thousands of small Jewish merchants and manufacturers.
On the one hand it fights the anonymous trade, which supposedly competes with it because the anonymous trade pays no taxes; and on the other hand it does not agree to the lump-sum collection (ryczałt) of the turnover tax, which would have been a salvation for the whole of trade. And therefore it would be right of the government finally[?] to put this tax on a lump-sum basis, just as it has already done with sugar, cement and other articles of first necessity, and just as the small merchant is exempt from paying turnover tax on these products.
If the standpoint of big industry in its struggle against the small manufacturer and merchant is still somehow understandable, it is in no way possible to understand how representatives of Jewish organisations openly and with full sharpness fight the small merchant.
The largest tax-paying element today is not the big manufacturer but precisely the small year-round merchant. So if one wants to crush the small merchant, one will thereby take away from the government a strong tax-paying element. Let big industry adapt itself to today's crisis times, let it content itself with a quite small profit percentage — then it will not need to fear so much the competition of the small merchant, nor need to look for means of getting rid of him.
M. Gordon [M. Gardan].
A Little Feuilleton. — My Programme for the Municipal Elections.

Water. I hold that the most necessary thing in a person's life is water.
Water is needed not only for internal use, but also for external use.
Even more than a person needs to use water for drinking, he needs to have it for washing himself.
Especially in need of it are the communal activists, whose hands and faces are often unclean.
I would therefore strive with all my strength to water the whole of Zagłębie.
The journalists, who need water most of all for their profession, will get water from the Przemsza [the river through Będzin and Sosnowiec] completely free.
The milk dealers will get water at greatly reduced prices; likewise the "weigers" [so printed; probably a misprint for "wine dealers"] will be able to enjoy cheap prices for water.
Roads. Since it has been established that the citizens of the town tear their shoes walking and running all day to the banks, I shall endeavour that the roads leading to the banks, and mainly to the Magistrat [town hall], be paved; special attention will be paid to the streets leading to the "zimne d..." [so printed, deliberately truncated]. Thereby two aims will be achieved: both the citizens and the "zimnikes" will not tear their shoes so often, and they will also spare their feet.
Lighting. I shall devote all my powers so that the town uses as much electric energy as possible — not like the Małobądz[?] power station, which is stingy with a kilowatt of energy for the citizens.
Electricity will be exploited in various fields, for example:
The bakers will raise the prices of bread with special little electric machines that will help the bakers in the work of raising prices; the municipal taxes will be collected with the help of electric apparatus that can roll thousands of złoty out of people's pockets in one minute; and so that the colossal difference between the upper and lower streets should not catch the eye, only the lower streets will be lit and not the upper ones.
Sanitation. In the new town council, in which I shall occupy a distinguished post, special attention will be paid to the sanitary condition.
Efforts will be made so that not only the citizens' pockets will always be found in a sanitary condition, but the streets too: for every spit on the pavement one will be fined a hundred zł. Nobody minds if you spit in someone's face — just not in the street; likewise it will be forbidden to cough and sneeze in the street, only at home.
All this is just the beginning of my future programme: about the rest — another time.
Rebus.
Radio Bulletin

[Radio — radio bulletin: Poland, Vienna, England.]

Polish Radio's preparations for the summer season.

For the coming summer season Polish Radio is preparing a special programme.

Unlike past years, when the summer programme, in order to spare the better artistic forces, stood at a lower level than the winter programme, this year the summer programme will stand at the same height as the winter programme.

The work on assembling the summer programme is in full swing. A whole series of projects is being considered and worked out which will make the summer programme interesting and instructive, — will give the maximum of entertainment and a pleasant way of spending time by the radio set.

Unexpected result of a radio survey.

The Vienna radio station a short while ago sent questionnaires to all its radio subscribers. It did so in order to learn from the answers to this survey about the wishes and demands of its radio listeners. The survey brought quite unexpected results: the greater part of the radio listeners demand only cabaret music. Of all instruments the zither is the most beloved, and the press news should be given to them not at the end but at the beginning of the evening broadcast.

Characteristic is the hostile attitude of the radio subscribers toward the "fair sex" that appears before the microphone as announcer ("Speakerin"). The sharpest opponents of the woman announcer are women; they reproach her with bad manners, with a note of disdain in her voice and other feminine failings. Many of the women listeners found an opportunity to unburden their hearts and told in the survey preposterous gossip about the women who appear on Vienna radio. It is said that if the Vienna radio station wanted to publish all this gossip, a real women's war would break out in Austria. The men, on the other hand, proved more discreet, although there was no lack of "gossipers" among them too.

But the greatest surprise for the Vienna radio station was the result of the survey on the question: do the radio listeners want opera music? It turned out that the Viennese population, which used to love operas and operettas so much, does not want to hear operas on the radio at all.

Radio survey for motorists.

The research office of Polish Radio, in connection with the cycle of lectures for motorists now being broadcast on the radio, has published a survey and sent questionnaires to all schools in Poland. The survey's purpose is to learn the opinion of the radio listeners on the usefulness and expediency of these lectures for motorists.

The filled-in questionnaires should be sent to Polish Radio, Warsaw, Zielna 24, to the "Biuro Studjów" (research office).

24-hour clock in England

For the first time in the history of England, the 24-hour clock was introduced on the night of the 21st to the 22nd of this month.

Almost all European states have already been using this clock for several years. The railways, post, telephone, telegraph and radio regularly use the 24-hour clock.

It went hardest, however, with the English. This conservative people, which still cultivates the customs and traditions of centuries, could by no means bring itself to discard the old faithful clock of its great-grandfathers, who divided the hours of the day into "before noon" and "after noon".

At last, however, the English gave in, and they too have reformed the clock to a 24-hour one.

From now on all English radio stations will announce the time according to the new form, as for example: twenty-two o'clock, etc.
Perished for the Sanctification of the Name.

[Serial story — the Ukrainian pogroms of 1919.] By H. Akerman.
(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919).
Had the Angel of Death come to them for their souls, it would not have been as great a calamity for the Hornsteins as the tidings the rabbi had brought them. The Hornsteins wept bitter tears before the rabbi and begged him to give them his advice on what to do. But the rabbi did not want to give them any advice. He could not tell them yes, that they should send their virtuous daughter into the arms of the wild beasts, and again he could not tell them no, because on her now hung the life of an entire congregation of Jews, of four hundred and fifty Jewish souls, men, women, children. The rabbi too wept that it had fallen to his lot to carry such a dark mission. And the rabbi, with tears in his eyes, left their house and wished the Hornsteins that God might put the right thought into their minds about what to do.
Reb Chaim Hornstein and his wife Gitl were now left alone and had to decide what to do.
Had someone cut their bodies with knives just then, no blood would have flowed and they would have felt no pain, so petrified were their hearts.
Apart from Chana they had no other children, and Chana was dearer to them than their own lives — and now God had brought them to such a trial!
But an answer had to be given, because the slaughter-knife was hanging over their throats.
After much weeping and lamenting, the first to consent to the terrible step was the father. The mother lamented and wept and tore the hair from her head. But Reb Chaim Hornstein comforted her and told her that it was a privilege that God had chosen precisely them for such a trial, to bring their only daughter as a sacrifice, just as God had tested our father Abraham when He bade him bring his only son Isaac to the Binding. He spoke words of comfort to his wife, while hot tears ran from his own eyes and his heart was torn to pieces. He spoke to her in broken phrases, because tears were choking her [?; printed thus, probably for "him"] in the throat.
And Reb Chaim further said to his wife: it is no small matter to save several hundred Jewish souls from certain death. And if their daughter will be one night in impurity, what is that compared with saving so many Jewish lives?
And the grief-stricken mother Gitl, after several hours of anguish and pain, also consented.
And now there was still the question: how does one tell it to her, to the daughter herself? How will their mouths open to speak such words to their innocent child, to their one and only Chanele, to the apple of their eye? For a long time they racked their heads and hearts and could by no means find the courage to talk with her, until at last they decided not to speak to her about it, but to write it down for her on paper and hand it to her.
The father wrote the paper and the mother also signed it as proof that she too consented, and they laid the letter in her room.
Chana found the letter and read it through, and she burst into loud wailing. Fear fell anew upon her parents [printed "עטטערן", a misprint for "עלטערן"]. When the first screams had passed and the spasms grew quieter, the parents talked with her about it; they choked back their tears and did not cry in front of her, because they wanted to give her heart, so that she would be strong.
Chanele heard them out. She did not speak; she did not say "yes"; she only kept silent, but her face grew frozen, her eyes deeper and somehow so determined, and the parents understood, without words from their daughter, that she consented. The father went to the rabbi and told him that Chanele would go.
No one in Bilovka [?] knew what was happening at the Hornsteins' — except the rabbi and his wife, the rebbetzin.
It was the night of Tisha be-Av. The Jews of Bilovka crept little by little out of their hiding places and sat in the synagogue on the ground and bewailed the destruction of the Temple and their own destruction.
But the Hornsteins — Reb Chaim in the men's synagogue and his wife in the women's synagogue — wept over the kinot [lamentations] louder than everyone. Chana too came with her father into the synagogue and wept and prayed to God that He might show her a miracle in the great trial she had to withstand.
After the kinot all the Jews went home. And Reb Chaim Hornstein with his wife and their daughter went home, and the rabbi went along with them, and sat the whole evening until around midnight in the Hornsteins' house and talked with Chana and her parents about the mission it was her fate to carry out, and comforted her and persuaded her not to lose heart afterwards, because she would always remain a virtuous Jewish daughter. And before leaving, the rabbi took leave of her, blessed her and kissed her on her forehead.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: He Wanted to Save His Helper's Life and Perished a Tragic Death

[Head of the local page; Będzin — accident and funeral; Brit HaChayal and the Revisionists.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 12 Iyar 5694 — piątek 27 kwietnia 1934 [Friday, 27 April 1934].)
Będzin
He wanted to save his helper's life — and perished a tragic death.
A terrible catastrophe. — Up to 10 thousand people take part in the funeral of the victims.
Będzin is still under the heavy impression of the terrible accident which happened in Będzin last Friday at about 6 o'clock in the evening, and which cost the lives of
2 young Jewish victims.
The 44-year-old Matek Winer and his worker, the 16-year-old Mendel Fryc.
Lightning-fast the tragic news spread through the whole town. From mouth to mouth went the sad tidings that on Magrushever[?] [Modrzejowska?] Street No. 87, 5 people had been suffocated in a privy pit (cesspit). At the siren signals masses of people ran to the place where the terrible catastrophe had happened. Still more painful is the fact that there was torn away the one so beloved by the whole town,
Matusz Winer, of blessed memory,
who fell a victim when he let himself down into the pit to save his helper, his favourite Mendele, may he rest in peace.
How did the accident happen?
As we are told, the accident happened in the following circumstances:
In the above-mentioned house Winer was working in a well (shaft) that was connected to the sewer pipes. The work was almost finished, but Mendele, coming up out of the well, remembered that he had left a small board down below, which he was sorry to lose; and although Matek told him it was not worth going down into the well again for the sake of a board, the ever-nimble[?] Mendele went down like a squirrel and came back with the board. Suddenly, however, an iron clamp broke off, which also caused the sewer pipe to open, and from the strong smell of gas Mendele lost consciousness and fell into the depths of the well. When Matek saw that Mendele, his worker, was in danger, he risked his life and went down; to his help came a second worker, Baumgarten, and also the caretaker (stróż) of the house, who likewise lost consciousness from the gases.
The alarm raised by the residents of the house unfortunately was of no use at all in the tragic accident. Instead of telephoning the neighbouring police commissariat so that police would come with gas masks, the fire brigade was telephoned, and they arrived when the victims had already been dragged out. Fryc was already dead, but Winer still showed weak signs of life. Here again urgent help was lacking, and while he was being taken to hospital in a droshky (cab) he died.
As soon as the disaster had happened, the town was wrapped in deep mourning. The Sabbath day was turned into a day of mourning and grief. Potocka[?] Street, on which the house of the deceased stands, was full of people who were literally frozen by the deep pain.
In front of the entrance to the deceased's house there was posted
A guard of honour of „Brit HaChayal“
in honour of their tragically perished commander and helper in all fields. For a part of „Brit HaChayal“ Matek Winer was also a caring father.
On Saturday evening a meeting took place in the premises of the Revisionist organisation, at which the funeral committee was formed of representatives of the Artisans' Union, „Brit HaChayal“ and Betar. Every society and organisation announced the death of Matek Winer by means of klepsydras (black-bordered death notices).
On Sunday, the day of the funeral, already from early morning Potocka[?] Street looked like a place under siege. From minute to minute the number of people grew; from all the surrounding[?] towns of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia came uniformed and non-uniformed detachments of „Brit HaChayal“ and members of the Revisionist organisations. In the surrounding streets there were many thousands of people from all strata of the Jewish population. To pay the last respects came the rabbinate, delegations, and also the police commissioner with several przodowniks (police sergeants), the district (powiat) doctor, firemen and respected Christians, with whom Matek was very well liked.
The keeping of order at the funeral and its whole management were carried out by the district commander of „Brit HaChayal“, Mr. Maniek Glidman, but because of the crowd of many thousands of heads the order could not be as it should.
At about 12 o'clock there began
The funeral.
The deceased was brought into the beit midrash which he had set up in his house. There he was eulogised by the director of the yeshiva „Yismach Yisrael“, R' Szmuel Zylbersztajn, who in a few words described the good deeds of the tragic victim.
Behind the bier walked the family of the deceased, behind them the funeral committee, delegations from a detachment of children of the „Morchi“ [read: „Mizrachi“] school, „Brit HaTzohar“, „Brit HaChayal“, artisans and about 10 thousand people. Such a huge funeral had never yet been seen in Zagłębie. Tram traffic on Kołłątaja — Małachowskiego Streets was stopped[?] for half an hour until the funeral procession had passed. The funeral committee wanted the funeral to go along Sączewska[?] and Kołłątaja and to stop for a while at the premises of the „HNTs.“[?] and the Revisionists, but the official (referent) of the Starostwo did not permit it. At the bridge on Czeladzka Street the funeral of the second tragically perished victim, Mendele, joined it. The wailing reached the very heart of heaven.
About 2—3 thousand people accompanied the tragic victims up to
The cemetery
Before the entrance stood larger detachments of „Brit HaChayal“, who by order of the commander Mr. Glidman let in only the next of kin and the delegations. But unfortunately the crowd forgot where it was and broke the fences in order to get inside.
At the open grave eulogies were given: in the name of the Revisionists by Mr. A. Diament, of the Artisans' Union by Mr. Goldsztajn, of Betar by L. Turner, and of „Brit HaChayal“ by the commander Mr. Glidman, who ended his funeral speech with the call to sing „HaTikvah“.
Slowly, with heavy steps, the crowd leaves the fresh graves of the two young, beloved, tragic victims.

As the shochtim report, a few days ago a certain Cyhan[?] came into the slaughterhouse and declared that, as a contributor to the "Placig"[?], he wished to confer with one of the shochtim. In addition[?] he demanded that the meeting take place "between four eyes", but he did not succeed in this, and having no choice he held the "interesting" conversation in the presence of all the shochtim.
During the conversation Mr. Cyhan declared that, although he knows that abuses amounting to tens of thousands of złoty are being committed in the slaughterhouse, he would not publish this in the paper if the shochtim admitted it. He would also, he said, prevail upon his colleague not to write about it either.
When the shochtim declared that they were not afraid of the paper writing after all, the contributor stressed several times: "You don't understand me."
—
At the Sunday session of the kehilla board the slanders of that rag were discussed, and it was resolved to bring the editors to account in court.
A separate suit will also be filed by the shochtim.

The 1st and 3rd of May in Zagłębie

The 1st of May in Zagłębie passed, on the whole, quietly. The workers' holiday was not celebrated at all the mines. The largest Jewish demonstration was that of the Right Poale Zion, who marched to Dąbrowa to join the demonstration of the P.P.S. there. The demonstrators' slogans were directed only against Betar, „Jewish fascists“, „Long live the Histadrut“, etc.
The demonstration of the Left Poale Zion was broken up by the police on Kołłątaja Street; the demonstrators fled, leaving behind part of the instruments of their own orchestra.
On Małachowskiego Street a Communist youth demonstration was broken up.
The demonstrations of the „Bund“ were not disturbed. In the afternoon a May academy was held in Sosnowiec by the „Bund“. Several participants were arrested and taken to the police station; the next morning they were released.
*
The celebrations of the 3rd of May began on Wednesday evening. The houses and balconies were decorated with state flags. The monument on 3rd of May Square was decorated particularly splendidly.
In the synagogues the appropriate prayers were held for the President of the State and Marshal Piłsudski.
In the Będzin synagogue the director of Fürstenberg's gymnasium, Dr. Einhorn, spoke, and in the Sosnowiec synagogue — the teacher Goldberg.
Then a parade took place of: the army, school youth, organisations. The local Hitlerites in their uniforms also officially took part in the parade; Betar and „Brit HaChayal“ therefore refused to take part in marching together with Hitler's comrades.
The participation of the „local“ Hitlerites aroused great bitterness among the Jewish population.

What's New on the Election Front?

On the election front it is still quiet; there are even quiet negotiations and still quieter combinations. Since mandates are important[?] (printed "vor-han vikhtsig"), and not every side has enough desire and enough strength to put up Jewish lists also in the other districts, various means are being tried. One side wants to push the other away, to lead it astray, to create, faits accomplis[?]; instead of a general bloc, attempts are made to create a bloc from which certain sides are to drop out — and this is to be done at the last minute, when the opposing side will no longer manage to put up a list of its own. And since all sides are playing this game, only at the last minute will one find out who has fooled whom...
We are not publishing any details, although the so-called "strategic" plans are precisely known to us. We simply do not want to increase the chaos and disorient Jewish society even more. We hope that in the end the petty ambitions will give way to the seriousness and importance of the question, and that the Jewish population will after all obtain in the city councils such a representation as will want to, and be able to, truly defend its interests.

In connection with the forthcoming elections the Ministry of the Interior has clarified that the chairmen of the separate (district) electoral commissions have the right to demand of every voter that he prove the identity of his person with a document.
If the voter does not possess a proper document, he can bring 2 trustworthy witnesses who are to confirm that he is the person who figures on the voters' list.
A negative decision of the chairman cannot be appealed.
One must therefore alert all Jewish voters to provide themselves in good time with proper documents. Apart from ordinary passports, photographs certified by the police, sick-fund (Kasa Chorych) identity cards, student identity cards, etc. can serve this purpose.
All those who have no documents must think about it already now, otherwise they may lose the possibility of taking part in the elections.
Exhibition of Ben Zion Zuckerman in Będzin

Yesterday, Thursday, in the club (on Kołłątaja Street in Będzin) the festive opening of the picture exhibition of Ben Zion Zuckerman [Ben Cijon Cukierman] took place.
The exhibition is one of the most beautiful and richest that Będzin has seen[?] ever (printed "es iz geven"). Ben Zion Zuckerman is represented here with rich creations from among his most colourful pictures, both in form and in content.
Zuckerman is today one of the greatest painters. His works are known all over the world; they adorn the studies of barons, wealthy men and other famous personalities.
The artist spent the last years in the Land of Israel and drew his painterly inspiration from there. His picture exhibitions in all the larger cities of Poland and Galicia met with very great moral and material success. The entire press, the non-Jewish too, responded warmly to the work of B. Zuckerman.
One must believe that the exhibition will have its due success here. It is very important that the exhibition also be visited by the pupils of the elementary and secondary schools, in order to become acquainted with Zuckerman's works from the Land of Israel and from the Jewish ghetto.
The exhibition is open daily from 10 in the morning until 7 in the evening.

The Town Council Elections in the Light of the New Law

2.
The chairman of the main electoral commission checks every list and determines whether the list complies with the regulations. In the case of defects he calls upon the authorised representative to remove the defects within 10 days; otherwise the whole list or individual candidates may be annulled.
There is no appeal against these decisions.
Combinations of lists (a bloc) are not permitted.
The regulations provide that if only one valid list exists, no election takes place and the candidates of the single list are recognised as councillors.
The main electoral commission must publish: 1) all candidate lists and their numbers, 2) the day of the election and the voting hours, 3) the polling stations and 4) the particulars of the election organisation.
The voting.
Voting takes place at the polling stations from 9 in the morning until 7 in the evening without a break.
At the ballot box there may be present scrutineers (trusted men) from each list (1 person from each list) on the basis of special credentials issued by the list's authorised representative and confirmed by the main electoral commission.
On election day no campaigning may be conducted within an area of 100 metres around each polling station. All persons who contravene this rule or disturb the peace, even scrutineers, may be removed from the polling station.
Voting is done on ballot slips, which must be white.
Each slip must contain the number and possibly the name of the list and the names of the candidates.
A slip is valid: 1) even if it has no number or name — if all the candidates appearing on the slip come from one list; 2) if it has the number or name of the list and at least 1 candidate. Candidates from different lists may not appear on a ballot slip.
Each voter has as many votes as there are candidates [to be elected] in the district. He may vote for several candidates or give all his votes to one. In that case he must write the candidate's name on the slip as many times as the number of votes he has.
The ballot slip may be printed or handwritten.
The members of the electoral commission have[?] the right to demand documents from the voter showing that he is the same person who appears on the list.
If the voter does not have sufficient documents, he may call upon 2 known witnesses.
Against the commission's decisions in these matters there is likewise no appeal.
It is therefore advisable that all voters, and especially those whose names or nicknames may raise doubts, provide themselves with documents in good time.
The count.
Immediately after the election the counting of the slips and of the votes cast must take place, and the following is recorded in the minutes: 1) how many slips each list received, and 2) how many votes each candidate received.
The following slips are declared invalid: 1) those in unstamped envelopes, 2) those not white, 3) those not filled in or illegible, 4) those containing candidates from different lists and 5) those without candidates.
If a slip has the number or name of one list and candidates from other lists, only those candidates are struck out and the slip is recognised as valid.
After the district electoral commissions, and then the main electoral commission, have established the number of slips cast for each list and the number of votes of each candidate of each list, the distribution of mandates takes place — first of all between the lists and then between the candidates of each list.
The counting system.
Instead of explaining the counting system theoretically, we shall illustrate the whole matter with an example:
Będzin, which has up to 50 thousand inhabitants, elects 40 councillors. The administrative authority has divided the town into 3 districts (constituencies).
In one of the districts, which elects 8 councillors, there are 4000 eligible voters. 4 candidate lists were submitted, on which 3600 valid slips fell, for example:

candidate A. 1320 votes

candidate D. 2400 votes

The distribution of the 8 mandates is done in this way: the number of slips of each list is divided by 1, 2, 3 etc., and then the largest figures receive the 8 mandates, for example:

The mandates should have gone to candidates B. and G., but under the law the list leader has certain privileges and receives the surplus votes; therefore the total number of the list's votes is divided by 2 (mandates): 7420 divided by 2 is 3710; the surplus of the second candidate: 4400—3710, i.e. 690 votes, is credited to the 1st candidate: 1320 plus 690.

Finally the mandates go to: A. and B.
List no. 2 has 5 mandates. All its candidates are elected.
From list 3 the first candidate is elected.
The remaining candidates are recognised as substitutes.
Protests against the election.
The election is invalid:
1) if it has been established that abuses, forgeries and the like were committed;
2) if the electoral regulations were broken.
Election protests must be lodged within 7 days after the election. Entitled to do so is such a number of voters as has the right to sign a candidate list.
Election protests are settled by the starostas — in smaller towns, and by the voivodes — in larger towns.
The regulations also provide that the same authorities have the right to annul ex officio, even without a protest, the entire election or the election in districts, and also individual candidates.
The regulations set no time limit for the ex-officio annulment of the election or of candidates. This will undoubtedly be an important factor in the composition of the town councils.
The electoral regulations also provide the procedure for supplementary elections in the case of the town councils becoming incomplete, i.e. when 20 to 30 per cent of the candidates are lacking.
Important for every voter is the rule that all applications and certificates in electoral matters are free of any stamp duty or administrative fee for the local self-government bodies.
