The Minister Said and the Small Trader Spoke

(After the regional small traders' conference in Sosnowiec.)
One fine morning — it was last week — I open the daily papers and my eyes light up: all the newspapers were suddenly flooded with big headlines across the full width of the large papers, announcing no more and no less than: "Poland's economic situation keeps improving." And this is not some report sucked out of one's thumb, in which one should place no trust. The telegram was distributed by the Polish Telegraph Agency, and the words were spoken at the opening of the Poznań Fair by the Minister of Commerce, Dr. Zaoshitski [Zarzycki].
We are approaching — the minister said — little by little the level of the year 1931. And were it not — the minister went on — for the bad situation in the economy, we would long since have been past the crisis. The minister therefore arrives at the conclusion that, in order to save the difficult situation, one must first of all help agriculture, because the peasant is the main consumer.
According to these words, then, it turns out that all citizens in the country are well and fine, and only the peasant is badly off. And since everything is so good, it is truly a terrible injustice if all the elements in the country will not [?] improve agriculture, which finds itself in a difficult state.
We do not really know whether this should be called short-sightedness, an unwillingness to look with open eyes, or simply not giving oneself any account of the real state of affairs. Otherwise one cannot understand the conclusions and the arguments. That the peasant is badly off, that he gets nothing from his hard work — about that there are no two opinions. But, firstly, who is actually well off, and who in fact should help him? Has the government not gone into the situation of the peasant more than into that of the town citizens? And secondly, let us look with open eyes: why has life in the village become harder — is it not because life in the town has become worse? Is it not because the worker, the clerk, the merchant and the industrialist began to feel abnormal and could not afford to live as people lived in former times? Why then did the peasant's lot become worse, why did he have to cheapen his products? Is it not because the town could no longer [?] afford to buy? And since this is so, life in the town became bad even before it did in the village — so how does one arrive at the conclusion that only in the village is it still not good? And since when has the situation in the town improved? Since when do we hear [?] of a revival in industry, in commerce and in the crafts?
Perhaps it is measured by the yardstick of the constantly raised tax assessments, in which no account at all is taken of the fact that the population cannot pay them?
What is there much to talk about — here a conference of small traders came about [printed "tsushtanr"] in Sosnowiec, and what groans and cries of woe were carried away from that gathering! The large and important conference, which had many questions, serious and important questions, to solve, was turned into a mourning meeting. People were so lost, so helpless, as each began to unpack the bundle of troubles he had come loaded with. And nothing, God forbid, was exaggerated; on the contrary, not everything that oppresses was spoken out, not all the suffering found an echo, because people did not forget that this is not what they had gathered for, and that this would not improve the so painful Jewish question, which keeps growing worse and harder.
Thus, for example, a delegate from Miechów relates that there the Polish Hitlerites [hitlerowcy] agitate openly and freely at the markets that no one should dare to buy from any Jew, or else he will be put in the pillory; they post themselves in front of the Jewish shops and do not let any Christian in to buy.
Then the Zawiercie delegate relates that, regardless of the fact that the town is almost dead and no trace has long remained of the Zawiercie of former days, the tax office takes no account of it and the tax assessments keep on rising. Thus, this year they were raised threefold compared with a year ago. The desperate delegate cries out bitterly that the situation is utterly catastrophic and that ruin threatens 1500 Jewish families.
And another delegate, from Czeladź, relates that with them antisemitism rages on all fronts, so that the whole little town is "adorned" with Hitlerite slogans. He tells a characteristic fact as well: his own shop was covered with these very slogans, and when his saleswoman dared to tear down such a placard, she was administratively punished for this "sin".
It goes without saying that one cannot — and incidentally need not — sit down and take down in shorthand all the sufferings and cries of woe that could be heard at the conference. The three facts mentioned suffice to form an idea of the situation we are in, and how "easy" it is for the middle class to earn its daily piece of bread.
It is enough that on the one hand the citizen must toil hard until he earns enough for the citizen's taxes and all kinds of administrative expenses connected with the business, and only after that should something fall to him as well — and they do not even let him begin to earn, so that he does not get the possibility to pay his civic taxes, and consequently no longer attains a living for himself.
From a purely business standpoint it would certainly have paid the government first of all to react to the adventurist deeds of all sorts of hooligans, who above all want nothing more than to fish in troubled waters. This is how Jewish families are ruined and their goods and chattels go to waste. When such a ruined merchant is left owing taxes and they come to take away his last belongings, the government gets nothing more from him, because he no longer trades and remains lost both to himself and to the government.
Why deceive ourselves, why look with closed eyes — is it any wonder that people talk and agitate the mob, that the Jews are the most dangerous element and that they are to blame for all troubles? It is an old rule that the crowd, the common mass, can be persuaded of anything in the world — all the more so when it is a matter of ill against Jews.
So, on the one hand, the dark individuals are allowed to run riot, pouring poison into the cup that Jewish suffering never fails to fill, and on the other hand the taxes become ever larger and more oppressive. No account is taken of the fact that turnovers are far from what they were in the good old times; no one looks at the fact that incomes are minimal; the office [?] has fixed such-and-such, and the matter is settled. One must — as the saying goes — weep and pay [printed "count"].
How many firms have already gone under because of these squeezed-out compulsory taxes? And what does the government get from these "dead" ones? They bring no benefit to the living and do not disturb the dead...
The entire Jewish community is downcast because the Jew is lain in wait for on all sides. Everywhere he is unwanted, everywhere he is superfluous. Hardly ever has the Jew been in such a plight as today. Like rubber we are elastic in bearing all sorts of troubles, and that is no wonder either: the long history of exile has raised us as hardened people, and therefore we are not frightened when it falls to us to take new sufferings upon ourselves — we then accept them, willingly or unwillingly, with love.
True, we are downcast, we are in a pessimistic mood, because from all sides dark elements lie in wait for us, wishing to uproot, exterminate and destroy us. We must be steadfast. We must not lose our equilibrium, but one must not rely on miracles, and we must be vigilant. We must apply every means within our power to protect and defend our rights, both as Jews and as human beings and citizens.
The most important thing is not to deceive ourselves and not to think about illusions that are far from being realised.
We must therefore be represented everywhere; the representation must be authoritative and responsible. People who take upon themselves the mission of representation must know and understand their responsibility in the full sense of the word and its meaning; otherwise they may not [?] take on the people's mission, and in such a case they must be brought before the people's judgment, because in this way they harm and weaken our national interests, and the later consequences are sad, and the whole people suffers from them — this is what one must know and remember in the present hard time, when the minister spoke and the small trader talked.
R. Les [?].
A Little Feuilleton — I Believe

[Feuilleton — satire; Nazi Germany, Hungary and Austria.] I believe — that our teacher and master Adolf Hitler will yet one day become a great penitent (baal teshuvah) — and Göring-Goebbels will yet fast fast-days and study a chapter of Mishnah, and people will apply to them the old verse:
"Where penitents stand, the perfectly righteous cannot stand" — because[?], because there will be — begging your pardon — a smell.
I remember today's Hungarian premier Gömbös as an "awakening[?] Hungarian" with his "awakened" good deeds towards Jews — and then I read his "repentance, prayer and charity", his "I have sinned, I have done iniquity, I have transgressed".
I tell this in comparison with the following:
The Christian Social leader in Austria, Comrade Kunschak, always used to devour a hundred Jews for breakfast, a hundred — for lunch and a hundred for supper.
Today — honey-or milk drips from Kunschak's mouth; a penitent, a perfectly innocent saint — and in a speech he says:
"We shall not, God forbid, persecute any Jews. Let them only preserve their faith and nation; we do not want any assimilation."
When Kunschak talks like that, then — I believe that Hitler-Göring-Goebbels will yet become Jewish Shabbos-goyim.
S.
Poverty in Disguise (From Today's Crises)

[Story — the economic crisis; poverty and a merchant's suicide.] From outside one could see nothing at all. Even when one went in to visit them, one noticed little at the G. family. Those close to them did, it is true, suspect something. They already felt and understood something — that things at the G.s' were not rosy[?] — but that such want, such poverty reigned there, that nobody could have believed. Even the very closest[?], who used to be on more intimate terms with the G. family, did not know either that things there had gone so far that they were going hungry.
There, at the G.s', people knew, a fine household had long been kept; they lived respectably, the home had plenty of everything, and he himself, Mr. G., a solid householder, a merchant, ran a fine business — and yet all of a sudden such poverty reigns. Nobody had expected it; in truth it was a bitter, disappointing fact, which only Mr. G. himself with his wife and children knew. He felt the bitter taste of the crisis; life grew harder. The takings stopped completely, and the money owed to him by customers — nobody wants to pay back a penny. But for that his creditors are not silent. Without regard to the fact that others are breaking him and will not pay him their debts, and that everyone knows it, his creditors will not let up and want to ruin him, so that he should never rise again, not even at the resurrection of the dead — taking no account of the fact that G. had long been an honest and reliable merchant from whom many people had lived and earned their livelihood.
His creditors are merciless towards him, breaking him materially and morally. They take from him whatever they possibly can. His business is already emptied out. Even the household goods are being sold at auction. It has gone so far that he no longer even has the means to buy out a trade licence (patent). Mr. G. is forced to give up his business of many years. He liquidated it and, thanks to the creditors, took to trading in something else — perhaps he would after all earn something towards bread for his wife and children; but it came to nothing[?], and from then on everything only got worse. In his home they are simply starving, but they try with all their might so that the street should not know of it.
It was mostly the wife who concealed the poverty. As a modest Jewish woman she quietly suffered want, if only no one would know what was going on in her home. One thing gave her no rest — her husband; she noticed well how he went about without courage, despairing and full of melancholy. Her heart began to dread the thought that he might, God forbid, commit suicide, though he had never mentioned it. She sensed with her woman's instinct that her husband, the long-established merchant, who in all his life had never wronged anyone, would not bear the shame. With all her strength, with all her womanly sense, she watched over him, and thereby hoped to avert her own already unhappy situation, which she could do nothing to help. Unfortunately, it seems[?], Mrs. G. had not yet drained the whole cup of pain and troubles; the misfortune was stronger than the weak, worn-out Mrs. G. Weeks and days dragged on like a long chain of sufferings, until once she woke up from sleep with a heavy heart. Outside the electric light had already gone out. A blue strip of sky cut in through the windowpanes. Mrs. G. glanced at the other bed, but to her horror she did not find her husband there. She leapt out of bed as if half alive[?] and went into the kitchen. There a terrible sight met her: on a hook her husband was hanging by a rope. In his neck there was a deep cut. A great outcry arose; neighbours came running. Mr. G. was taken down from the rope already stiff and cold. The doctor could only certify death.
On the table a letter from the suicide was found, in which he asks his wife and children to forgive him for the grief he has caused them — "I could no longer — he writes in the letter — bear the shame from the creditors and the sorrow of my wife and children going hungry". I also ask that good people have pity and not let my wife and children perish of hunger, but help them as far as possible.
The people who knew G. lamented that such an honest and fine man had ended his life so tragically.
P. Polier.
When the Hour Strikes

[Opinion — municipal council elections.]
L. Goldsztajn
(On the election turmoil.)

Only a short time separates us from going to the ballot boxes; the election calendar gives us a few more days, and then — it will be too late. Then we will look around and see that we are a completely torn camp, a camp without a leader, without a programme, without a path. Then we will look around and see how a few little people bustle about among [?] us, waving their paper flags and calling to the dispersed [?] and the scattered.
And they [?], the masses, wander about and do not know whom to follow.
But perhaps it is not yet too late! The great mass still has a minute's time to reflect, so that the thousands who are called voters want, even now, while there is still time, to ask:
— Who are you? What do you want? Whom shall we follow? To whom shall we entrust our fate?
These very questions we must now put in all their [?] sharpness to the few activists who make the "politics", who trade and haggle in mandates and in "ideologies", so to speak..
When political groupings come out and fill the street with the cry that the economic groups weigh nothing, that only they have the right to speak in the name of the thousands of voters, that the mandates are due to them alone; and then the economic organisations come in turn and confuse people's minds [printed "מחות" for "מוחות"], saying that the "parties have nothing to do here and that they alone represent the whole of Jewry (Klal Yisrael); and when someone comes along and shouts: I have a "shtibl" [small prayer house] with three hundred worshippers — pardon, voters; and when a couple of young men come and lay down an organisation with five hundred names, and there is a panic, a chase after "little benches" [seats], a scramble of mandate-grabbing — it is sad, very sad.
But that is not all; there is an even sadder aspect to it! It is clear that the political situation in the country has a certain line. It is also clear that life demands of us a more or less positive attitude towards that line; but that does not mean that the mandate-grabbers should run about and each of them promise mountains of gold, each of them promising to give more...
— That is the most tragic thing of all.
Therefore one would like to say to these gentlemen, who call and rouse, who hover around the bowl and create [?] blocs:
— Do not share out honours among yourselves; be reasonable, hand over the mandates to such hands as are worthy of them, choose capable, tried and tested people. And if a party or organisation does not have such people in its ranks, it must give way and hand over its mandates to those who can bear the heavy burden, and let this or that grouping not go about saving its prestige — for the prestige of Klal Yisrael is a thousand times greater!
— Moderate your appetites a little, do not come to the table demanding so much, for quality is greater than quantity.
— Step aside and let into the town council the little intellectual strength that we, alas, possess in such small measure. They too can defend all the parties, even with all their right and left wings, because they too can defend the Agudah, the Mizrachi, the workers no worse than they themselves would do it.
— Show [?] that you are not out to grab "little benches", but seek out the best and finest that we have, and put the mandates into their hands!
— For otherwise you will only provoke apathy and indifference among the thousands of voters, and for the loss of Jewish mandates no one will be to blame but you yourselves.
What Are They Shouting About?

It may well be that even the Agudah ringleaders [Agudat Israel] are wondering how I — whom they have removed from the kehilla — still take an interest in kehilla matters[?] and even go to the trouble of addressing public opinion with my remarks on questions closely connected with the present kehilla's work. Umehai ta'ama [and for that very reason] I want to reassure these gentlemen of the "Agudah" that they should not be mistaken and think that because, by base denunciations, they have removed me — for the time being, or "removed" me entirely — from the kehilla, my work in this field has stopped. My work as a Zionist I shall continue. We Zionists understand that the Agudah demoralises Jewish life; they are the destroyers of a Jewish revival, they shatter Jewish honour. Against this demoralisation we must wage a merciless struggle, and I shall always be the first to fight these gentlemen, both inside and outside the kehilla. We Zionists have to a great extent succeeded in tearing the mask off the Agudah and placing them before the judgment of the public, and we shall go on doing so until we have unmasked them completely.
Now to the matter itself: the Agudah people have made a great noise in town, since[?] [i.e. claiming that] they were badly wronged in the assessment of the last kehilla budget; they hold meetings, write ugly denunciations, trumpet about, and do not forget to babble along the way that the kehilla simply took revenge on the Agudah people and that they alone, poor things, fell victim to sinners who sit in the kehilla.
To this one must first of all tell them that they are greatly mistaken; their outcry will not find the slightest echo, because public opinion already knows these pitiful faces well. It has long been known that their tumult is nothing but a means of provoking the Jewish street, since in all there are some 20—25 shouters; this proves that the present kehilla went about assessing the budget with a system. The system is that people of little means are exempt from burdens, while the well-to-do are, on the other hand, obliged to carry the burdens of the Jewish population in Będzin.
Had these Agudah shouters been honest for one minute, they would have seen that the progressive part of the Jewish population today cares more for religious needs than the Agudah people. This further proves that the kehilla drew up the budget this year in an honest way; it made no distinction by party but went only by the clear principle: whoever can, must pay. True, it may happen that mistakes are made regarding individual people, but that always happens; for that there is, after all, the way of appeals, of clarifications — but by no means resorting to denunciations, provoking public opinion — and provocation must be answered as it deserves. For, in truth, what is the Agudah leader from the Old Market [Stary Rynek] shouting about? How long ago was it that he signed a pledge of several hundred zł. for the mikveh and then laughed at everyone and did not pay a single grosz? And does he really think, this "Torah-true" Jew, that Mr. Fürstenberg or even Mr. Goldsztaub[?] and the like will forever maintain the mikveh and all matters of sacred institutions in general, while the "fine" Jews will discharge their duty by rolling their eyes to heaven and shouting before the whole world that they love the Torah dearly?
To all these shouters, and especially to the Agudah leader, one must say that we simple people have a different notion; we say that Jews who love the Torah — and especially one who is a leader of the Agudah and has a few złotys besides — such a Jew must be the first to carry the burdens for sacred institutions, for the mikveh, for charity etc. [o"ch]. This comedy must come to an end at last, where in the shtibl they say that they pay elsewhere, and elsewhere they say that they pay, poor things, a lot of money in the shtibl.
Also to all the other shouters, who are used to and brought up on the idea that you can get everything out of them — only not giving money? — not that! They must be told that the kehilla is — together with all its other tasks — also an educational institution: one must educate the Jewish population, one must teach them that one has to carry the duty together with everyone — and let the gentlemen shouters learn from the progressive part of the Jewish population, many of whom, like Messrs. Gutman, Fürstenberg and Szajn[?], have of their own free will burdened themselves with a larger assessment, because these people have an interest in such an institution as the gmina [the Jewish community]; these people would like to see a kehilla that can and should achieve things for Jewish interests. And you, the "Torah-true" gentlemen, you are the destroyers; you do not even have an interest in the religious institutions having a proper appearance. The time when you wanted to persuade everyone that you would study and the sinners would give money for you — is over; you must carry the burden for the Jewish kehilla together with everyone; you will have to uproot from yourselves the thought — you are not privileged aristocrats [meyukhosim].
And therefore we tell you — the present kehilla has taken the first step: no revenge whatsoever against anyone has been taken, no distinction between religious and non-religious; the only thing that galls you is that you were always favoured and paid pennies for the kehilla, and now you have been put on an equal footing with everyone — for the mouldy system cannot go on ruling as it has until now. Never yet has the budget been drawn up so seriously and so sincerely as now [printed: "as until now"].
The upshot of my writing is to tell you that your shouting will be a voice in the wilderness; the street knows that all your ways are accompanied by falsehood.
The town has come to realise that among you there are only a few troublemakers [awanturnicy], destroyers, wreckers. You cannot look on calmly where things are being created and worked on. The Jewish street receives your outcries with disdain. You have lost trust, because it is well known that your morality is nothing but hypocrisy.
A. Liozer[?].
Letters from Home

[Będzin — feuilleton: letters from town; municipal elections, football, the community and cantors.]
B"H, on the day of the Torah portion "and they journeyed and they encamped"...
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
"Praised be the Name whom I am not worthy to mention." At least once I have the privilege of writing you a happy tiding. My letters to you are always Books of Lamentations: only crisis, only unemployment, only gmina [municipal/community] muddle[?] and other kinds of "cancers". If only we were rid of them the sooner the better, sweet Father! Yes, Reb Shlomo, I give praise for the fact that the crisis on the Jewish street has weakened a little and the lamentations have stopped for a while. One sees plainly that Divine Providence watches over the people of Israel. Take, for example: how could we have borne it, when spring has warmed up[?] so, the sun has come out of her "muter pas"[?] and the heat torments, and if that is not enough for you, you receive newspapers[?] from everywhere, from which you learn that the "shatsert"[?] have honoured themselves with "shlishi" [the third Torah call-up], the boycott [of German goods] grows like the flowers on Third[?] of May Square, Hitlerites marching with the "Błyskawica"[?] have received ...[?] with a friendly face... Well, where would we have found so much strength to live through so many troubles and calamities!
What does the Holy One do, as it were? He puts a thought into the nations of the world that they should call — elections...
That is the only remedy that makes the people of Israel forget its day-to-day troubles. It is an opiate[?] that leads[?] Reb Yisroel far, far astray, right down to the forty-nine gates of impurity.
— Elections upon you, Israel!...
They fuss[?] and sweat, grab, run, a grab[?] here and a grope[?] there; every one of them is ready and willing to sacrifice himself — pardon me, I mean to abandon the community of Israel — so long as he is one of the "elect", one of the community's emissaries...
———
At this very moment, in this present minute, as I write you this letter, the collective child has been born — "Blok Bl"n"[?].
The public wish each other mazel tov and rub their hands with joy, but the pessimists, the sober ones, are somewhat melancholy; they are not with everyone, since the "child" — so they say — is an "eighth-monther" [a premature, non-viable baby]. Even greater is the fright that the "Agudah" leaders, who are known as the first to create "Jewish unity", were elsewhere at the time of the birth and were studying the motto[?] A. G. "majority in number and majority in building"...
That, Reb Shlomo, is how the election fair looks here, from which, it seems, we will have no joy. But be that as it may, I am already content that the laments about the crisis, the boycott and the Hitlerites have stopped for a while...
———
Now, Reb Shlomo, a second piece of news that will surely satisfy you. You surely remember how Jews of olden times fulfilled with self-sacrifice the commandment of redeeming captives. The commandment of redeeming captives once played a great role among Jews. No sooner had the squire thrown his tavern-keeper into jail for an unpaid debt than good Jews ordered horses harnessed to a wagon and drove from city to city, from town to town, went from house to house and collected donations to ransom the imprisoned Jew.
— Redeeming captives.
But today too, in the twentieth century, in the football epoch, the commandment is observed again, only in another form. For instance, once honest, pious Jews occupied themselves with this commandment, and today —
— who do you think?
— the Jewish football teams [drużyny] of Będzin and Sosnowiec.
To the account of the "merits" that "football culture" has on the Jewish street one must enter one more meritorious item, the item of
— "redeeming captives"...
As is well known, "the jealousy of scribes increases wisdom" [printed thus], and jealousy over "goals" increases the lust for snatching good "shooters" [strikers]. Before every match [mecz] there takes place — (so we are informed) — a hiring and a trade in "live merchandise"; pardon, we mean
— good "goal shooters"...
The prices depend on the qualifications of the "shooter"; needless to say, if the shooter or the "backs" are Ślązacy [Silesians], the rate is higher; one shrinks from no price at all, so long as the bought[?] player brings the proper victory...
Here one quite often meets sweaty young fellows collecting donations; there are people who judge the young fellows unfavourably and suspect them of bad ways, but as I have learned, a holy mission is being carried out by them: they are striving to ransom several[?] players from foreign hands, from a foreign domain —
— "redeeming captives"... — a great commandment, after all...
———
In answer to your request about the "white" ["Weiss"] story, I inform you that it really happened so. A small "Leibele" [little lion] came here and drove out a big strong "white one" ["Weissn"]... But I will reveal a "secret" to you: by driving out the "white one", the gmina has been blackened completely... If the situation does not improve, I am sure that the very same "heroes" will cry:
— "Give us the white one"...
In my next letter I will write, God willing, who the candidates for the new city councils are. Have a good Sabbath, wishes you
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! Here in our town the cantor question is topical again. A cantor has applied who has first-rate "instruments" [voice] but "knowledge"[?] — none. The wits of Będzin say, however, that the surest candidate will be the one who has what lies underneath, in the pocket — that's what they mean... Especially at a time when the mikveh building has to be completed...
H.N.Sh.[?]
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Behar-Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Behar-Bechukotai
The Portion
—o—
a) "And you shall do My statutes" (Lev. 25:18)
"And you shall do My statutes" — you shall keep My commandments even when "you dwell in the land in safety, and the land yields her fruit, and you eat your fill"; even when things go so well for you, do not forget God either, to whom you turn when things are bitter for you... Devash ve-Chalav.
—o—
b) "And if your brother becomes poor and his means fail with you, then you shall uphold him" (ibid. 25:35)
The late rabbi of Lublin, R. Meir Shapira of blessed memory, once came to a rich man to ask for some donation for a good cause. The rich man had a ready excuse: he could not. So the clever rabbi said to him:
— Why, you are a veritable holy of holies..
The rich man did not understand, and the rabbi explained: the Gemara says, "Israel are holy — there is one who has and does not want [to give], and one who wants and has not." Jews are holy: some have to give and do not want to, and some want to give and have not. Well, you do not want to give and — as you say — you also have nothing to give, so you are a doubly holy one, a holy of holies..
• • •
Up to here it says "And you shall do My statutes" — in the plural, and so with most of the commandments; for charity it says only in the singular: "then you shall uphold him". Because charity is not laid on the community at large, and no one can excuse himself: let the other fellow do the mitzvah. The commandment of charity is addressed to every single individual — "you shall uphold him". On you lies the commandment — says the Torah to every Jew separately..
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
• • •
"Righteousness lodged in it, but now murderers" (Isa. 1:21).
If it comes to doing someone harm, with you it is "but now" — right away. "But now murderers": you are already hurrying to the murder. But if, on the other hand, it comes to righteousness, to doing some charity — then it is "lodged in it": you are in no hurry, you let it stay overnight, it is not burning... R. Yehonatan Eybeschütz.
• • •
"A poor man is counted as dead."
A dead man is remembered only at the burial; afterwards he is already forgotten. A poor man, too, is remembered only when the slaughter-knife is already lying at his throat and he comes with an outcry. A while goes by — and he is forgotten as one forgets the dead... R. Yehuda Leib of Volkovisk [Vilkaviškis].
• • •
"Righteousness shall go before him" (Ps. 85:14).
Before his death every miser gives charity, bequeathing in his will for charitable purposes. But it ought to be "righteousness shall go before him": his charity should come before him, and not that he should arrive in the World of Truth before the charity, before his will is distributed... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
c) "You shall keep My Sabbaths and revere My sanctuaries" (Lev. 26:2)
"And revere My sanctuaries": you shall have awe and respect for My sanctuaries, the synagogues — not talk and quarrel in them (and it goes without saying that the desecration of the sanctuaries occurs mainly on the Sabbath, when people gather in the synagogue..) Binyan David.
—o—
d) "If you walk in My statutes" (ibid. 26:3)
"That you toil in the Torah." Rashi.
That the toil — your day-to-day work, your trade and dealings — should also be in the Torah, according to the ways of the Torah. (When one trades and observes "you shall not wrong one another", "you shall not rob" — that too is learning Torah). Devash ve-Chalav.
• • •
Of the Jewish king it is said that he should keep a Torah scroll with him: "and it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life". The Chatam Sofer interpreted: "and he shall read therein all the days of his life" — his whole life's path he should live according to the Torah...
—o—
e) "And I will give peace in the land" (ibid. 26:6)
"And you shall eat your bread to the full and dwell in your land safely" — and when things go so well for you, you will surely want still more: "whoever has a hundred wants two hundred"; so a special blessing comes: "And I will give peace in the land" — you will be content with yourselves... That is a special blessing: to be happy with one's lot. Ktav Sofer.
• • •
"He satisfies every living thing with favour" (Ps. 145:16) — God gives every living being "ratzon", contentment with what it possesses. That is a gift against the order of nature. Hafla'ah.
—o—
f) "And I will walk among you" (ibid. 26:12)
"And you shall not be terrified of Me. Could it mean you shall not fear Me? Therefore it says: and I will be your God." Rashi.
"And I will walk among you" — I, God, will be found within you; "you shall not be terrified of Me": outwardly you will not tremble before Me, you will not ostensibly sway before Me, but fear of Me you shall indeed have — in the heart...
R. Menachem Mandil Krengil.
• • •
"How beautiful are your steps in sandals" (Song 7:2) — "your steps [pe'amayikh]": the beating of your heart (pa'am — the beating of the heart). The beating of your heart before God is good when it is "in sandals [ba-ne'alim]", locked away from the outward eye... Rabbi Mendele of Kotsk [Kock].
—o—
g) "And you shall eat the flesh of your sons" (ibid. 26:29)
You will send your children out to earn for you; you will take away from your sons and daughters their sacred books and schoolbooks and have to send them to work for you (that is what it means: "and you shall eat the flesh of your sons" — you will eat their flesh...). That is a curse from the Rebuke [Tochacha].. Sde Tevuot.
—o—
Avot.
b) "Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven will endure, and one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not endure" (ch. 5:17)
A dispute that is not for the sake of Heaven will not endure, because soon a different conjuncture will arise, soon you will bribe the quarrelsome man and he will give in to you — and the dispute is over... Whereas a dispute for the sake of Heaven will endure: neither of the parties will give in if they mean it for the sake of Heaven... Magen Avot.
• • •
"Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven."
The whole dispute must be for the sake of Heaven, so that not the slightest ulterior motive and no dishonesty be mixed into it, not even a hair's breadth... Chosen Yeshuot.
A Gaggle of Geese...

A riddle [?] of the election-list signatories on the Jewish street.
R' Aharon was greatly shamed before his little wife and before his father-in-law:
"A fine fellow you are — look at Velvele, he is no greater sage than you. He has no livelihood either, just like you; he too gnaws the bones at his father-in-law's, and nevertheless he manages [?] with those bones: he runs to meetings, turns up here and turns up there, comes among people, talks with squires, offers an opinion, people think well of him, he is making himself a councillor, the whole magistrate [city hall] will yet listen to him, and most likely he too will get to lick a little bone — what else? All this one doesn't do for nothing!"
After such moral lectures R' Aharon went off to his shtibl and found another such idler and another such one:
"Let's do something!"
"What, so to speak, is there to do today?"
"Velvele can, and we can't?"
"Who says he can? There he runs, there he sweats, tears himself apart, the spodik [fur hat] tolerates [?] a head."
"And we can't?"
"And what will you get out of it?"
"And as it is, what have you got?"
In short, the three idlers agreed that they too must do something.
Between Mincha and Maariv someone banged on the bimah.
"Gentlemen, the Chęciny Hasidim must not let this pass! The Gerers are grabbing everything. Let's do something, let's run, let's go!"
Hearing that the Gerers were running, the Chęciny Hasidim also decided to run!
But where to? To whom?
Aharon asked his wife; the wife [asked] a neighbour, and that one had found out from Velvele's so-and-so's wife where the squire lives, who he is and how one speaks to him.
The next morning a delegation of the Chęciny Hasidim, with R' Aharon at its head, went off to the squire:
"Mister election-maker, we Hasidim have come to tell you that we are here too; we think even more of you than the Gerers do. Our shtibl has resolved to do just as you will order; we want nothing, we only want to spite and needle the Gerers, so they shouldn't think they are already everything — we too can do the same:"
The squire was not surprised; he did not even laugh any more. He was already used to such "re-legations" which his agents had begun sending him from various shtiblekh, and R' Aharon received from him a pat on the shoulder:
"Fine [?], what decent little Jews [żydki] you are. I like such ones."
The delegation left happy.
"Did you hear what he said!.."
"He gave me his hand too.."
"Mine he shook well."
"And mine he squeezed like this!"
"A fine goy..."
"And now the Gerers will die a strange death... Oy, how it will grieve them.. They thought the whole buttered cake was theirs... Now we too have found the address and can do the same!.."
— — —
Dear readers, what we are telling you here is, God forbid, no fantasy, apart from the blocs and little blocs. With the "waltz with figures" [Polish: walc z figurami] of the official election-makers on the Jewish street, the disease has caught on in quite a few shtiblekh as well, and every shtibl considers it a duty and an honour to send a few Hasidim over to the squire and inform him that the Gerers are like the Chęciny Hasidim, the Żarki Hasidim like the Wolbrom Hasidim, and all of them want only the good fortune of reciting the blessing "who has given of His glory"...
When two such Jews meet, they open the conversation with this formula:
"Let's do something!"
"We too can make elections!"
Right: if Baruch can and Zerach can, why shouldn't Gronem be able to, and, I beg you, can't R' Gimpel, God forbid, do the same? And today — such a Jew as R' Itche Ber and such a doer as Hersh Zalman!
Why indeed shouldn't the squire know that he, R' Itzikl or R' Sender, is also a bit of a somebody in Będzin.
The Jews of Będzin now give the impression of a gaggle of geese: whoever wants takes a little whip in his hand and becomes a goose-driver...
A Shvartser ["A Black One"].
I've Become a Useful Person...

I have become a useful person. People need me, they look after me, I am entered on a couple of dozen lists, I am called to meetings, people write me letters, send me circulars, greet me — in a word, people seek my company. I feel fine, I feel like a bridegroom on his wedding day. My door never shuts; packs of letters are already lying at my place, and invitations to sessions and confidential consultations; my opinion counts, my smile, my glance; I am living through the true honeymoon days... I have various neighbours around me; well, they differ in their leanings — they seek me out, they urge me to visit them, to come to them as a guest as often as possible; some of them simply scold[?] me: how is this, Mister neighbour, aren't you ashamed, so utterly[?] never to drop in on us? They smile at me like that, right into my eyes, as if they could not do otherwise. Some of them get angry: how is this, whoever heard of such a thing, that a neighbour should never need a loan from a free-loan fund, or ask for a bit of advice?
I have become a useful person for them — that is, I can be of use to them at the elections, and in this field there is competition between them, between my neighbours. Here I have one neighbour who is a Zionist and the second an Agudah man [Agudat Yisrael], and they have been lying in wait for me for weeks. The Zionist wants me to sign his list, and the Agudah man won't let me sign, and both of them always grab me and conduct a debate over my head. I leave them to it, and they quarrel. The day before yesterday[?] they grabbed me and began to quarrel over me with the vilest words, such as: thief, swindler, provocateur, hangman, fascist, Hitlerite, murderer, traitor. I left them and went away.
Towards evening the two of them found me. Each held a sheet of paper and begged me to sign; it is very useful to them — they explained to me very seriously.
"Why quarrel?" I asked them. "You both want me to sign this for you. So I agree — but tell me, who are the candidates?"
For a while they both looked at each other like two drenched[?] hens; then they began begging me again not to break the "unity" and not to destroy their fine neighbourly feelings towards me.
The Zionist smiled ironically and the Agudah man was embarrassed. He began to blush and muttered something quietly to me: you are not a good neighbour, you only want us to quarrel — why?
So both of them lie in wait for me every day and want a signature from me. For them I am a useful person; both send me invitations by post. Besides the two neighbours I have a whole list of merchants-niks, Beit-Lechem-niks, small-traders-niks, Moshav-Zekenim-niks [old-age-home-niks], "Morchi"-niks [sic; probably Mizrachi-niks], Al-HaMishmar-niks, Et-Livnot-niks, splitter-niks, "Hausher"-niks[?], benefactor-niks, Thou-shalt-not-covet-niks, Thou-shalt-not-commit-adultery-niks, No-bribes-niks, Musar-niks, interest-niks [usurers] — who want me to sign for them and help support them, so that, for heaven's sake, they get elected to the City Council, in order to be able to do favours and bring salvation to all Israel...
All of them make various faces at me, and they smile at me with glazed eyes, with God-fearing countenances, with trimmed[?] little beards, with drunken eyes, with red noses, with crooked shoulders, with long hands, with little wooden swords in their hands, with sly little "unity" eyes, with quiet thievish steps, with dark hidden intentions, mixed with all the colours, starting from black, blue, red, brown — all of which together arouses disgust in me.
And believe me, if it weren't a pity for me to forgo the pleasure of this grab-and-run fair, now that I have, almost for once, become a bit of a useful person — I would long ago have sent them all to the devil [lit. "to the black year"]. But what does it help, when I nevertheless[?] crave to be a useful person...
Shiele.
Have Turnovers Grown?

The merchants have already received the "nakazy" [payment orders] for the new turnover tax for the year 1933. Most merchants received demand notes for much larger sums than they had expected, and much more than they are able to pay.
In this year's assessment the assessment commissions still officiated; the assessment of the year after next will already take place without their participation, on the basis of the new tax law. But one can by no means say that at the last assessment the assessment commissions defended the merchants strongly enough in the valuation of their turnovers.
The year 1933 was in any case not better and not livelier than the previous critical years. True, in some branches the turnover did not fall any further, but it certainly did not grow. In other branches the turnover even became smaller still.
In women's and men's ready-made clothing the turnovers were smaller. Turnovers were also smaller in such branches as paper, writing materials, haberdashery (galanterie), food, iron and the colonial-goods (grocery) branch.
As one will see, the turnovers in the most important branches of trade in 1933 were barely, barely the same as in the previous years.
From the assessment, however, it looks as though this year there had already been a great revival. A large part of the merchants were assessed a turnover tax double that of [printed: "in"] 1932, and many merchants were assessed at 50 to 60 percent more. For this part of the merchants such an assessment came as a great surprise. They had by no means reckoned that the assessment would be higher this year.
Even more surprised were the merchants who had had a "rimszalt" [ryczałt — flat lump-sum taxation], and from whom it was taken away on the grounds that their turnovers had greatly increased.
With the present shortage of credit and of cash, this high assessment of turnover is, to put it mildly, a great hardship for the merchants. Most merchants must fight very many difficulties in order to be able to buy goods for cash, because no credit is given. One has to borrow money at interest; one often sells below cost only in order to be able to buy and sell, only in order to be able to go on trading. In such a situation, assessing the turnover even higher means putting the small and middle merchant in a situation with no way out,
Spring Moods

Spring. The world gives the impression that it is celebrating a holiday, a joyous occasion, a great feast.
Everything is so light, so mobile, so fluttering, as if about to fly off into the distant, deep infinity.
An inner feeling, something growing, something rising, pushes you out into the street, beyond the town, to the river — and there you come alive.
Something in you swells and glows[?]. You rise up and turn back to yourself — and as soon as you look for yourself [printed "di" for "du"] — you find yourself again.
You begin to feel the rustle of your soul. You remember it and catch its call. You feel — how something quivers there inside and knocks like a prisoner in jail, how something demands and longs, and and [sic] a glowing feeling of pure love for everything and everyone embraces you, and it gnaws, it draws you to the point of the soul's expiring.
Heaven and earth. Endless expanses of earth, a holy breadth bursts open, swallows you like a windstorm and shouts, calls, wakes...
Wakes you so long, until you become a man of the earth — and you reach the level where you begin truly to understand and appreciate many values which until now rang like little bells, like an echo, like phrases.
Balloons.
Red, yellow, white and blue balloons... How beautiful they look from afar, how pleasant it is to look at them. They flutter so quietly, without clamour, and somehow they are always straining to break out into the wide world; the light little wind gives a puff, and at once they toss about, like the waves of the sea, down and up — light, round, coloured balloons. In each of them a little coloured soul romps — and flying, quivering, they look like little living creatures that frolic, preen[?], hurry and chase one another, as if they never had any time. Balloons exert an illusory influence. They make one forget time and bring one closer to space, to infinity and motion — and they always pull upward, agitate for the sky, only for the sky. But all this is so only from afar.
Hardly do you come close to the pretty, lovely, beckoning toy and begin to touch it... to examine, to inspect, than you see at once how poor, pale, dull it is; moreover the unpleasant smell arouses disgust.
But if you want to get to the bottom of the truth... then crrrash — it bursts and a cheap ugliness is revealed to you.
So it is too with many ideas...
N. Tz.
Radio Bulletin

[Radio — buyer's guide and the summer programme; followed by a short item: Będzin — Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land, excursion.]
How to choose a radio set.
Which set should I buy? Everyone who wants to join the ranks of the great radio family asks himself this question. We want to point out a few rules that one needs to know in order to find one's way when buying a radio set.
If it is a valve (tube) set, with which one should also be able to hear foreign radio stations, one must know that what matters here is not only the number of valves but above all the assembly, or better said the model according to which the set was built. The first valve of the set has the task of catching the current from the aerial. The first valve is called the "audion" or detector valve. The task of the second valve is to amplify the current of the first valve, thanks to which the sounds in the loudspeaker[?] come out stronger. With a one- or two-valve set one can usually hear well only the local and a few very strong foreign radio stations.
All the foreign radio stations can be heard well only with a 3- or 4-valve set. The task of the first valve in a 3- or 4-valve set is first of all to amplify the very weak signals from the aerial. Besides that, a 4-valve set has the advantage of being selective, i.e. one station does not disturb another and the sounds come out clean. With a 4-valve set the aerial must be a very short one. It is best to take a couple of metres of electric wire and use it as an aerial.
Those who want to hear well only the local radio stations are advised to buy a detector set, because no larger set will render the voice as cleanly and clearly as the ordinary crystal detector. With a good aerial and earthing one can even pick up several strong foreign stations with the detector[?]. The valve sets also have the drawback that they pick up all the stray noises from electric motors, X-ray machines, etc. The detector set, on the other hand, knows nothing of all these noises, and that is precisely why the number of detector enthusiasts keeps steadily growing.
What will the radio give us in summer?
The main season of radio is winter, when the evenings are long, when because of the frost and snow one does not feel like going out of the warm house. In summer, by contrast, one spends as much time as possible in the open air, and it is natural that in summertime people listen to the radio less. The radio programme too must be a light one and have an entertaining character. Therefore all the radio stations of the world work out a special summer and winter plan for the radio programmes.
In Poland the summer radio season begins on 3 June and will last until 1 September. During these months we shall above all have a considerable preponderance of music.
First of all the summer programme will take into account all the features that distinguish the summer. The microphone will wake radio listeners as early as 6.30 a.m. with a cheerful hour-long broadcast. Only on Sundays and holidays will the radio start operating at 8.30 a.m.
An interesting change will also take place in the midday hours, from 12 to 15, during which the radio will give cheerful and pleasant music. Doctors have long drawn attention to the favourable effect of music during meals.
As was to be foreseen, in summer serious music will be greatly reduced[?], and during the heat the radio waves will cheer us up with light and merry music.
As for lectures, it has been seen more than once that even the most interesting lecture can become boring if it lasts too long, especially in summer, when the mind tires more quickly. Therefore in summer lectures will last at most 15 minutes, feuilletons and talks no more than 12 minutes.
A very useful rubric will be the broadcasts called "What to read". In these broadcasts radio listeners who like to read books will receive the most necessary critical guidance on the most interesting and instructive books that have appeared on the book market.
This, in general outline, is the summer programme of Polish Radio.
More music and less talk — that is the radio's slogan for the summer.

[Serialized story — the Ukrainian pogroms of 1919; final installment.]
A. Akerman.
(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter in the time of the Ukrainian pogroms of 1919.)

The rabbi came to the Hornsteins' house and comforted them and their daughter over the misfortune that had befallen them. And to Chanele the rabbi said that by the deed she had done she had raised herself to the rank of a righteous woman. Although the Hornsteins knew full well that through their daughter many Jewish lives had been saved — the proof being that Volosenko [Wołosenko; the pogrom ataman] had indeed kept his word and left Bilokhke [?] with his pogromists — nevertheless the two of them went about broken and gloomy, seeing how their daughter suffered. And neither of them, neither Reb Chaim nor his wife Gitl, could open their mouth to comfort their daughter. Can one comfort a mourner while the dead lies before his eyes? Could they really tell their daughter that she was pure, when she had lain a whole night in a [—] with swine?

But their cup of sorrows, it seems, was not yet full. A still greater misfortune befell the Hornsteins, one they had not reckoned with.

They had reckoned that with time their only daughter, Chana, would little by little forget the shame, that they would all move away to another town, and that the wounds in their hearts would heal with time.

So the parents thought, but Chana decided to act otherwise. Right after, on that very night when she came home from Volosenko and poured out her bitter heart before her parents and told them what had happened to her, late at night, when everyone in the house was already asleep, she took her clothes and doused them with kerosene, went down to the old synagogue, went inside the ruin and set herself on fire.

Chana's clothes were at once wrapped in flames, and from the flames the synagogue caught fire too. A great blaze broke out, and the whole shtetl came running together.

Reb Chaim's house was somewhat far from the synagogue, and so the Hornsteins were among the last to come running to the fire.

When the Jews of Bilokhke had put out the fire, only then did they see a burnt woman's body lying there. The body was so badly burnt that they could not recognize who the woman or girl had been.

Meanwhile the Hornsteins were running about like mad and searching for Chana. High above the whole tumult their voices carried in the night: "Chanele! Chanke!" And when the news was heard that a burnt woman had been found, their hearts sank. They ran up to the dead body, and the most terrible thing did indeed happen: in that little heap of ash they recognized their Chanele! Chaim and Gitl Hornstein kept fainting, and it took long hours before they were revived.

On the second day after the fire the burnt eighteen-year-old girl was buried, together with ash from the old synagogue of Bilokhke.

All the Jewish inhabitants of Bilokhke followed the funeral, and from the oldest elder to the youngest child, all walked behind the bier and all shed bitter tears; and the Hornsteins strewed ash upon their heads and sat shiva for their only daughter.

And no one in Bilokhke except the rabbi and the rebbetzin knew the true reason why Chana Hornstein burned herself, and perhaps they do not know it to this day.

When the Hornsteins rose from shiva, they felt that they could no longer go on living in Bilokhke. And Reb Chaim Hornstein decided to sell off his property and leave for America.

When the Hornsteins had sold off all the property that remained to them, the first thing they did was to pledge the building of a new synagogue on the site of the old synagogue, which had been burnt to ash together with their daughter, so that the synagogue should be a memorial to their daughter's soul. And at the shloshim, thirty days after their daughter's tragic death, they set up a tombstone on her grave in the Bilokhke cemetery, on which these few tragic words were engraved:

"Here lies the modest and holy maiden, Mrs. Chana daughter of Gitl Hornstein."

(The End.)

Annual General Meeting of the “TOZ” Society.

[Będzin — health and welfare.]
(M.F.) It is already a rule with us: at meetings where one is not personally interested, a minyan or two minyans of people gather. The number present from all three towns, Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa, reached as many as... 26 members — out of a total number of 415 members.

The session is opened by the president of the outgoing board, Dr. S. Weinzieher, who proposes President Rubinlicht as chairman of the meeting. From the activity report given by the vice-president, Advocate Kohn, and the secretary, Dr. Liberman, we learn that during one year of its existence the board succeeded in increasing the number of members, which had amounted to 83, to 415 as of today. During this time 9 lectures were held on medical-hygienic subjects. Under the medical supervision of “TOZ” there are in Zagłębie 6 schools (mainly religious ones, which do not enjoy the assistance of the municipality), with 1200 children. The school doctors examined or sent for treatment nearly 500 children; recently the society, with the help of the Central office, purchased a quartz lamp, with which 100 children have so far been irradiated. A feeding campaign is also being conducted, from which up to 150 children benefit daily. For this campaign 1200 litres of milk, nearly 500 kilos of baked goods, butter, eggs etc. have been used so far. In addition, 90 kilos of cod-liver oil were distributed among 350 children. To the summer colonies last year 61 children were sent for the whole of August[?]. The preparation of this year's colony is in full swing, and the number of children sent will probably be much larger. That is a short summary of the activity of the reorganised branch.

[Sosnowiec — labour; mine strike.]

We have written many times about the high-handedness of the caretaker of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah: it is not the administration that has the say over the municipal building, but Saki [?] the stróż [caretaker]. Zuckerman's Picture Exhibition

[Art — exhibition; cinema.] The painter Ben-Zion Zuckerman comes from the Paris art academy, the "École des Beaux-Arts", from where he brought with him the virtues of French painting.
Light and foaming like champagne, graceful and full of temperament like the Parisiennes — these are the chief qualities of the French school.
That does not mean, however, that Zuckerman holds fast to certain stereotyped forms of the aforementioned school. The artist has merely assimilated the choicest artistic values and, with the help of his talent, created an original, strongly individual painterly conception.
Zuckerman is represented at the exhibition by a large number of watercolours and oil paintings of the Palestinian landscape and of various local types there.
Zuckerman's palette is a very rich one. He works with a broad colour scale and his landscapes constitute a splendid composition of colours. He exploits brilliantly the wonderful play of light and shadow of Palestinian nature and transfers it to his canvases with so much grace and verve that it captivates the viewer and chains him to his pictures.
The task of an artist is not to copy nature faithfully — nature, which often allows itself to be banal and yet does not shock; the artist must correct nature, perfect it, add to it artistic refinement and an individual mood.
Zuckerman belongs to those fortunate painters who see nature through their own individual, artistic prism and create entirely new values with the help of their [—] intuition.
Besides landscapes Zuckerman also paints portraits, which are distinguished by the expression of the most important character traits of the persons painted. Here too one notices the specific Zuckermanian approach to the treatment of a portrait. In his portraits the artist brings out, besides the strong likeness, also the personality — the spiritual and the deeply human that lies hidden in his models.
Graphic technique, too, is not foreign to Zuckerman. A fairly large number of pen drawings testify that in this field as well the artist occupies a very important place.
It is an exhibition that everyone who has a sense of aesthetics, of a splendid play of colours and subtle drawing, must see.
In the desert of everyday greyness, Zuckerman's picture exhibition is a refreshing oasis for the spirit. His pictures pursue one like a sweet dream long after one has left his exhibition.
Sh. R.
The exhibition is open every day from 10 in the morning. We advise the Jewish public to visit the rare exhibition of Ben-Zion Zuckerman, who is one of the most important artists in the Jewish world.
It is especially important that the school youth visit the exhibition, in order to become acquainted with the creations of Eretz-Israel life.
—o—
From the Silver Screen.
"Yizkor" is the name of the picture now showing at the "Światowid" cinema. An old picture, but newly corrected and modified so that the silent film has become a sound film.
Its plot is, as usual, stereotyped: a count's daughter falls in love with the handsome young man Leibke, but Leibke remains faithful to his people, his faith and his Jewish bride, so that the Hungarian countess cannot win him — that is already Jewish chutzpah... As usual there is also no lack of a court intriguer, who intrigues against the handsome Jewish huntsman Leibke and angers the count until the count issues an order to bury Leibke alive. The beautiful countess tries once more to persuade Leibke, but seeing her failure she poisons herself, and then comes the finale — Leibke is buried.
The picture has very moving moments that shake the viewer. The music for the picture is very nicely fitted. The "Kol Nidre" is, it is true, weakly sung, whereas the quartet that sings the "Shiviti" sounds very harmonious.
The picture is worth seeing, above all for the artist Maurice Schwartz, who plays truly masterfully.
Elge.

In the course of the week a real election fever reigned in the Jewish street; people literally forgot the antisemitic waves sweeping over us and threw themselves entirely into the election whirl[?]. Every party and grouping bitterly defended its position and fought for a respectable „seat“ in the new city council.
The attempt to create a united Jewish bloc in Będzin ran into difficulties on the ground of party and personal ambitions, which led to the Jewish „unity“ going out with 5 Jewish bourgeois lists, counting[?] the one bloc of: the intelligentsia, Zionists, merchants, „Mizrachi“, „Hitachdut“ and Revisionists[?]. —

In Honour of the Holiday.

[Shavuot — literary sketch (feuilleton).]
L. Goldsztajn
(A Little Mood).
...So what do you want, dear reader, that I should tell you today?
[—] — about our sad life, about our bitter fate, how Jews, poor things, groan under the heavy yoke of making a living, how Jews torment themselves day in, day out?
What shall I write today about our „unity“, about our „oneness“ — so-called[?] — which our good and bad friends exploit so!
Or perhaps, dear reader, you would rather we talked today about our „Land“, about our cradle[?], where we were born, where mother rocked us and sang us the songs of Zion?
But all this only turns into sadness!.. And how can we greet the holiday in such a sad mood?
— After all it is [—] the Festival of First Fruits, after all it is a holiday, when the sun warms so „[—]“ and „fine“, when everything grows green and blossoms..
Let us forget, at least for one minute, the heavy, hard weekday life; let us for at least one minute be Sabbath-like, holiday-like Jews.
— At least one minute...
• •
— Do you still remember, when you were small, Shavuot in the shtetl? The most beautiful, the brightest, the sunniest holiday of all holidays, and father sits and tells you that precisely[?] on this holiday the Jews received the Torah on Mount Sinai — the Torah which the whole world snatched up and from every letter of which it made laws; and then he tells the beautiful story of Boaz and Ruth, which takes your breath away; and then father sits and recites the Tikkun, recites without end, without finish... until... outside it begins to dawn, and when — you know[?] — a piece of sky is red as a fiery flame, the morning sun tears itself out onto God's bright world. And you hear from afar the rustling of the half-ripe ears of grain in the fields; you [printed „di“] feel the scent of the soft grass on the meadows; you hear the quiet flowing of the little river that winds around the shtetl.
• •
And there, far, far in the East, day is already dawning; there the peaks of the mountains are already bathed in the first rising rays of the sun, and on the fields where Boaz and Ruth walked, soft golden ears of grain have again sprouted from the earth, and the desolate roads have been covered with palms.
And there the silver Jordan flows and tells secret-filled[?] stories of the heroic Maccabees; there stands a great mute Wall and tells a two-thousand-year-old story of a Temple, of a Holy of Holies; and roaring beat the waves of the sea, beating like a human heart; and loudly echo the voices of young pioneers[?], who sing a song, sing with heart, with hope:
— Am Yisrael Chai, Am Yisrael Chai [the people of Israel lives]...
• • •
— It is Shavuot!
Let us be for a minute Sabbath-like, holiday-like; let us for a minute forget our bitter fate.
— It is Shavuot, it is a holiday, a beautiful one, a wonderful[?] one..

The Gentile Woman of the “Talmud Torah”

[Sosnowiec — community and education.] A rare city, our Sosnowiec: in everything it is original and in every matter — truly enchanting. What could not happen in any city is with us a quite ordinary, self-evident matter, at which one simply[?] does not even stop.
Public affairs play hardly any role here. Nor is that any wonder, for when does one occupy oneself here with the community? Only once one already feels good at heart and has already done[?] everything else. Only then can one allow oneself a glance at how things stand in that society. And since people are worn out enough — it is not easy nowadays to earn a living — one can indeed only rarely concern oneself with these “superfluous matters”.
Recently it happened that the caretaker [stróżka] of the Talmud Torah set her dog on the Talmud Torah children, who had come[?], as usual, on Sabbath to learn a chapter.
But one must not think that we are dealing here with an ordinary caretaker: she is in fact the owner or co-owner of the Talmud Torah building, since she stands on the first mortgage with four thousand zl. To avoid any mistake, it must be said that the money was not borrowed from her; rather, a debt for her pension accumulated. Well, is that not a disgrace for the city in general and for the local Talmud Torah wardens in particular?
Could one imagine in another city that a pension of pennies should grow into a legendary sum of 4,000 zl., which should be allowed to be registered on a first mortgage? Can people with a clear public sense imagine anything like it? Which city would have been capable of bringing such a matter, or one like it, to so sad and simply shameful a state?
We have touched on this matter more than once in the columns of our paper; we told the leaders of the institution that they must not remain indifferent to the question, that they must reckon with such a ragged[?] management, which brings no honour at all — neither to the city nor to the leaders of the above institution.
Cities that run a normal public economy cannot conceive how such abnormal phenomena are permitted. But let us say this is a lost cause and yesterday cannot be brought back — one can nevertheless correct the error made so long ago. How can one tolerate such a course of action, and nothing — it bothers no one and no one is even ashamed? Would this have had a place anywhere else? In the smallest, poorest shtetl, where a Talmud Torah looks like a poorhouse, such disregard would have had no place. And here, in so important a kehilla as Sosnowiec and with such a building as the Talmud Torah owns, people remain so apathetic to the question, as if everything were in the best of order. Has such a thing ever been heard of? Sosnowiec is, after all, not some godforsaken shtetl of a few minyans of Jews where no remedy can be found — so why does nobody care? Why is there no reaction to such a disgrace? Why does no one see to liquidating the matter? Can a kehilla like Sosnowiec truly find no way to get rid of the gentile woman and clear the mortgage? Must one first talk about such[?] cardinal questions and raise them before the public? Do people not understand by themselves that this should have no place in such a centre as Sosnowiec? True, it is a thing that has already happened — so why not free oneself of it? After all, it is said that a poor community does not die[?] — so why should the debt not be extinguished? One must free oneself of such a burden, which brings no little shame both to the city and to the leaders.
When the children come there it does not look as if they had come into the Talmud Torah, but rather to the caretaker [stróż], before whom they tremble and shake.
A city must not let itself be treated so; measures must be taken to wipe away the stain and to free itself of the shameful burden. It is tragic enough that such a thing could happen, which shows the “model order” that was kept there.
It is therefore important that the present board should begin right now to think of a way to settle the question definitively. An action must be undertaken in which the whole city should take part, for after all a Talmud Torah is an institution that belongs to the whole city.
It would therefore be advisable for the board to convene an extraordinary meeting on the question, at which it would be discussed in what way the question is to be settled definitively. On no account may such a question be left to go stale[?]. It is a disgrace for the city and a humiliation for the institution, which is in fact an educational establishment.
Dr. Papuri.
The Victims. A Little Feuilleton.

[Będzin — feuilleton.] The war between the two gangs[?] [rotes] on the territory of Gzichów[?] is already “almost” over, and if one still hears somewhere the ring of a slap, or even the squeal of a knife-stab, these are no more than the last chords, which will not be heard for long either.
But what is to be done meanwhile with the other victims?
We do not mean those who got beaten — nonsense, a blow passes.
Nor do we mean the kosher sweethearts, the young men and girls, who cannot now allow themselves to stroll on the Gzichów grounds, or even late in the evening on Kościuszko Street — never mind: as long as the couple is kosher, it will find its resting place.
We mean the treyf couples — a married man with a strange woman and a married woman with a strange man.
At the beginning of spring, when nature runs riot and it is the very season of treyf romances and “left-hand” loves, when the heart longs to meet “the chosen one” (she or he) somewhere behind the town, far from human eyes, you have to fear not his wife or her husband, but — a plain hooligan...
There they are, the heroes of the left-hand loves, who now wander about, poor things, like stray stars and cannot come together — they are the true innocent victims of the hooligan attacks, and they will now have to make use of the Gerer Rebbe’s advice.
When the “Agudah” — so they tell — was about to publish the “Togblat” in Warsaw, the publishers came to the Gerer Rebbe for advice.
— Rebbe! — they say — in a newspaper one must print a novel, otherwise it does not draw; should we too print a novel?
— And what, pray, is such a thing as a novel? — asks the Rebbe.
— A novel — they explain to him — is a story about a fellow who loves a strange woman...
— A strange woman? — the Rebbe starts — God forbid, it is not allowed! Rather make a novel in which the fellow loves his own wife and does not think about strange ones...
That is now the only advice for the heroes of left-hand loves — to conduct a romance with their own wives.
Onkelos.
